items.title: What a statistical study does with data
items.core_explanation_md:
A statistical study turns a pile of numbers into a decision in four steps, always in this order:

| Phase | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| Collect | Gather numerical data from the right source |
| Classify and tabulate | Sort the raw data into groups and show it in a table |
| Analyse | Apply formulas and methods that suit the question |
| Interpret | Draw conclusions from the results |

Why bother? Statistics does six jobs: it states facts in definite form, simplifies complicated data, gives a way of comparing, studies how two or more variables move together, supports policy making and helps forecast.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The word "statistics" here means numerical (quantitative) data that can feed further calculation. If a step is skipped, the later ones suffer: analysis done on badly classified data gives a neat-looking but meaningless answer.

self_check.prompt_text: From memory: list the four phases of a statistical study in order, and name three of the six functions of statistics.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Collect, classify and tabulate, analyse, interpret. Functions: present facts definitely, simplify data, compare, study relationships between variables, help in policy making, help in forecasting (any three).

items.title: Statistics in banking, and where it stops
items.core_explanation_md:
Banks lean on statistics because their decisions rest on large numbers of accounts and transactions. Credit policy, for example, is set after studying profitability, demand and time deposits, credit ratios and customer numbers, and the policy itself rests on probability theory.

Four limits keep this honest:

- **Aggregates, not individuals.** Statistics describes groups; it says little about one particular borrower.
- **Numbers only.** Purely qualitative facts must first be turned into numbers before statistics can handle them.
- **Averages, not certainties.** Results are true on average over the long run, because a sample stands in for the whole.
- **Bias in, bias out.** Careless or dishonest data collection ruins the whole investigation.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A useful habit: before trusting a statistical claim, ask who collected the data and how. The first three limits are built into the method; the fourth is a failure of people.

self_check.prompt_text: A manager says "statistics proves that this borrower will default". Which limitation of statistics does that statement ignore?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Statistics deals with aggregates and long-run averages, not with individual cases; it can say how likely default is across a group, not what one borrower will do.

items.title: Population and sample, parameter and statistic
items.core_explanation_md:
Two pairs of words carry most of this unit.

| Group-wide | Part-wide |
| --- | --- |
| **Population**: every observation you want to draw conclusions about | **Sample**: a part of the population actually studied |
| **Parameter**: a number describing the population (fixed, usually unknown) | **Statistic**: a number computed from the sample, used to estimate the parameter |

Example in a bank: the population is the balances of all savings accounts in a region. Average balance of all of them is a parameter. If you look at 400 accounts and compute their average, that average is a statistic, and you use it to estimate the unknown parameter.
items.expanded_explanation_md: We sample because the population is often too large, too costly or too slow to study in full. The sample must be representative, otherwise the statistic will mislead about the parameter. A statistic is also called an estimator.

self_check.prompt_text: You compute the average loan size of 250 randomly picked accounts out of 40,000. Is the result a parameter or a statistic, and what does it estimate?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It is a statistic. It estimates the parameter: the average loan size of all 40,000 accounts.

items.title: Attributes, variates, discrete and continuous
items.core_explanation_md:
Ask one question of any characteristic: *can it be written as a number?*

- No: it is an **attribute** (type of account, branch location, religion, colour).
- Yes: it is a **variate** (balance, age, number of dependants). A variate is then split by the values it can take:

| Kind of variate | Takes | Banking examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Discrete | Separate, countable values | Number of loan accounts a customer holds; cheques returned in a month |
| Continuous | Any value in a range, whole or fractional | Account balance in rupees and paise; time taken to process a loan |

Counting gives discrete data; measuring gives continuous data.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Watch out for rounded measurements. Age is continuous in principle, even though it is often reported in whole years; the courseware lists "age in years" as discrete, so read the question for how the variable is being recorded.

self_check.prompt_text: Classify each: (a) type of deposit scheme, (b) number of ATMs in a district, (c) time a customer waits at the counter.
self_check.expected_takeaway: (a) attribute, (b) discrete variate, (c) continuous variate.

items.title: Primary or secondary data, census or survey
items.core_explanation_md:
Data comes from one of two places, and is collected on one of two scales.

| | Primary data | Secondary data |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Collected | First time, directly from respondents | Earlier, by someone else, for another purpose |
| Usual methods or sources | Direct interview, questionnaires | Records, published reports, banks, research bodies, the internet |
| Cost in money, time, effort | Higher | Lower |
| Fit to your question | Designed for it | Must be checked |

The same figures can be primary for one user and secondary for another: a statistical table is primary for the office that gathered it and secondary for the analyst who reuses it.

On scale: a **census** covers every unit of the population, while a **sample survey** covers a part and generalises to the whole, which works only if the sample is representative.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Choosing is a trade-off. If a good secondary source already answers the question, using it saves money and time. If it does not fit, primary collection is worth its cost.

self_check.prompt_text: A bank wants customer opinion on a new app feature. Would you start with primary or secondary data, and why?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Primary data (for example a questionnaire), because existing records will not hold opinions on a feature the customers have only just seen.

items.title: Classifying data: four bases and how many ways
items.core_explanation_md:
Classification sorts raw data into groups that share a characteristic. It shrinks a long list into a few classes you can compare, and it is the step before tabulation.

**Base** (what you sort by):

| Base | Sorted by | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Qualitative | A quality or attribute | Deposit accounts by type of scheme |
| Quantitative | A numerical characteristic | Borrowers by loan amount |
| Geographical | Place | Deposits by state |
| Chronological | Time of occurrence | Quarter-wise gross NPAs (a time series) |

**Number of ways** (how many characteristics at once): one characteristic is *one-way*, two is *two-way* and more than two is *multi-way*.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A table with branch type down the side and account type across the top is a two-way classification. Adding a third characteristic, such as year, makes it multi-way.

self_check.prompt_text: Name the base and the number of ways: customers classified by city and by gender.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Geographical and qualitative bases, classified two-way.

items.title: Class width, class mark and class boundaries
items.core_explanation_md:
Each class in a frequency table has a lower limit and an upper limit. Two quantities describe it:

- the **width** says how big the class is;
- the **class mark** is the middle of the class, used to stand for every value in it.

In an **exclusive** series (0-10, 10-20, ...) a value equal to the upper limit is counted in the next class. In an **inclusive** series (60-69, 70-79, ...) both limits belong to the class. To get continuous classes from an inclusive series, widen each class by half the gap between one upper limit and the next lower limit: these are the **class boundaries**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: If you are asked for a class width when only the data are given, divide the range (largest minus smallest value) by the number of classes wanted. Boundaries are what make inclusive classes safe to use in calculations that treat the variable as continuous.

formula_spec.latex_expression: \text{width} = U - L,\quad m = \frac{L + U}{2},\quad L_b = L - \frac{g}{2},\quad U_b = U + \frac{g}{2}

variables.name: Gap between the upper limit of one inclusive class and the lower limit of the next

assumptions: For width and mark, use the limits of the class as given (exclusive) or its boundaries (inclusive); both give the same width and mark for equal-width inclusive classes.
Classes of equal width cover the observed range without a break.
common_errors: Using 1 instead of half the gap when widening inclusive limits (the adjustment is half of the gap, so 0.5 for a gap of 1).
Counting a value equal to an upper limit in the lower class of an exclusive series.
Subtracting limits of an inclusive class to get the width (9 - 5 = 4) instead of using boundaries (9.5 - 4.5 = 5).

self_check.prompt_text: Inclusive classes run 1-5, 6-10, 11-15. Give the boundaries of the middle class and its mark.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Gap is 1, so adjust by 0.5: boundaries 5.5 to 10.5; mark (6 + 10)/2 = 8.

items.title: Relative, percentage frequency and frequency density
items.core_explanation_md:
Raw class frequencies are hard to compare across tables of different sizes, so express each as a share of the total:

- **Relative frequency** is a fraction of 1;
- **Percentage frequency** is the same share out of 100.

When classes have unequal widths, a bigger class naturally collects more observations. **Frequency density** removes that effect by dividing by width, so you can see where observations really crowd together.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Relative frequencies of all classes add to 1 (or to 100 for percentages), which is a handy check on your arithmetic. Density only matters when widths differ; with equal widths it just rescales the frequencies.

formula_spec.latex_expression: rf = \frac{f}{N},\quad pf = \frac{f}{N}\times 100,\quad fd = \frac{f}{w}

variables.name: Relative frequency, percentage frequency, frequency density
variables.unit: fraction, per cent, observations per unit of the variable

assumptions: N is the sum of all class frequencies in the table.
Width is measured in the same unit for every class.
common_errors: Dividing by the number of classes instead of the total frequency.
Forgetting the factor 100 for the percentage frequency.
Comparing raw frequencies of classes of different widths instead of their densities.

self_check.prompt_text: A class holds 18 of 75 observations. What are its relative and percentage frequencies?

items.title: Cumulative frequencies: less-than and more-than
items.core_explanation_md:
A cumulative frequency answers "how many observations are at or below this point?" or "at or above?" without adding up the table each time.

| Type | How it is built | What the last or first entry shows |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Less-than | Add class frequencies from the lowest class upwards | The final entry equals the total |
| More-than (greater-than) | Add them from the highest class downwards | The first entry equals the total |

The two always pair up: the less-than count at a boundary plus the more-than count at the same boundary give the total.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Each cumulative value is tied to a class boundary, not to a class. "Less than 30" means everything below the boundary 30.

self_check.prompt_text: Classes 0-10, 10-20, 20-30 have frequencies 5, 9, 6. Write the less-than cumulative frequencies.
self_check.expected_takeaway: 5, 14 and 20 (cumulative counts below 10, 20 and 30).

items.title: Turning loan-size classes into boundaries and class marks
items.core_explanation_md: A bank groups fifty new term loans by size in ₹ lakh using inclusive classes 1-5, 6-10, 11-15 and 16-20, with frequencies 8, 20, 12, 10. Convert the classes to boundaries, find the class width and the mark of each class.

worked_steps.description: Find the gap between the upper limit of one class and the lower limit of the next.
Half the gap is the adjustment.
Subtract it from each lower limit and add it to each upper limit.
Width of any class from its boundaries.
Class marks from the original limits.
Check that the frequencies add to the loans counted.

items.final_answer_with_unit: Boundaries 0.5-5.5, 5.5-10.5, 10.5-15.5, 15.5-20.5 (₹ lakh); width ₹5 lakh; class marks ₹3, 8, 13 and 18 lakh

self_check.prompt_text: Why do the boundaries, not the limits, let us treat loan size as continuous?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Because the boundaries leave no gaps: 5.5 belongs to the end of one class and the start of the next, so every possible loan size, such as ₹5.7 lakh, falls in exactly one class.

items.title: Shares, density and cumulative counts for savings balances
items.core_explanation_md: A bank samples 120 savings accounts and groups the average balance (₹ thousand) in exclusive classes of unequal width: 0-10 (40 accounts), 10-20 (36), 20-40 (30) and 40-80 (14). Find the percentage frequency and frequency density of each class, and both cumulative frequencies.

worked_steps.description: Total frequency.
Percentage frequency of each class: frequency / 120 x 100, to 2 decimals.
Widths of the classes.
Frequency density = frequency / width.
Less-than cumulative frequencies, adding from the lowest class.
More-than cumulative frequencies, adding from the highest class.
worked_steps.intermediate_result: 120, 80, 44, 14 (for the classes taken lowest to highest)

items.final_answer_with_unit: Percentage frequencies 33.33, 30.00, 25.00, 11.67 (sum 100.00); densities 4.00, 3.60, 1.50, 0.35 accounts per ₹ thousand; less-than 40, 76, 106, 120; more-than 120, 80, 44, 14

self_check.prompt_text: Which class has the most accounts per ₹ thousand of balance, and why is that different from the class with the most accounts?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The 0-10 class has the highest density (4.00); here it is also the largest class, but the 40-80 class shows how a wide class can hold many accounts while being thinly populated (density 0.35).

items.stem_md: Which description fits "the number of dependants in a borrower's household"?

options.text_md: An attribute, because a household is a group of people
options.explanation_md: Dependants are counted, so the characteristic can be written as a number; an attribute cannot.

options.text_md: A continuous variate, because it can be any value
options.explanation_md: The count can only be whole numbers, 0, 1, 2 and so on, not any value in a range.

options.text_md: A discrete variate, because it takes separate countable values
options.explanation_md: A count of people takes distinct whole-number values, which is the definition of a discrete variate.

options.text_md: A parameter, because it describes the whole population
options.explanation_md: A parameter is a summary of a population, not a kind of characteristic.

items.correct_explanation_md: A characteristic that can be expressed in numbers is a variate, and one that takes only separate, countable values is discrete. Dependants are counted in whole numbers.

options.text_md: Primary, because the analyst is using it for the first time
options.explanation_md: Primary data is collected first-hand by the investigator; first use by the analyst does not make it primary.

options.explanation_md: The presence of numbers does not decide the type; the source of collection does.

options.text_md: Secondary, because someone else collected it earlier for their own purpose
options.explanation_md: The data already existed and was collected by another agency, which is the meaning of secondary data. It may have been primary for the compiler.

options.text_md: Neither, because published data is a census
options.explanation_md: A census is a way of covering a population, not a type of source.

items.title: Why banks sample, and the symbols that go with it
items.core_explanation_md:
Studying every item is rarely possible: the population may be huge, testing may destroy the item, and time and money are limited. So you take a **sample**, measure it, and generalise to the **population**. A full count (a **census**) is the exception.

Keep the notation straight; the letter tells you which world a number belongs to:

| | Population | Sample |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Size | N | n |
| Mean | mu | x-bar |
| Standard deviation | sigma | s |
| Name of such a number | parameter | statistic |

Sampling is only as good as the sample: if it is not representative, every conclusion drawn from it is shaky.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Why this matters in a bank: a credit-quality review of 20 lakh loan accounts cannot read every file. A sample read carefully tells more than a census read carelessly, provided the sample is well chosen.

self_check.prompt_text: From memory: which letters stand for population size, sample size, population mean and sample mean?
self_check.expected_takeaway: N, n, mu and x-bar respectively.

items.title: Judgement samples, random samples and bias
items.core_explanation_md:
There are two ways to choose a sample.

| | Judgement (non-random) | Random (probability) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Who picks | Someone's knowledge or opinion | Chance, with known probabilities |
| Strength | Quick, convenient, good for a pilot | Every item has a chance of selection |
| Weakness | Its validity cannot be tested; rigorous statistical analysis is not possible | Needs a list of the population and more effort |

**Bias** creeps in when you pick the people most likely to have strong views, for example surveying only those directly affected by a policy. The report then describes that group, not the public. Random selection avoids this, and it allows the reliability of the estimate to be worked out.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A judgement sample is not worthless: a branch manager choosing three typical branches to pilot a new form is sensible. The mistake is treating the pilot result as if it were a scientifically drawn sample.

self_check.prompt_text: Why can the reliability of an estimate be worked out for a random sample but not for a judgement sample?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Random selection gives known chances of inclusion, so statistical theory applies; a judgement sample depends on the chooser's opinion, so its representativeness cannot be tested.

items.title: Simple random sampling: equal chances, with or without replacement
items.core_explanation_md:
In **simple random sampling** every possible sample has the same chance of being picked, and so does every member of the population.

Small example: from four officers A, B, C, D choose two. There are six possible pairs (AB, AC, AD, BC, BD, CD), each with probability 1/6, and each officer is in three of the six, so each has a 1/2 chance of being chosen.

Two ways to draw:

- **Without replacement**: a chosen item is set aside, so it cannot appear twice.
- **With replacement**: the item is put back before the next draw, so it can be chosen again.

For big populations, slips in a box do not work. Give each member a number and read numbers from a computer or a table of random digits, where every digit from 0 to 9 is equally likely.
items.expanded_explanation_md: An "infinite" population in statistics does not mean literally infinite. It means one too large to list in reasonable time, treated as if it never runs out.

self_check.prompt_text: Five officers, sample of two without replacement. How many possible samples are there, and what is the chance that a particular officer is in the sample?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Ten possible samples; each officer is in four of them, so the chance is 4/10 = 2/5.

items.title: Stratified or cluster sampling: which one, and why
items.core_explanation_md:
Both start by dividing the population into groups. They differ in what the groups look like, and so in what you do next.

| | Stratified | Cluster |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Groups | **Strata**: similar inside, different from each other | **Clusters**: much alike each other, varied inside |
| What you sample | Items at random from **every** stratum | A random few clusters, then **every** item in them |
| How many from each | In proportion to stratum size, or equal numbers weighted afterwards | Whole clusters |
| Use when | The population is already in groups of different sizes | The groups look like small copies of the whole, and cost matters |

A quick test: *is there little variation within groups and a lot between them?* Use stratified. *Is it the other way round?* Use cluster.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Stratifying a bank's customers into retail, small business and corporate makes sense because they behave very differently. Treating each branch as a cluster of a mixed customer base, and surveying all customers in a few branches, is cheaper and works if branches resemble one another.

self_check.prompt_text: Customers fall into three very different segments of different sizes. Which method, and how would you set sample sizes?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Stratified sampling, with the number drawn from each segment proportional to its share of customers (or equal numbers, weighted later by share).

items.title: Sampling distributions and standard error
items.core_explanation_md:
Take one sample and you get one mean. Take another sample of the same size and you get a different mean. If you could take **every** possible sample of that size, the collection of all their means is the **sampling distribution of the mean**. The same idea gives a sampling distribution for a median or a proportion.

Two facts to carry away:

- the sample means cluster around the population mean (their average equals it), and they are less spread out than the individual values;
- the standard deviation of that distribution is the **standard error**. It measures how far a sample mean is likely to stray from the truth by chance alone.

Smaller standard error means a better, more reliable estimator.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Do not confuse the two spreads. The standard deviation describes how individual items vary. The standard error describes how the sample *means* vary. The second is always smaller for n greater than 1.

self_check.prompt_text: What does the standard error of the mean measure, in one sentence?
self_check.expected_takeaway: How much sample means vary from sample to sample, because of chance, around the population mean.

items.title: Standard error of the mean and the z value of a sample mean
items.core_explanation_md:
For samples of size n from a population with mean mu and standard deviation sigma (infinite population, or sampling with replacement), the sampling distribution of the mean has the same centre as the population and a smaller spread:

- centre: mu of x-bar equals mu;
- spread: the standard error is sigma divided by the square root of n.

To find how likely a sample mean is to fall beyond a given value, measure the distance in standard errors and use the standard normal table: z is the sample mean minus mu, divided by the standard error. Areas on opposite sides of zero are added, on the same side subtracted.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The z value is unit-free, so the same table serves rupees, days or percentages. If the population is normal, this works for any n. If it is not, use it when n is at least 30 (central limit theorem).

formula_spec.latex_expression: \sigma_{\bar{x}} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}},\qquad z = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu}{\sigma_{\bar{x}}}

variables.name: Standard normal value of the sample mean

assumptions: Population infinite, or sampling with replacement (otherwise apply the finite population multiplier).
Population normal, or n large enough (at least 30) for the central limit theorem.
Simple random sampling.
common_errors: Dividing by n instead of its square root.
Using sigma instead of the standard error as the denominator of z.
Adding table areas for two z values on the same side of zero instead of subtracting.

self_check.prompt_text: sigma = 40 and n = 25. What is the standard error, and how many standard errors above mu is a sample mean 12 above mu?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Standard error = 40/5 = 8; 12/8 = 1.5 standard errors.

items.title: The central limit theorem in practice
items.core_explanation_md:
Real populations are rarely bell-shaped: loan sizes, deposit balances and claim amounts are usually skewed. The **central limit theorem** rescues us:

- whatever the shape of the population, the mean of the sampling distribution equals the population mean;
- as the sample size grows, the **shape** of the sampling distribution of the mean approaches the normal curve.

In practice you do not need an enormous sample. Use the normal approximation when **n is at least 30**; for fairly well-behaved populations even about 15 may be enough. The payoff: you can make probability statements about a sample mean without knowing the shape of the population.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The theorem is about sample means (and sums), not about individual values. A skewed population stays skewed; it is the distribution of the averages that becomes bell-shaped.

self_check.prompt_text: A population of account balances is heavily skewed. Can you use the normal table for the mean of a random sample of 50 accounts? Why?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Yes. With n of at least 30 the central limit theorem makes the sampling distribution of the mean approximately normal, whatever the population shape.

items.title: Finite population multiplier and the 5 per cent rule
items.core_explanation_md:
Sampling **without replacement** from a **finite** population gives more information per item than the plain formula credits, because each item drawn leaves fewer unknowns. The standard error is multiplied by a correction, the **finite population multiplier**, which is below 1.

The **sampling fraction** n/N tells you whether it matters. If the sample is a tiny share of the population, the multiplier is almost 1 and can be dropped. The accepted rule: when n/N is **less than 0.05**, skip the multiplier.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Notice what precision depends on. With the multiplier dropped, the standard error depends only on n, the absolute size of the sample, not on how big a slice of the population it is. A sample of 400 from a very large population is as precise as 400 from a larger one.

formula_spec.latex_expression: \sigma_{\bar{x}} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} \sqrt{\frac{N - n}{N - 1}},\qquad \text{sampling fraction} = \frac{n}{N}
assumptions: Population finite and sampling without replacement.
The multiplier may be omitted when n/N is less than 0.05.
common_errors: Applying the multiplier when sampling with replacement.
Using N - n over N instead of N - n over N - 1.
Forgetting that the multiplier is inside a square root.

self_check.prompt_text: N = 65 and n = 16. Is the sampling fraction large enough that the multiplier matters, and what is the multiplier?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Sampling fraction 16/65, about 0.25, is above 0.05, so it matters. Multiplier = square root of 49/64 = 7/8 = 0.875.

items.title: More sample, less error: diminishing returns
items.core_explanation_md:
Because the standard error is sigma over the square root of n, it falls as the sample grows, but ever more slowly:

| Sample size | Standard error when sigma = 100 |
| --- | --- |
| 10 | 31.63 |
| 100 | 10 |

A tenfold bigger sample cuts the error to roughly one-third, not one-tenth. To halve the error you must **quadruple** the sample.

So the right sample size is a decision, not a maximum: compare the value of the extra precision with the cost of collecting the extra observations.
items.expanded_explanation_md: This is the law of diminishing returns borrowed from economics. A common reasoning error is to think that sampling "half as many" accounts gives half the accuracy. It costs you far less than that, which is why modest samples are used so often.

self_check.prompt_text: If you want the standard error to drop to one-third of its present value, by what factor must the sample size rise?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Nine times, because the standard error varies as 1 divided by the square root of n.

items.title: What an average is for, and what makes one good
items.core_explanation_md:
A long list of numbers is hard to hold in the mind. An **average** squeezes it into one representative value, and lets you compare one group with another. There are three families:

| Average | Idea |
| --- | --- |
| Mean (arithmetic, geometric, harmonic) | A calculated value from all the data |
| Median | The middle value of the ordered data |
| Mode | The most frequent value |

A good average is clearly defined, simple, uses every observation, can be used in further algebra, is stable between samples, is not dominated by extreme values and is easy to interpret. No single average ticks every box, so choosing one means deciding which property matters for the question at hand.
items.expanded_explanation_md: This is why you will see the median for incomes (extreme values do not dominate), the mean for totals that must add up, and the mode for "what is the most common outcome".

self_check.prompt_text: Name two properties of a good average, and say which average gives up the property of using every observation.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Any two of: rigidly defined, simple, uses all observations, algebraic treatment, stable under sampling, not unduly affected by extremes, easy to interpret. The median and the mode do not use every observation.

items.title: Arithmetic mean: raw, grouped, combined and corrected
items.core_explanation_md:
One idea, four situations:

- **Raw data**: add the values and divide by how many there are.
- **Grouped data**: multiply each value (or class mark) by its frequency, add, and divide by the total frequency.
- **Combined mean**: you cannot just average two group means; weight each by its group size.
- **Corrected mean**: if one value was recorded wrongly, rebuild the total (mean times n), take out the wrong value, put in the right one, and divide again.

A missing value or frequency is found by writing the mean as an equation and solving for the unknown.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The corrected-mean method is the same as adjusting a ledger total: you do not recount everything, you reverse the error. Combined means appear whenever branches, products or customer segments are pooled.

formula_spec.latex_expression: \bar{x} = \frac{\sum x}{n},\quad \bar{x} = \frac{\sum f x}{\sum f},\quad \bar{x}_c = \frac{n_1 \bar{x}_1 + n_2 \bar{x}_2}{n_1 + n_2}

variables.name: Observation, or class mark for grouped data
Means of the groups being pooled

assumptions: For grouped data the class mark stands for every value in the class, so the grouped mean is an approximation.
The corrected mean uses the same n as the original.
common_errors: Averaging two group means without weighting by group size.
Using the class limit instead of the class mark for grouped data.
Correcting the mean directly instead of correcting the sum.

self_check.prompt_text: A mean of 50 observations is 40. One value recorded as 90 should have been 60. What is the corrected mean?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Original sum 2,000; corrected sum 2,000 - 90 + 60 = 1,970; corrected mean 1,970/50 = 39.4.

items.title: When the arithmetic mean misleads
items.core_explanation_md:
The mean is the workhorse: it uses every observation, is easy to compute and supports further algebra. Its strength is also its weakness, because every value pulls on it.

- **Extreme values** drag it. One very large loan moves the average loan.
- **Skewed data**: it sits away from where most observations lie.
- **Open-end classes** such as "above 50 lakh" have no class mark, so the mean cannot be computed properly.
- **Ratios and percentages**: averaging rates with the arithmetic mean can give a wrong answer.
- It may equal no actual value (an average of 2.4 children).

When these problems bite, look to the median, or to the geometric or harmonic mean for rates.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A useful test is to compare the mean with the median: if they are far apart, a few extreme observations are probably doing the work.

self_check.prompt_text: Why is the arithmetic mean a poor choice for a table whose last class is "above 50 lakh"?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The open-end class has no upper limit, so it has no class mark to multiply by its frequency, and the mean cannot be computed accurately.

items.title: Geometric and harmonic means, and how they compare with the arithmetic mean
items.core_explanation_md:
Use the right mean for the kind of quantity:

| Mean | Formula idea | Use it for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Arithmetic | Sum divided by n | Values in the same units |
| Geometric | nth root of the product | Growth that compounds: average annual growth, index numbers, portfolio return |
| Harmonic | n divided by the sum of reciprocals | Rates and ratios in different units, such as speed |

Geometric needs all values positive. For positive values that are not all equal, **AM is larger than GM, which is larger than HM**. For exactly two numbers, AM x HM = GM squared.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Why the geometric mean for growth? Growth factors multiply, so the single constant factor that gives the same overall result is their geometric mean, not their arithmetic mean. The courseware prints the order as AM > HM > GM; the standard result, which the worked examples here confirm, puts GM above HM.

formula_spec.latex_expression: GM = \left(x_1 x_2 \cdots x_n\right)^{1/n},\quad HM = \frac{n}{\sum 1/x_i},\quad AM \times HM = GM^2 \text{ (two numbers)}

variables.name: Positive observations (growth factors for GM, rates for HM)

assumptions: All values positive for GM and HM.
For HM to be the right average of speeds, the distances travelled at each speed must be equal.
AM x HM = GM squared holds only for two values.
common_errors: Using the arithmetic mean of growth rates to describe compounded growth.
Taking the harmonic mean when different distances are covered at different speeds without weighting.
Applying AM x HM = GM squared to more than two numbers.

self_check.prompt_text: An account grows by factors 1.20 and 1.05 over two years. Which mean of the two factors gives the constant yearly factor?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The geometric mean, the square root of 1.20 x 1.05 = 1.26, which is about 1.1225.

items.title: Median and quartiles, raw and grouped
items.core_explanation_md:
Sort first. Then:

- **Raw data**: with an odd count take the middle value; with an even count average the two middle values.
- **Grouped data**: find the **median class**, the first class whose less-than cumulative frequency goes beyond N/2, then interpolate inside it.
- **Quartiles** work the same way with N/4 (Q1), N/2 (Q2, the median) and 3N/4 (Q3).

In each case the interpolation starts at the lower limit of the class, adds the fraction of the class still needed and scales by the class width. Make sure the classes are continuous (use boundaries for inclusive classes) before you start.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The median is the safe choice when extreme values or open-end classes are present, because it needs only the order, not the size, of the outer values.

formula_spec.latex_expression: \text{Median} = l_1 + \frac{N/2 - cf}{f}\,(l_2 - l_1),\quad Q_1:\ N/4,\quad Q_3:\ 3N/4

variables.name: Lower and upper limits of the median (or quartile) class
Cumulative frequency of the class before it

assumptions: Classes are continuous, in ascending order.
The median class is the one whose cumulative frequency first exceeds N/2 (N/4 or 3N/4 for quartiles).
common_errors: Using the class frequency instead of the preceding cumulative frequency for cf.
Forgetting the class width factor.
Using N/2 for every quartile.

self_check.prompt_text: N = 80 and the cumulative frequencies of the first three classes are 10, 30 and 55. Which class holds the median, and which holds Q1?
self_check.expected_takeaway: N/2 = 40, first exceeded by 55, so the third class; N/4 = 20, first exceeded by 30, so the second class.

items.title: Mode, and the mean-median-mode relation
items.core_explanation_md:
The **mode** is the value that occurs most often. In a frequency table, the **modal class** is the class with the highest frequency. The mode is then placed inside it by pulling it towards the more crowded neighbour: if the class after the modal class is fuller than the one before, the mode sits above the middle of the modal class.

A distribution can have two modes (bimodal) or more (multimodal).

For moderately skewed data the three averages are tied together: **Mode = 3 x Median - 2 x Mean**. If two are known, estimate the third.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The relation is an empirical rule, not an identity. It works well for single-peaked, only mildly skewed distributions and poorly for very uneven ones.

formula_spec.latex_expression: \text{Mode} = l_1 + \frac{f_1 - f_0}{2 f_1 - f_0 - f_2}\,(l_2 - l_1),\qquad \text{Mode} \approx 3\,\text{Median} - 2\,\text{Mean}

variables.name: Frequencies of the classes before and after it

assumptions: Equal class widths.
The relation with the median and mean holds only approximately, for moderately skewed single-peaked data.
common_errors: Taking the middle of the modal class without adjusting for the neighbours.
Swapping f0 and f2.
Treating the three-median-two-mean relation as exact.

self_check.prompt_text: Modal class 20-30 has frequency 30, the class before has 20 and the class after has 10. Is the mode above or below the middle (25) of the class?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Below: the class before is fuller than the one after, which pulls the mode down. 20 + (30 - 20) / (60 - 20 - 10) x 10 = 23.33.

items.title: Choosing between mean, median and mode
items.core_explanation_md:
Pick the average that matches the question and the shape of the data.

| Average | Best when | Weak when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Arithmetic mean | Totals matter; data roughly symmetric | Extreme values, skew, open-end classes |
| Median | Skewed data, extreme values, open ends | You need further algebra, or every value must count |
| Mode | You want the most common value | The distribution has no clear peak or several |
| Geometric mean | Compounded growth | Zero or negative values |
| Harmonic mean | Rates over equal distances or equal amounts | Zero values |

If the data are **positively skewed**, expect mean > median > mode; if **negatively skewed**, the reverse.
items.expanded_explanation_md: When in doubt, report the mean and the median together. A large gap between them tells the reader the data are skewed.

self_check.expected_takeaway: The mean will be larger; the median is the better typical value because large balances do not drag it.

items.title: Dispersion: how spread out the data are
items.core_explanation_md:
Two sets of branch deposits can have the same average and be very different: one steady, one swinging wildly. An average hides that. **Dispersion** measures the scatter.

| Absolute (in the units of the data) | Relative (a pure number, for comparison) |
| --- | --- |
| Range | Coefficient of range |
| Quartile deviation | Coefficient of quartile deviation |
| Mean deviation | Coefficient of mean deviation |
| Standard deviation | Coefficient of variation |

Use an **absolute** measure within one series. Use a **relative** one to compare series measured in different units or with very different averages.
items.expanded_explanation_md: As with averages, a good measure is well defined, uses all observations, is simple, allows algebra and is stable between samples. The standard deviation does best on most of these, which is why it is the standard.

self_check.prompt_text: You want to compare the spread of loan amounts (in rupees) with the spread of loan tenures (in months). Absolute or relative measure?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Relative, because the units differ; use the coefficient of variation.

items.title: Range, quartile deviation and mean deviation
items.core_explanation_md:
Three ways to measure scatter, from rough to thorough:

- **Range**: largest minus smallest. Quick, but uses only two observations.
- **Quartile deviation**: half the gap between the upper and lower quartiles. It ignores the extremes, so it is steady.
- **Mean deviation**: the average of the absolute distances from an average (the mean, or the median, which gives the smaller value). It uses every observation, but throwing away the signs makes it awkward for further algebra.

Each has a coefficient that divides by a comparable quantity, so you can compare series.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Remember what each coefficient divides by: the sum of the extremes for range, the sum of the quartiles for quartile deviation, and the average used for mean deviation.

formula_spec.latex_expression: R = x_{max} - x_{min},\quad QD = \frac{Q_3 - Q_1}{2},\quad MD = \frac{\sum f |x - \bar{x}|}{\sum f}

variables.name: Range: (max - min)/(max + min); QD: (Q3 - Q1)/(Q3 + Q1); MD: MD divided by the mean

assumptions: Absolute deviations are used in MD (signs ignored).
Class marks stand for the values in a grouped table.
common_errors: Dividing the range by the mean instead of by max + min for the coefficient.
Forgetting to take absolute values in MD.
Using Q3 - Q1 without halving for QD.

items.title: Standard deviation, variance and coefficient of variation
items.core_explanation_md:
The **standard deviation** squares each deviation from the mean (so the signs cannot cancel), averages the squares, and takes the root to get back to the original units. The average of the squares is the **variance**.

A shortcut avoids computing every deviation: **mean of the squares minus square of the mean**.

The **coefficient of variation** expresses the standard deviation as a percentage of the mean, which makes different series comparable. The series with the smaller CV is the more consistent.
items.expanded_explanation_md: This unit divides by n (the whole data set is treated as the population). Later, when estimating from a sample, a different divisor is used; check which the question intends.

formula_spec.latex_expression: \sigma = \sqrt{\frac{\sum f (x - \bar{x})^2}{N}} = \sqrt{\frac{\sum f x^2}{N} - \bar{x}^2},\qquad CV = \frac{\sigma}{\bar{x}} \times 100
assumptions: Divisor is N, not N - 1.
The mean is not zero when CV is used.
common_errors: Squaring each frequency-weighted total instead of squaring the mean (mean of squares less square of the mean).
Taking the root before dividing by N.
Reporting the variance when the standard deviation is asked.

self_check.prompt_text: Mean 60 and standard deviation 9. What is the CV, and what does a smaller CV in another branch tell you?
self_check.expected_takeaway: CV = 9/60 x 100 = 15 per cent; the branch with the smaller CV is more consistent.

items.title: Reading a standard deviation and comparing consistency
items.core_explanation_md:
A standard deviation by itself needs a yardstick. Is 20 big? For deposits averaging 80 it is large; for 200 it is modest. That is the job of the **coefficient of variation**.

| Branch | Mean daily transactions | Standard deviation | CV |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | 200 | 30 | 15 per cent |
| B | 80 | 20 | 25 per cent |

Branch B has the smaller standard deviation but the larger CV, so its volumes swing more *relative to its size*. Branch A is the more consistent. Quoting the standard deviation alone would have given the opposite impression.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The standard deviation gives more weight to extreme items (squaring magnifies large deviations), so a few outliers can inflate it. Always look at the data behind the number.

self_check.prompt_text: Two series have the same mean. The first has standard deviation 12 and the second 8. Which is more consistent?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The second: with equal means the smaller standard deviation also means the smaller CV.

items.title: Skewness and kurtosis: shape beyond average and spread
items.core_explanation_md:
Two distributions can share a mean and a standard deviation and still look different.

**Skewness** is lopsidedness.

| Skew | Longer tail | Order of the averages |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Positive | Right | Mean > median > mode |
| Symmetric | Neither | All equal |
| Negative | Left | Mean < median < mode |

It is measured with the **third central moment** (the average cube of deviations from the mean): positive means a longer right tail, negative a longer left tail, zero a symmetric shape.

**Kurtosis** is peakedness and tail weight, measured from the fourth central moment as mu4 divided by mu2 squared. Taller and sharper with fat tails is **leptokurtic**; like the normal curve is **mesokurtic**; flatter with thin tails is **platykurtic**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A caution on conventions. In this form, mu4/mu2 squared equals 3 for the normal curve, so leptokurtic means above 3. The courseware compares the value with 0 (the "excess" form, measured as mu4/mu2 squared minus 3). Check which form a question uses.

self_check.prompt_text: Mean 52, median 48, mode 44. Is the skew positive or negative, and which tail is longer?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Positive skew (mean > median > mode); the longer tail is on the right.

items.title: Moments, skewness and kurtosis for five observations
items.core_explanation_md: Five daily collections (Rs thousand): 2, 4, 6, 8 and 20. Find the mean, the second, third and fourth central moments, the skewness measure beta1 and the kurtosis measure beta2, and describe the shape.

worked_steps.description: Mean.
Deviations from the mean.
Second central moment: mean of squares of deviations.
Third central moment: mean of cubes.
Fourth central moment: mean of fourth powers.

items.title: Scatter diagrams: seeing a relationship before measuring it
items.core_explanation_md:
Before any formula, **plot the pairs**. Put one variable on the horizontal axis (the one you use for prediction, the **independent** variable) and the other on the vertical axis (the **dependent** variable, the one you want to predict). Each customer, branch or month becomes one dot.

| Pattern of dots | Relationship |
| --- | --- |
| Rise from left to right | Direct (positive) |
| Fall from left to right | Inverse (negative) |
| Shapeless cloud | None |
| Falls then rises, or bends | Curvilinear |

If a straight line can run through the dots, the relationship is **linear**. The tighter the dots hug the line, the stronger the relationship and the better the predictions. This unit deals only with linear relationships.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Two scatter diagrams can both show a direct relationship yet differ in strength. A diagram only gives a rough feel; correlation puts a number on the strength and regression gives the line for predicting.

self_check.prompt_text: Branch advertising spend is plotted against new accounts opened. Which variable would you put on the horizontal axis if you want to predict accounts from spend?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Advertising spend: it is the independent variable, the basis of the prediction.

items.title: Correlation coefficient r
items.core_explanation_md:
The correlation coefficient asks: when x is above its average, is y usually above its average too? Multiply each pair of deviations, average the products (the **covariance**), then divide by the two standard deviations so that the answer has no units.

For hand calculation use the sums version. Tabulate x, y, x squared, y squared and xy, total each column, and substitute. It avoids computing every deviation.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Dividing by the standard deviations is what keeps r between -1 and +1 and makes it comparable across problems: rupees against months gives the same kind of number as kilograms against metres.

formula_spec.latex_expression: r = \frac{\operatorname{cov}(X,Y)}{\sigma_x\sigma_y} = \frac{N\sum xy - \sum x \sum y}{\sqrt{N\sum x^2 - (\sum x)^2}\,\sqrt{N\sum y^2 - (\sum y)^2}}

variables.name: Standard deviations of x and y (divisor N)

assumptions: The same N pairs are used in every sum.
Standard deviations use divisor N, matching the covariance.
common_errors: Mixing divisors (N for covariance, N - 1 for a standard deviation).
Confusing the sum of squares with the square of the sum.
Reporting r outside the range -1 to +1 (a sign that an arithmetic slip occurred).

self_check.prompt_text: cov(X, Y) = 12, sigma_x = 3, sigma_y = 5. What is r?

items.title: Reading the value of r
items.core_explanation_md:
r is a **dial** from -1 to +1.

| r | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| +1 | Perfect direct linear relationship: all points on an upward line |
| Near +1 | Strong direct relationship |
| Near 0 | Weak or no *linear* relationship |
| Near -1 | Strong inverse relationship |
| -1 | Perfect inverse linear relationship: all points on a downward line |

Two habits keep you honest. First, the **sign** gives direction and the **size** gives strength, so -0.9 is stronger than +0.5. Second, r = 0 says there is no *linear* relationship, not that the variables are unrelated: a curved pattern can have r close to 0.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A computed |r| above 1 is always an arithmetic mistake. Check your sums.

self_check.prompt_text: Which shows the stronger relationship: r = -0.85 or r = +0.60?
self_check.expected_takeaway: r = -0.85: strength is the size of r, and the sign only shows the direction (here inverse).

items.title: The least-squares regression line
items.core_explanation_md:
Regression draws the one straight line that fits the dots best in the **least squares** sense: it makes the total of the squared vertical gaps between the dots and the line as small as possible.

The line is y-hat = a + bx.

- The **slope** b says how much y changes, on average, for one unit increase in x. Positive slopes rise, negative slopes fall.
- The **intercept** a is where the line cuts the y-axis. Because the line passes through the point of averages, a = y-bar minus b times x-bar.

To predict, put the given x into the equation.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Notice that b is a covariance divided by the *variance of x*, not by a standard deviation: it carries the units of y per unit of x, so it has units, unlike r.

formula_spec.latex_expression: \hat{y} = a + bx,\quad b = \frac{\operatorname{cov}(X,Y)}{\sigma_x^2},\quad a = \bar{y} - b\bar{x}

variables.name: Slope of the line
variables.unit: units of y per unit of x

assumptions: The relationship is linear.
x is the independent variable and y the dependent variable; the line predicts y from x.
common_errors: Dividing the covariance by sigma_x instead of its square.
Computing a with the wrong sign.
Using the line to predict x from y.

self_check.prompt_text: x-bar = 20, y-bar = 70 and b = 2. What is a, and what does the line predict for x = 25?

items.title: Standard error of the estimate: how good is the prediction?
items.core_explanation_md:
A regression line always gives *a* prediction, but how reliable is it? Measure the gaps between actual y and the line's y-hat. Square them, add, divide by **n - 2** (two quantities, a and b, were estimated from the data) and take the root.

A **small** Se means the dots hug the line and predictions are accurate. As a working rule from the courseware, the actual value is expected within about one Se either side of the prediction roughly two-thirds of the time, and within two Se about 95 per cent of the time.

If you have already found a and b, the sums form saves finding every y-hat.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Se is in the units of y, so judge it against the size of the y values: an Se of 5 matters less when y is around 60 than when it is around 10.

formula_spec.latex_expression: S_e = \sqrt{\frac{\sum (y-\hat{y})^2}{n-2}} = \sqrt{\frac{\sum y^2 - a\sum y - b\sum xy}{n-2}}
assumptions: The line has been fitted by least squares to the same data.
The divisor is n - 2.
common_errors: Dividing by n or n - 1 instead of n - 2.
Using y-bar in place of y-hat.
Forgetting that Se has the units of y.

self_check.prompt_text: Sum of squared residuals is 36 and n = 11. What is Se, and what band does two Se give around a prediction of 50?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Se = sqrt(36 / 9) = 2; the band is 50 plus or minus 4, that is 46 to 54 (about 95 per cent).

items.title: Limits of correlation: line only, careful data, no causation
items.core_explanation_md:
A high r is not the end of the analysis. Three cautions:

- **Linear only.** r measures straight-line association. Points laid out on a perfect circle have r near zero even though the pattern is exact.
- **Homogeneous data.** If you mix two different groups in one sample, r can look high when there is no real relationship inside either group. That is **spurious correlation**.
- **Not causation.** r near 1 shows that two variables rise and fall together. It does not show that one causes the other: annual rice consumption and road accidents both climbed together over twenty years, yet neither drives the other.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Before acting on a correlation, ask what else could drive both variables, and look at the scatter diagram, not only the number.

self_check.prompt_text: Deposits and the number of ATMs in a town both rise for ten years and r = 0.95. Can you conclude that more ATMs cause more deposits?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No. A high r shows they move together, not that one causes the other; growth in the town's economy could drive both.

items.title: The four components of a time series
items.core_explanation_md:
A **time series** is a set of readings taken at regular intervals: monthly deposits, quarterly profit, yearly new accounts. Four forces shape it:

| Component | What it is | Banking example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Secular trend** | Smooth long-term drift, up or down | Steady growth of digital transactions over a decade |
| **Cyclical** | Swings above and below the trend over several years, uneven in length | Credit growth rising and slumping with the business cycle |
| **Seasonal** | Regular pattern within a year | Cash demand peaking around festivals each year |
| **Irregular** | Random, unpredictable shocks | Flood closing branches in a district for a week |

Real data mix all four. Time series analysis tries to pull them apart.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A quick test: if the pattern repeats on a calendar rhythm (every year, every quarter), it is seasonal. If it swings over several years with no fixed length, it is cyclical.

self_check.prompt_text: Quarterly cash withdrawals jump every December. Which component is that, and what distinguishes it from a cyclical swing?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Seasonal variation: it repeats on a fixed calendar rhythm within the year, while cyclical swings last longer than a year and vary in length.

items.title: Linear trend with coded time
items.core_explanation_md:
Fit the straight line y-hat = a + bx exactly as in regression, but use time as the independent variable, and **code** time so the arithmetic is easy.

- **Odd number of years**: let x be the year minus the middle year (..., -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, ...).
- **Even number of years**: the middle falls between two years, so subtract the mean and **double** the result to get whole odd numbers (..., -3, -1, 1, 3, ...).

Because the codes add to zero, the formulas shrink: **a is simply the mean of y** and **b = Sum xy / Sum x squared**.

To forecast, first convert the future year to the same code: x = 2 x (year minus mean year) for an even series.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The most common slip is plugging the calendar year (2026) into the equation instead of its coded value. Always code the target year with the same rule you used for the data.

Time points are equally spaced.
Coding rule for the forecast year matches the rule used for the data.
common_errors: Forecasting with the calendar year instead of the coded value.
Forgetting that the doubled code changes the meaning of b (change per half-year).

items.title: Cyclical variation by the residual method
items.core_explanation_md:
Once the trend is fitted, what is left over is cycle plus irregular noise. To see the cycle, compare each actual value with its trend value:

- **Per cent of trend** = actual / trend x 100. Above 100 means above trend.
- **Relative cyclical residual** = (actual - trend) / trend x 100. Positive means above trend, negative below.

Plot these over time. Stretches above 100 and then below 100 reveal the cycle.

The method describes the **past** cycle. It cannot forecast the next one, because cycles do not repeat at fixed intervals.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The relative residual is just per cent of trend minus 100. Using either is fine; check which one a question asks for.

formula_spec.latex_expression: \text{per cent of trend} = \frac{y}{\hat{y}}\times 100,\qquad \text{relative cyclical residual} = \frac{y - \hat{y}}{\hat{y}}\times 100

items.title: Seasonal index by ratio to moving average: the six steps
items.core_explanation_md:
A seasonal index says how a quarter usually compares with an average quarter, with 100 as average. To build it from quarterly data:

1. **Moving total** of four quarters, sliding one quarter at a time.
2. **Moving average**: divide by 4.
3. **Centre** it: average each pair of consecutive moving averages, so the result lines up with an actual quarter. (Skip this for an odd period like 7 days.)
4. **Ratio**: 100 x actual / centred average, for every quarter that has one.
5. **Modified mean** of each quarter's ratios, dropping the highest and lowest to cut out extreme cyclical and irregular effects.
6. **Adjust** so the four indices total 400: multiply each by 400 divided by the sum of the modified means.

The moving average smooths out seasons and random bumps, leaving trend plus cycle, so the ratio isolates season plus irregular.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Why centre? A four-quarter average naturally falls between two quarters. Averaging two neighbours moves it onto a quarter so you can divide that quarter's actual by it.

self_check.prompt_text: Why are modified means rescaled so the indices total 400?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Seasonal indices are based on 100 per quarter, so across four quarters they must average 100 and total 400; the modified means may not, so they are scaled by 400 divided by their sum.

items.title: Using a seasonal index: deseasonalise, then forecast
items.core_explanation_md:
Two uses, one inverse of the other:

- **Deseasonalise** (remove the season): actual / (index / 100). This shows trend, cycle and irregular movement only, so you can compare quarters fairly. A quarter that looks weak may simply be a seasonally weak quarter.
- **Forecast with the season** (put it back): estimate the trend on deseasonalised data, then multiply the deseasonalised forecast by index / 100.

Example: a deseasonalised forecast of 2,000 for a quarter whose index is 90 becomes 2,000 x 90/100 = 1,800.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Always check the direction. Dividing by the index removes the season; multiplying by it restores the season.

items.title: Irregular variation, the combined model and forecasting models
items.core_explanation_md:
**Irregular variation** is what is left after trend, cycle and season are taken out: random shocks such as a flood or an unusually cold winter. We cannot predict it, but over time it tends to even out.

To handle all four components in one series:

1. deseasonalise the data with the seasonal index;
2. fit the trend line to the deseasonalised data;
3. compute per cent of trend to see what remains (cycle plus irregular).

For forecasting from a series' own history there are three families of models:

| Model | Idea |
| --- | --- |
| Autoregressive (AR) | Predict from a combination of the variable's own past values |
| Moving average (MA) | Model the error as a combination of present and past errors |
| ARMA | Both together |
items.expanded_explanation_md: All time-series forecasting assumes the future will resemble the past. When structure changes (a new regulation, a crisis), the forecast can fail.

self_check.prompt_text: In what order do you treat the components of a quarterly series with all four present?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Deseasonalise with the seasonal index, fit the trend to the deseasonalised data, then use per cent of trend to look at cycle and irregular variation.

items.title: Factorials, permutations and combinations
items.core_explanation_md:
Counting comes before probability. Three tools:

- **n factorial** (n!): multiply n by every whole number below it. By agreement 0! = 1.
- **Permutation** P(n, r): ways to **arrange** r items chosen from n, where order matters (a first, second and third officer in a ranking).
- **Combination** C(n, r): ways to **select** r items from n, where order does not matter (a committee of three).

Every selection of r items can be arranged in r! orders, which is why P(n, r) = r! x C(n, r).

When a task has stages, multiply the ways at each stage: choosing 3 of 7 officers and 4 of 6 clerks gives C(7,3) x C(6,4).
items.expanded_explanation_md: Ask one question: "does swapping two chosen items give a different outcome?" If yes, permutation; if no, combination.

formula_spec.latex_expression: n! = n(n-1)\cdots 1,\quad P(n,r) = \frac{n!}{(n-r)!},\quad C(n,r) = \frac{n!}{r!\,(n-r)!},\quad P(n,r) = r!\,C(n,r)
assumptions: Items are distinct and chosen without repetition.
common_errors: Using a permutation when order does not matter.
Adding the ways for different stages instead of multiplying.
Forgetting that C(n, r) = C(n, n - r).

self_check.prompt_text: How many different panels of 3 can be chosen from 8 officers, and how many ways to fill the posts of chair, secretary and treasurer from the same 8?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Panels: C(8,3) = 56. Posts: P(8,3) = 336, which is 3! = 6 times 56.

items.title: Sample space and events: the vocabulary
items.core_explanation_md:
A **random experiment** has several possible outcomes, and you cannot say beforehand which will occur: tossing a coin, rolling a die, checking whether a loan will be repaid. List every possible outcome and you have the **sample space** S. An **event** is any collection of outcomes, a subset of S.

| Type of event | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Certain | Contains every outcome |
| Impossible | Contains none (the empty set) |
| Mutually exclusive | Cannot happen together |
| Equally likely | No reason to prefer one outcome |
| Exhaustive | Together they cover the sample space |
| Complementary | Exhaustive **and** mutually exclusive: exactly one of the pair happens |

On one throw of a die, "odd" and "even" are complementary. "Odd" and "multiple of 3" are neither mutually exclusive (3 is both) nor exhaustive (2 is neither).
items.expanded_explanation_md: The complement of A is "A does not happen". Every event and its complement are complementary, so their probabilities add to 1.

self_check.prompt_text: Are "loan approved" and "loan rejected" for one application mutually exclusive, exhaustive, or both?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Both (if no third outcome such as "pending" exists): they cannot happen together and between them cover all outcomes, so they are complementary.

items.title: Classical probability: favourable over possible
items.core_explanation_md:
When all outcomes are equally likely, count them:

P(A) = number of outcomes in A divided by number of outcomes in S.

The answer always lies between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain).

Counting is where the work is. Use the tools:

- **Selections**: combinations. Two balls from 10 white and 11 black give 210 possible pairs; both white can happen in C(10,2) = 45 ways.
- **Arrangements**: factorials. For "two items always together", glue them into one item, arrange, then arrange inside the glue. For "never together", subtract the "always together" count from the total.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The formula works only if the outcomes you count are equally likely. Counting "heads or tails" outcomes of a biased coin would not give the right probability.

formula_spec.latex_expression: P(A) = \frac{n(A)}{n(S)},\qquad 0 \le P(A) \le 1
assumptions: Outcomes are equally likely, exhaustive and mutually exclusive.
common_errors: Counting outcomes that are not equally likely.
Using a permutation count for n(A) and a combination count for n(S) (or the reverse).
Reporting a probability above 1.

self_check.prompt_text: Two dice are thrown. What is the probability that the total is 7?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Six of the 36 equally likely outcomes give 7 ((1,6), (2,5), ..., (6,1)), so 6/36 = 1/6.

items.title: The addition rule and the complement rule
items.core_explanation_md:
"A **or** B" means at least one of the two happens. Adding P(A) and P(B) counts the overlap twice, so subtract it once:

**P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B).**

If A and B are mutually exclusive there is no overlap and the last term is zero.

The **complement rule** is often quicker: P(A does not happen) = 1 - P(A). In particular, P(neither A nor B) = 1 - P(A or B).

For a card drawn from a pack: P(red) = 26/52, P(picture) = 12/52, P(red and picture) = 6/52, so P(red or picture) = 32/52 = 8/13.
items.expanded_explanation_md: For "at least one" questions, work out the complement ("none") and subtract from 1. It usually saves a lot of arithmetic.

formula_spec.latex_expression: P(A\cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A\cap B),\qquad P(A^c) = 1 - P(A),\qquad P(\text{neither}) = 1 - P(A\cup B)

variables.name: Probability that at least one occurs

assumptions: A and B are events of the same sample space.
For mutually exclusive events P(A and B) = 0.
common_errors: Forgetting to subtract the overlap.
Subtracting the overlap when events are mutually exclusive (it is zero anyway).
Using 1 - P(A) - P(B) for "neither" without removing double counting.

self_check.prompt_text: P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4 and P(A and B) = 0.2. What are P(A or B) and P(neither)?

items.title: Conditional probability, multiplication and independence
items.core_explanation_md:
Learning that B has happened changes the odds of A. **Conditional probability** restricts attention to the world where B happened:

P(A given B) = P(A and B) / P(B).

Rearranged, it gives the **multiplication rule**: P(A and B) = P(B) x P(A given B).

If knowing B tells you nothing about A, the events are **independent**, P(A given B) = P(A), and the rule simplifies to P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B).

For a two-stage process, add over the first-stage outcomes (total probability): P(B) = P(B given A1) P(A1) + P(B given A2) P(A2).
items.expanded_explanation_md: Do not confuse independent with mutually exclusive. Two mutually exclusive events with positive probabilities are never independent: if one occurs the other certainly does not, so P(A and B) = 0, which differs from P(A) x P(B).

formula_spec.latex_expression: P(A\mid B) = \frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)},\quad P(A\cap B) = P(B)P(A\mid B),\quad \text{independent: } P(A\cap B) = P(A)P(B)

variables.name: Probability of A given that B has occurred

assumptions: P(B) is greater than zero.
Independence is assumed only when the events genuinely do not affect each other.
common_errors: Multiplying P(A) and P(B) for events that are not independent.
Dividing by P(A) instead of P(B) (check which event is "given").
Treating mutually exclusive events as independent.

self_check.prompt_text: P(A) = 0.8 and P(A and B) = 0.6. What is P(B given A)?

items.title: Putting the rules to work: odds, two stages and independence checks
items.core_explanation_md:
Three tasks come up often.

**Odds to probability.** Odds of m to n in favour mean probability m/(m+n); odds of m to n against mean probability n/(m+n) in favour. Odds against of 2 to 1 means a probability of 1/3.

**Two stages.** When the second stage depends on the first, split by the first stage and add: P(rejected) = P(rejected given branch A) P(branch A) + P(rejected given branch B) P(branch B).

**Independence check.** Compute P(A) x P(B) and compare with P(A and B). Equal means independent; different means the events influence each other.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Tree diagrams help: each branch carries a conditional probability, multiply along a path, add across paths that lead to the same event.

self_check.prompt_text: Odds against a stock rising are 3 to 2. What is the probability that it rises?

items.title: Random variables and their distributions
items.core_explanation_md:
A **random variable** turns an outcome into a number: the number of cheques returned today, the time a customer waits, the return on a portfolio.

| | Discrete | Continuous |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Values | Countable (0, 1, 2, ...) | Any value in a range |
| Example | Accidents, arrivals, age in years | Weight, percentage of marks, waiting time |
| Description of probabilities | **Mass function** f(x): P(X = x) | **Density function** f(x): probability is area under the curve |
| Rule | Each f(x) is at least 0; all f(x) add to 1 | f(x) is at least 0; total area is 1 |

For a continuous variable the probability of any **single exact value** is zero; probabilities belong to intervals.

The **cumulative distribution function** F(x) = P(X is at most x) works for both types. It never decreases, starts at 0 and ends at 1.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A probability table is a valid mass function only if no probability is negative and the probabilities total exactly 1. That is the first check on any distribution you are given.

self_check.prompt_text: A table of probabilities for X = 0, 1, 2 reads 0.5, 0.4, 0.3. Is it a valid distribution?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No: the probabilities add to 1.2, not 1.

items.title: Expectation, variance and standard deviation of a discrete variable
items.core_explanation_md:
The **expectation** is the long-run average: weight each value by its probability and add.

The **variance** measures scatter about that average: the expected squared deviation. A shortcut is the mean of the squares minus the square of the mean. The **standard deviation** is its square root, back in the original units.

Changing units is easy: adding a constant b shifts the mean by b and leaves the variance unchanged; multiplying by a multiplies the mean by a and the variance by a squared.
items.expanded_explanation_md: If a payoff is 500 times a count plus a fixed 100, the expected payoff is 500 times the expected count plus 100, and the standard deviation is 500 times that of the count. The fixed 100 does not add any spread.

formula_spec.latex_expression: E(X) = \sum x f(x),\quad V(X) = E(X^2) - [E(X)]^2,\quad E(aX+b) = aE(X)+b,\quad V(aX+b) = a^2V(X)
assumptions: The probabilities form a valid distribution (they total 1).
common_errors: Taking E(X squared) as the square of E(X).
Adding b to the variance of aX + b.
Forgetting to square a in V(aX + b).

items.title: The binomial distribution
items.core_explanation_md:
Use the binomial when you count **successes** in a **fixed number n of independent trials**, each with the **same success probability p**. Typical bank cases: the number of loans, out of 20, that go bad, if each does so independently with probability 0.05; the number of cheques, out of 50, returned.

The chance of exactly x successes is the number of ways to place them times the probability of each such sequence: C(n, x) p to the x times q to the (n - x), where q = 1 - p.

Handy summary figures: mean np, variance npq. The **mode** is the whole-number part of (n + 1)p; if (n + 1)p is itself a whole number there are two modes, one below it.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Check the conditions before using it. If trials influence one another, or p changes from trial to trial, the binomial formula will give wrong probabilities.

formula_spec.latex_expression: P(X=x) = \binom{n}{x}p^x q^{n-x},\quad E(X) = np,\quad V(X) = npq,\quad M = (n+1)p

variables.name: Probability of success in each trial

assumptions: Fixed number of trials.
Each trial has two outcomes, success or failure.
Trials are independent with constant p.
common_errors: Using the binomial when p changes between trials.
Forgetting the combination factor C(n, x).
Reporting only the integral part of M when M is an integer (there are two modes, M - 1 and M).

self_check.prompt_text: n = 10 and p = 0.2. What are the mean, the variance and the mode?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Mean 2, variance 1.6, M = 11 x 0.2 = 2.2 so the mode is 2.

items.title: Shape of a binomial distribution
items.core_explanation_md:
The shape follows p:

| p | Shape |
| --- | --- |
| Less than 0.5 | Positively skewed (long right tail): small counts are the most likely |
| Exactly 0.5 | Symmetric |
| More than 0.5 | Negatively skewed (long left tail): large counts are the most likely |

The courseware measures skewness as (1 - 2p) squared over npq, which is zero only when p is 0.5, and kurtosis as 3 + (1 - 6pq)/npq, which moves towards 3 as n grows.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The sign of the skew is read from p. The squared skewness measure given in the courseware cannot itself be negative, so it shows how much asymmetry there is rather than which way.

self_check.prompt_text: Each of 60 loans repays with probability 0.7. Is the distribution of the number repaying skewed to the left or the right?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Negatively skewed (long left tail), because p = 0.7 is above 0.5.

items.title: The Poisson distribution
items.core_explanation_md:
The Poisson distribution counts how many times something happens in a **fixed interval** (a day, a page, a week) when the events occur at random at an **average rate lambda** per interval: misprints per page, wrong numbers dialled per day, customers arriving per hour.

The chance of exactly x events is e to the minus lambda times lambda to the x, divided by x factorial.

Two remarkable facts: the **mean and the variance are both lambda**, and for several independent intervals the total is Poisson too, with the rates added (ten pages at 1.2 misprints each give a rate of 12).

The mode is the whole-number part of lambda, or two modes (lambda - 1 and lambda) if lambda is a whole number.
items.expanded_explanation_md: For "at least" questions use the complement: P(X at least 2) = 1 - P(0) - P(1). Summing infinitely many terms is never needed.

formula_spec.latex_expression: P(X=x) = \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^x}{x!},\quad E(X) = V(X) = \lambda

variables.name: Average number of events per interval

assumptions: Events occur randomly and independently at a constant average rate.
The interval for lambda matches the interval being asked about.
common_errors: Using a weekly rate for a monthly question without rescaling lambda.
Computing "at least" probabilities by adding terms instead of using the complement.
Thinking the variance differs from the mean.

self_check.prompt_text: A branch averages 2.5 failed transactions an hour. What is the rate for a 2-hour period?
self_check.expected_takeaway: lambda = 5, because rates for independent intervals add.

items.title: Which distribution fits the question?
items.core_explanation_md:
Three questions pick the model.

| Ask | Binomial | Poisson | Normal |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| What is counted or measured? | Successes in n trials | Events in an interval | A measurement on a continuous scale |
| Is there a fixed number of trials? | Yes (n) | No upper limit | Not applicable |
| Parameters | n and p | lambda | mu and sigma |
| Mean and variance | np and npq | Both lambda | mu and sigma squared |

Examples: loans out of 20 that default (binomial); wrong numbers dialled in a day (Poisson); daily cash demand in rupees (normal).
items.expanded_explanation_md: The first two give probabilities for exact counts (a mass function). The normal gives probabilities for ranges (areas under a density), and the chance of exactly one value is zero.

self_check.prompt_text: Which model for "the number of customers arriving at a counter in a given hour"?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Poisson: events counted in a fixed interval at an average rate.

items.title: Credit risk and its three faces
items.core_explanation_md:
**Credit risk** is the chance of a loss because a borrower does not pay as promised. Three types appear in this course:

| Type | What goes wrong | Warning sign |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Credit default risk** | Borrower cannot repay in full, or is 90 days past due | Overdue instalments |
| **Concentration risk** | Too much exposure to one borrower, group or industry | One failure hurts the whole bank |
| **Country (sovereign) risk** | A government or central bank cannot or will not meet its obligations | Lending to a state in distress |

Probability theory enters because default is uncertain: lenders estimate a **probability of default** and use it to price and provision.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Concentration risk is about size, not about whether any one borrower is weak. A large exposure to a healthy borrower is still a concentration.

self_check.prompt_text: A bank lends 40 per cent of its portfolio to one steel group. Which credit risk is this?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Concentration risk: significant exposure to a single group or industry.

items.title: Value at risk for a normal portfolio
items.core_explanation_md:
**Value at risk** answers: "over a stated period, with a stated level of confidence, how much could the portfolio lose?" If returns are normal with mean r and standard deviation sigma:

- at **95 per cent** confidence, the worst return is r minus 1.65 sigma;
- at **99 per cent**, it is r minus 2.33 sigma.

Multiply that worst return by the portfolio value. A negative answer is a loss, and VaR is usually quoted as the size of that loss.

The period of the return and of sigma sets the period of the VaR: monthly inputs give a monthly VaR.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The multipliers come from the normal curve: 1.65 leaves about 5 per cent in the lower tail (exactly 1.645) and 2.33 about 1 per cent (exactly 2.326). The method assumes returns really are normal, which is a strong assumption in a crisis.

formula_spec.latex_expression: VaR_{95\%} = (r - 1.65\sigma)\times V,\qquad VaR_{99\%} = (r - 2.33\sigma)\times V

variables.name: Standard deviation of returns for the period

assumptions: Returns are normally distributed.
r and sigma are for the same period as the VaR.
common_errors: Using the 95 per cent multiplier for a 99 per cent VaR.
Mixing a daily sigma with a monthly return.
Quoting the negative number as a gain.

self_check.prompt_text: Portfolio Rs 2,00,000, mean return 6 per cent, sigma 5 per cent. What is the 95 per cent loss?
