items.title: Emotional intelligence and morale
items.core_explanation_md:
**Emotional intelligence (EI)** is the capability to manage your own emotions and influence those of others. Goleman argues that IQ alone does not predict success; EI, unlike IQ, grows through adulthood and can be learned. Five components:

| Component | Meaning | Elements |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Self-awareness** | Recognising your moods, emotions, drives | Emotional awareness, self-assessment, self-confidence |
| **Self-regulation** | Controlling disruptive impulses; thinking before acting | Self-control, trustworthiness, conscientiousness, adaptability, innovation |
| **Self-motivation** | Passion beyond money or status | Achievement drive, commitment, initiative, optimism |
| **Empathy** | Understanding others' emotions | Understanding and developing others, service orientation, leveraging diversity, political awareness |
| **Social skills** | Managing relationships | Influence, communication, conflict management, leadership, change catalyst, building bonds, collaboration, team capabilities |

**Morale** is the general mood of a person or group: confident, motivated, willing. High morale shows as confidence, cheerfulness, discipline and willingness; it depends on motivation, rewards and recognition. **Poor morale** lowers productivity and revenue and raises turnover.

**Boosters** include communicating often, welcoming ideas, recognising and sharing success, surveys and open-door access, an open forum, thank-you notes, a daily huddle, and measuring morale regularly. For negativity from faulty information, solve the problem systematically with the people affected.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware cites a Sirota Consulting finding (low-morale companies' share prices rose 3 per cent against an industry average of 16 per cent) without further detail; treat it as illustrative.

self_check.prompt_text: Name the five components of emotional intelligence.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Self-awareness, self-regulation, self-motivation, empathy and social skills.

items.title: Talent management: attract, develop, retain
items.core_explanation_md:
**Talent** has three Cs: **competence** (the head: being able to do), **commitment** (hands and feet: action) and **contribution** (the heart: doing it).

**Talent management** is anticipating the human capital an organisation will need and planning to meet it. The term was coined by McKinsey and Company after a 1997 study. It covers **acquiring, developing and retaining** talent. The courseware lists five interdependent elements:

1. Attracting the right talent
2. Onboarding
3. Creating a talent pool
4. Designing the talent career path
5. Retaining talent

Why it matters in banks: demand for skilled people exceeds supply. The courseware argues that new-generation employees are more loyal to their **careers than to their employer**, that turnover among highly talented staff will rise, and that they seek leisure, freedom at work, flexi-time and work-life balance.

Surveys of corporate talent management departments found its work included **succession planning, assessment, development and high-potential management**; compensation was not part of it.
items.expanded_explanation_md: If one element is out of step (for example attracting people without a career path for them), the whole structure weakens.

self_check.prompt_text: What are the three Cs of talent in the courseware?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Competence, commitment and contribution.

items.title: Succession planning and replacement planning
items.core_explanation_md:
**Succession planning** identifies and develops people who can take over from leaders who leave, retire or die. It is a business strategy for passing leadership roles on, by developing internal people with the potential to fill key positions.

| | Replacement planning | Succession (talent-pool) planning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Focus | Specific **back-up candidates** for given senior positions (the "truck scenario") | A **pipeline** of feeder groups through the leadership levels |
| Courseware view | Research suggests little effect on outcomes | The heart of effective succession planning |

**Objectives:** identify people with potential; give critical development experiences; engage leaders in developing high-potential staff; build a database for staffing key jobs.

**Benefits:** better commitment and retention; meets career development expectations; counters the rising cost and difficulty of external recruitment.

It is an integral part of **career planning** and touches recruitment, training and performance management.

**Banks:** the courseware finds Indian banks' approach (sporadic exposures, quick promotion to fill gaps) **inadequate**, and calls for a comprehensive strategy with **assessment centres and 360-degree feedback**, and management development programmes for senior executives focused on high-end **soft skills**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware quotes survey figures on small firms' lack of written succession plans and on how often firms pick the wrong people for manager roles; they illustrate the problem but were not independently checked.

self_check.prompt_text: How does replacement planning differ from succession planning?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Replacement planning names specific back-up candidates for specific positions; succession planning builds feeder groups across the whole leadership pipeline.

items.title: What shapes behaviour at work: four groups of factors
items.core_explanation_md:
Human behaviour is complex: it combines originating and responding behaviour, reflects a person's psychological make-up, and results from **biological, psychological and social** processes. **Employee behaviour** is how employees respond to specific circumstances at work.

Kurt Lewin's idea, as the courseware states it: behaviour is a **function of the person and the environment**. Neither alone explains it.

| Group | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| **Environmental** | Economic (employment level, wage rates, outlook); social (norms, cultural values, work ethic); political (stability, quality of the political system) |
| **Personal** | Age, sex, education, abilities, marital status, family background |
| **Organisational** | Nature of job, structure and design, leadership, compensation and reward system, growth opportunities, culture, facilities, personnel policies |
| **Psychological** | Personality, perception, attitudes, values, learning |
items.expanded_explanation_md: Two employees in the same bank can behave very differently in the same situation because the personal and psychological factors differ even when the organisational factors are identical.

self_check.prompt_text: Name the four groups of factors the courseware gives for behaviour.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Environmental, personal, organisational and psychological.

items.title: Individual differences and changing views of "man"
items.core_explanation_md:
Because people differ in needs and motives, **the same treatment will not motivate everyone**. If people were identical, standard rules and minimal judgement would do.

Managers' views of employees have changed:

| View | Idea | Limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Economic / rational man** | Motivated mainly by money | Ignores social needs |
| **Social man** (from the Hawthorne studies) | Wants to belong; treatment and recognition matter | Neglects the work itself; can be manipulative |
| **Creative man** (Argyris, Likert, McGregor) | Needs opportunities to use creativity and grow | Not everyone wants to grow on the job |
| **Complex man** (current view) | A complex being; personalities differ | Requires understanding individual personality |

Understanding personality helps managers **predict** behaviour such as absenteeism, turnover and work involvement, adjust their own behaviour, and take **preventive** steps in time.
items.expanded_explanation_md: This is why "one size fits all" HR policies underperform: they assume a single view of what people want from work.

self_check.prompt_text: Which view of employees holds that they are motivated mainly by money?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The economic or rational man view.

items.title: Seven assumptions about behaviour at work
items.core_explanation_md:
Technical competence is not enough: behaviour and **interpersonal skills** matter because people work in teams, and good teamwork creates **synergy**, an outcome greater than the sum of individual contributions.

The courseware lists seven basic assumptions about human behaviour at work:

| About people | About organisations |
| --- | --- |
| 1. Individuals **differ** | 5. Organisations are **social systems** |
| 2. The **whole person** matters | 6. There is **mutuality of interest** among members |
| 3. Behaviour is **caused** | 7. Organisational behaviour is **holistic** (combines 1 to 6) |
| 4. An individual has **dignity** | |

And a useful reminder: every person is in some respects **like all others**, **like some others** and **like no other**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The "like all others" level covers shared human traits; "like some others" covers groups such as introverts and extraverts or high and low risk takers; "like no other" is the individual's unique personality.

self_check.prompt_text: Which two of the seven assumptions concern organisations rather than people?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Organisations are social systems, and there is mutuality of interest among organisational members.

items.title: Personality and the Type A and Type B profiles
items.core_explanation_md:
**Personality** (Salvatore Maddi): a stable set of characteristics and tendencies that determine the commonalities and differences in people's psychological behaviour (thoughts, feelings, actions), with continuity in time. People do not change overnight; changes occur slowly.

Two classical views: **Cattell** (a pattern of **traits** that helps understand and predict behaviour; traits are permanent) and **Eysenck** (temperaments largely genetic; two primary dimensions, **extraversion** and **neuroticism**).

**Type A and Type B** (Friedman, Meyer, Rosenman):

| Type A | Type B |
| --- | --- |
| Restless, always moving, impatient | Easy going, relaxed about time pressure |
| Multitasks; starts a new task before finishing | Systematic and methodical |
| Squeezes more into less time | Plans so urgent matters are done on time |
| No time to relax | Balanced outlook on life; less competitive |

Both types are found among bank managers. The courseware describes a Type A manager as likely to have an untidy cabin and loses papers; a Type B manager works methodically.
items.expanded_explanation_md: These are tendencies, not boxes. The value for a manager is predicting how a person is likely to react to deadlines, delegation and pressure.

self_check.prompt_text: Which type of personality is restless, impatient and often multitasks?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Type A.

items.title: Erikson's eight stages, and what they look like at work
items.core_explanation_md:
Erikson described personality development as eight stages, each a tension between two outcomes. The courseware gives a workplace parallel for each:

| Stage | At work |
| --- | --- |
| 1. **Trust vs mistrust** | Depending on others for guidance; trust grows if they respond well |
| 2. **Autonomy vs shame and doubt** | Happy when functioning independently after induction; doubt after mistakes |
| 3. **Initiative vs guilt** | Taking initiative; guilt if resources are wasted |
| 4. **Industry vs inferiority** | Working hard for a place; low self-esteem if unsuccessful |
| 5. **Identity vs role confusion** | Proving oneself as a performing member; role identity may be diffused |
| 6. **Intimacy vs isolation** | Close contact at work or a sense of isolation |
| 7. **Generativity vs stagnation** | Developing others; stagnation if not |
| 8. **Integrity vs despair** | Near retirement: self-worth from achievements, or purposelessness |
items.expanded_explanation_md: Type A and B describe personality features; Erikson's model describes growth stages and their effects on mental personality. They answer different questions.

self_check.prompt_text: Which Erikson stage is linked to an employee near retirement who feels either self-worth or despair?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Stage 8, integrity versus despair.

items.title: Four theories of personality
items.core_explanation_md:
| Theory | Core idea | Workplace illustration |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Psychoanalytic** (Freud) | Personality = **id** (unconscious pleasure drive), **ego** (controls the id through reality), **super ego** (conscience, absorbed values). A balance among the three is needed | Over-strong super ego: guilt over trifles. Weak super ego: id runs loose. Daydreaming, forgetfulness, absenteeism, tardiness can be analysed this way |
| **Trait** | Traits are inherent, more heredity than environment | Describing people as aggressive, loyal, flexible, submissive |
| **Self-concept** (Carl Rogers) | Behaviour is consistent with the **image of oneself**, formed by interaction and feedback | A person with a self-image of high independence seeks challenge and recognition, not just pay or security |
| **Social learning** | Personality is mostly **learned** through reinforcement and punishment; person and environment interact | Praise reinforces good behaviour; frustration can reinforce aggression |
items.expanded_explanation_md: Positive feedback reinforces self-concept; negative feedback lowers self-regard and raises tension and anxiety, so feedback style affects development.

self_check.prompt_text: In Freud's scheme, which part acts as the conscience?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The super ego.

items.title: The brain and Holland's personality-job fit
items.core_explanation_md:
The courseware also links personality to the **brain**: through electrical stimulation of the brain (ESB) and **split-brain** psychology. As it summarises (and notes remains open to research):

| Left hemisphere (controls right side of body) | Right hemisphere (controls left side) |
| --- | --- |
| Speech and verbal, logical and mathematical, linear and detailed, sequential, analytic | Spatial and musical, holistic, artistic, emotional, intuitive and creative, simultaneous, facial recognition |

**Holland's personality-job fit theory:** satisfaction depends on how well personality matches the occupation. Six types:

| Type | Prefers | Examples of congruent jobs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Realistic** | Physical skills; shy, stable, practical | Mechanic, farmer |
| **Investigative** | Thinking, understanding; analytical, curious | Biologist, economist |
| **Social** | Helping others; sociable, friendly | Teacher, social worker |
| **Conventional** | Orderly, rule-regulated; efficient, unimaginative | Accountant, bank teller, file clerk |
| **Enterprising** | Influencing others; ambitious, self-confident | Lawyer, public relations specialist |
| **Artistic** | Creative, unsystematic; imaginative, emotional | Painter, musician, writer |
items.expanded_explanation_md: The practical message: a good match between personality and job raises satisfaction; a poor match raises dissatisfaction.

self_check.prompt_text: Which Holland type does the courseware pair with the job of bank teller?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The conventional type.

items.title: Diversity at work and the trap of homogeneous reproduction
items.core_explanation_md:
**Diversity** includes race or ethnicity and gender (the most recognised), and also disability, family background, age, lifestyle and culture.

Traditional HR systems were built on **homogeneity**: recruit from the sources that produced past successes; hire, promote and evaluate people who resemble the decision-makers. The courseware calls this **homogeneous reproduction**: only those who fit the dominant coalition pass through. Mass aptitude tests selecting similar abilities create another risk: when that ability becomes obsolete the whole group becomes redundant. Its example: banks in the 1970s and 1980s recruited for numerical ability to run rapid branch expansion; computerisation made it obsolete, and banks now need selling and marketing skills.

**Why diversity helps:** complementary skills; well-managed diverse workgroups show more **creativity, problem solving, cohesiveness and communication**, and organisations gain in performance and quality of product and service.

**Why it often fails:** diversity programmes are introduced **piecemeal**, without a holistic view or integration with other systems, and laws change rules without changing culture and beliefs.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A diverse workforce is also a source of adaptability: the organisation can respond to market changes, new technology and shifts in expectations.

self_check.prompt_text: What is "homogeneous reproduction"?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The tendency of selection and promotion to favour people like the decision-makers, letting through only those who fit the dominant coalition.

items.title: Managing diversity: three approaches and four problems
items.core_explanation_md:
**Three traditional HR approaches:**

| Approach | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| **Diversity enlargement** | Increases the **representation** of people from different ethnic and cultural backgrounds, changing demographic composition |
| **Diversity sensitivity** | **Trains** members about cultural differences to promote understanding |
| **Cultural audit** | **Surveys** to find what blocks non-traditional employees and how groups see the dominant culture; must link to HR systems, and should find similarities too |

**Problems:**

1. **Critical mass**: a few diverse recruits may feel isolated or like **tokens** (Kanter).
2. **Time**: it takes years for the organisation's profile to show the effort.
3. **Business conditions**: growth and frequent hiring speed progress; slow expansion or downsizing slows it.
4. **Piecemeal action** without integration with other HR systems.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A cultural audit is meant to be mutual: new culture and HR strategies should be designed so that all members can contribute their potential.

self_check.prompt_text: Which approach teaches employees about cultural differences through training?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Diversity sensitivity.

items.title: Gender issues at work: what the courseware reports
items.core_explanation_md:
The courseware's account, as far as it is taught here:

- Some jobs have long been associated with a gender for physical, social or emotional reasons, but the difference is **blurring**.
- **Powell (1987)** found gender did not significantly affect selection decisions; the more relevant information an evaluator has about the job and applicant, the **less gender-biased** the decision.
- Pay gaps persist: a UK survey (2001) found women earned **82 per cent** of men's average hourly earnings in full-time work.
- In India, representation of women is improving but still poor; banking, teaching and health care have been preferred by women, who often want **regulated working hours** for work-life balance.
- **Sexual harassment:** the courseware reports the Supreme Court's directive and then the **PoSH Act 2013** (the Sexual Harassment of Women at Work Place (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act), in force from **9 December 2013**, and says employers must report sexual harassment offences.
- McKinsey (2021), as cited: women have made gains in representation, especially in senior leadership.

**Left out on purpose:** the courseware also cites older equal-pay, factory, succession and criminal-law provisions. They were not checked against the law in force at the 30 June 2026 cut-off (several have since been replaced or reorganised), so this course does not teach them. Verify any such provision from current sources before relying on it.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The idea to keep: gender should not decide selection or pay, women need workplaces that respect safety and work-life balance, and employers carry a duty to prevent and report harassment.

self_check.prompt_text: Which Act do the courseware and the Supreme Court's directive lead to on sexual harassment at the workplace?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The Sexual Harassment of Women at Work Place (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act 2013, the "PoSH Act".

items.title: Motivation: what it is and how the theories are grouped
items.core_explanation_md:
**Motivation** (from Latin *movere*, to move) is, in an organisation, the **extent of an employee's willingness to respond to organisational requirements**. It is directed towards satisfying **needs** (motives), directly affects performance, and shows in **actual work behaviour**. In Kendra Cherry's words (as cited), it is the process that **initiates, guides and maintains** goal-oriented behaviour, and it involves biological, emotional, social and cognitive forces.

The courseware groups theories in three families:

| Family | Question | Theories in the courseware |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Content** | *What* motivates? | Maslow, Herzberg, Alderfer (ERG), McClelland |
| **Process** | *How* does motivation arise and lead to satisfaction? | Vroom, Porter and Lawler |
| **Contemporary** | Fairness, control, goals, reinforcement, job design | Equity (Adams), reinforcement, goal setting, job design |

It then covers ten: scientific management, human relations, Maslow, Herzberg, ERG, achievement motivation, Vroom, Adams, Porter-Lawler and reinforcement.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A highly motivated employee is not automatically a good performer, and a poor performer is not necessarily de-motivated; ability, role clarity and resources matter too.

self_check.prompt_text: Which family of motivation theories asks "what motivates people"?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Content theories.

items.title: Scientific management and the human relations model
items.core_explanation_md:
| | **Scientific management** (Taylor) | **Human relations** (Mayo) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| View of people | Motivated mainly by **economic gain** | Motivated by **social needs** too |
| Method | Study work scientifically; prescribe the best method; pay a **differential piece rate** | Give workers freedom, information and recognition; let informal groups work |
| Why workers accept authority | In return for **higher wages** | Because supervisors treat them **with consideration** |
| Criticism | De-humanised workers as factors of production; the "**rabble hypothesis**" (motivated by money alone) | Undue reliance on **social contacts**, which do not always motivate |

Taylor's three-step logic: (1) physical work can be studied to find the best method; (2) workers can be made efficient by prescribing how to do their jobs; (3) they will follow the prescriptions if the pay is linked to output.

Mayo's Hawthorne studies (Western Electric, 1920s and early 1930s) found that **interpersonal relations within the working unit** were the real centres of power; leaders were to facilitate cooperation and personal growth.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Neither extreme is enough: workers seek security, social fulfilment and a challenging job as well as pay.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the "rabble hypothesis"?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The assumption that workers are motivated mainly or only by the need for money.

items.title: Maslow's hierarchy of needs at work
items.core_explanation_md:
Maslow ranked human needs in five levels. A need becomes prominent when the one below it is reasonably satisfied. The courseware matches each level to workplace practice:

| Need | In the organisation | Managers can provide |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Physiological** | Salary and physical working conditions | Adequate pay and conditions |
| **Safety / security** | Job security, safe conditions | Pension, group insurance, provident fund, gratuity, grievance procedure; no arbitrary or discriminatory action |
| **Social** | A compatible work group, peer acceptance, friendly supervision | Encourage informal groups (that do not work against the organisation) |
| **Self-esteem** | Job title, merit, recognition, challenging work, responsibility | Performance feedback, involvement in goals and decisions |
| **Self-actualisation** | Excelling, advancing an idea, managing the unit | Autonomy, challenge |

**Criticisms:** not everyone climbs the ladder in order (artists and teachers pursue self-actualisation without satisfying lower needs), and the concepts are hard to measure. **Strength:** a useful scheme, since most people entering an organisation at lower levels first seek to satisfy lower needs.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The healthiest self-esteem rests on earned respect, not fame, status or adulation.

self_check.prompt_text: A bank offers pension, group insurance and provident fund. Which Maslow need level does this address?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Safety or security needs.

items.title: Herzberg's two factors: motivators and hygiene factors
items.core_explanation_md:
Herzberg asked about 200 accountants and engineers when they felt exceptionally good and exceptionally bad about their jobs (the critical incident method). Good feelings came from the **job content**; bad feelings from the **job context**. So the two sets are separate:

| | **Motivators (satisfiers)** | **Hygiene (maintenance) factors** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Relate to | The **job itself** (content) | The **surroundings** (context) |
| If present | Create a strongly motivating situation | Do **not** significantly motivate |
| If absent | No dissatisfaction, only no motivation | **Serious dissatisfaction**, lower performance |
| Items | Recognition, advancement, responsibility, achievement, possibility of growth, work itself (6) | Company policy and administration, technical supervision, relations with subordinates, salary, job security, personal life, working conditions, status, relations with supervisors, relations with peers (10) |

**Key insight:** the opposite of satisfaction is **no satisfaction**, not dissatisfaction. Removing dissatisfiers does not make a job satisfying. Fixing salary or conditions prevents dissatisfaction but will not by itself motivate.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware lists salary and job security among the hygiene factors, which sits uneasily with Maslow's treatment of them as basic needs; exams based on the courseware follow Herzberg's classification.

self_check.prompt_text: Is salary a motivator or a hygiene factor in Herzberg's theory?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A hygiene factor: its absence dissatisfies but its presence does not motivate.

items.title: ERG theory and McClelland's three needs
items.core_explanation_md:
**Alderfer's ERG** compresses Maslow's five levels into three:

| ERG need | Corresponds to Maslow |
| --- | --- |
| **Existence** (survival: pay, conditions, job security) | Physiological and safety |
| **Relatedness** (relationships, recognition) | Social and esteem |
| **Growth** (growing in career and as a person) | Self-actualisation |

Differences from Maslow: **three** levels not five; needs do **not** form a rigid ladder (several may operate at once); and **frustration regression**: if a higher need is frustrated, desire for a lower need increases.

**McClelland** proposed three needs:

| Need | Gains satisfaction from |
| --- | --- |
| **Achievement** | Reaching goals; money is a **scorecard**, not the aim; prefer independent, challenging tasks |
| **Power** | Controlling others and resources; drawn to military, civil service and political organisations |
| **Affiliation** | Interpersonal ties; given the choice, work with friends rather than the most competent person |
items.expanded_explanation_md: Frustration regression explains why employees blocked from growth may suddenly press for higher pay or better conditions.

self_check.prompt_text: Which ERG need corresponds to Maslow's self-actualisation?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Growth needs.

items.title: Process theories: expectancy and equity
items.core_explanation_md:
**Vroom's expectancy model** (also instrumentality, path-goal, or valence-instrumentality-expectancy theory): motivation depends on the reward an employee **expects** to get from performance. Assumption: people are rational and choose what maximises perceived benefit. Three elements:

| Element | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Expectancy** | Likelihood that effort leads to a certain outcome (probabilistic) | "If I work hard I will probably do well" |
| **Instrumentality** | Belief that performance will lead to the desired reward | "Good performance will get me promoted" |
| **Valence** | How much the person values the reward (perceptual) | One values status, another job security |

If any element is weak, motivation falls: no belief that effort pays, no belief that performance is rewarded, or a reward nobody wants.

**Adams' equity theory:** people compare their **inputs** (education, skills, experience) and **outcomes** (salary, promotion, perquisites) ratio with that of a **comparison person**. A perceived unequal ratio is **inequity**, and the person is motivated to reduce it (more so the larger the inequity): change inputs, change outcomes, distort perceptions, leave, change the comparison, or press the other to leave.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Equity thinking underlies why pay transparency and fair appraisal matter for retention: employees compare, and a perception of unfairness drives behaviour.

self_check.prompt_text: An employee believes strong performance will not be rewarded. Which Vroom element is weak?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Instrumentality.

items.title: Porter-Lawler and reinforcement theory
items.core_explanation_md:
**Porter and Lawler** combine the other ideas into a multivariate model: behaviour is determined by individual and environmental factors; people are rational, have different needs and decide between behaviours by expectations.

**Effort** (how much energy: depends on value of the reward and the effort-reward probability) leads to **performance** (depends on effort, **ability** and **role perception**) which leads to **satisfaction** (depends on actual rewards against perceived **equitable** rewards). Rewards can be **intrinsic** (accomplishment, self-actualisation) or **extrinsic** (working conditions, status). Intrinsic rewards are more likely to produce satisfaction that is related to performance. The model says **performance leads to satisfaction**, not the reverse.

**Reinforcement theory** (Skinner): behaviour is a function of its **consequences** (the law of effect); the individual's internal state is set aside. Applied in organisations it is called **OB Mod**.

| Standard term | Meaning | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Positive reinforcement** | Reward follows a behaviour | Behaviour repeated |
| **Negative reinforcement** | An unpleasant consequence is removed | Behaviour repeated |
| **Punishment** | An unpleasant consequence follows | Behaviour less likely |
items.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware uses "negative reinforcement" for behaviour that is followed by a punishing consequence and so not repeated. In the standard usage that is punishment, as in the table. Check which usage an exam question follows.

self_check.prompt_text: In Porter and Lawler's model, does satisfaction lead to performance, or performance to satisfaction?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Performance leads to satisfaction.

items.title: Motives, goals and incentives
items.core_explanation_md:
Behaviour is a response to things inside (thoughts, feelings) and outside (the environment). It is usually driven by a desire to reach a **goal**, though the person may not always know why.

| | **Motive** | **Goal / incentive** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Where | **Inside** the person | **Outside** the person |
| What | Needs, wants, drives, impulses: the "whys" of behaviour | The "hoped for" reward motives are directed at |
| Role | Arouse and maintain activity, set its direction | Evoke behaviour |
| Examples | Need for recognition | Tangible: increased pay. Intangible: praise, power |

To predict behaviour a manager must know which motive or need is active at a particular time.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The words motive and need are used interchangeably: both refer to something inside a person that prompts action.

self_check.prompt_text: Is a pay rise a motive or an incentive?
self_check.expected_takeaway: An incentive (a goal outside the person); the motive is the inner need it satisfies.

items.title: Money, appreciation, enlargement, enrichment and rotation
items.core_explanation_md:
Knowing the theories is not enough; managers need practical **techniques**. The courseware lists money, appreciation, job enlargement, job enrichment, job rotation, participative management and quality of work life.

| Technique | What it is | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Money** | Pay structure | A powerful motivator because it can buy what meets many needs, but with limited impact and diminishing return |
| **Appreciation** | Recognition | The most effective non-monetary incentive; satisfies self-esteem; must be objective and impartial |
| **Job enlargement** | **Horizontal** expansion: more tasks of the **same level** | Relieves boredom, diversifies skills; contradicts specialisation |
| **Job enrichment** | **Vertical** loading: more challenge, responsibility, decision-making, planning and control | Done by promotion or delegation |
| **Job rotation** | Moving a person to a **different job at the same level** | Common in banks; removes boredom; people may resist from inertia and fear of the unknown |

**Quick test:** adding tasks of the same level is **enlargement**; adding responsibility and authority is **enrichment**; moving to a different job is **rotation**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The right rotation period depends on the job and the learning curve: once a person reaches peak efficiency in a routine job and becomes over-confident, performance can slip.

self_check.prompt_text: A clerk is given two additional routine tasks at the same grade. Enlargement or enrichment?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Job enlargement.

items.title: Participation and quality of work life
items.core_explanation_md:
**Participation.** Employee participation in management associates employee representatives with decisions at every stage, from shop floor to board. It brings contributions to decisions and plans, satisfies the **power need**, makes people feel important and **reduces resistance to change**. In India, the courseware ties **workers' participation in management (WPIM)** to Article 43A of the Constitution (a Directive Principle) and treats it as an element of industrial democracy that rests on the human relations approach. Its motivational basis: people get satisfaction from taking part in decisions, doing an effective job and having **self-control rather than management control**.

**Quality of work life (QWL)** is the degree to which members of an organisation can satisfy important personal needs through their experience in it. Seven contributing factors:

1. Adequate and fair compensation
2. A safe and healthy environment
3. Jobs that develop and use skills and abilities
4. Growth and security (capabilities expanded, not made obsolete)
5. An environment for self-esteem and identity
6. Protection of rights to privacy, dissent and equity
7. A sensible balance of job, career, family and leisure
items.expanded_explanation_md: QWL means different things to different people: a safe workplace for a miner, dignified treatment for a shop-floor worker, promotion and creative tasks for a new probationary officer.

self_check.prompt_text: Name three of the seven QWL factors.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Any three of: fair compensation; safe and healthy environment; jobs that use skills; growth and security; self-esteem and identity; protection of rights; balance of work, family and leisure.

items.title: Role: rights, obligations and the role set
items.core_explanation_md:
A **role** is a set of expected behaviour patterns attached to a **position** in a social unit. It carries **rights and obligations**. Everyone plays many roles (worker, manager, parent, union leader). All the roles around the **self** form the **role space**.

| | **Role** | **Position** | **Job** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Nature | **Obligational**: defined by functions in response to others' expectations | **Relational and power-related** | **Prescriptive**: assumes a relationship with the supervisor |
| Emphasis | Relationships with **all** who have expectations of the holder | Place in hierarchy | Duties assigned |

The **role set** is the pattern of relationships between one **focal role** and the many others with which it interacts. A supervisor's role set holds the expectations of everyone the supervisor deals with. A role set map puts the focal role at the centre.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Role matters for integrating the person with the organisation: the organisation has structure and goals, the individual has personality and needs, and they meet in the role.

self_check.prompt_text: What is a role set?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The pattern of interrelationships between a focal role and the other roles it interacts with, with their expectations of the role holder.

items.title: Role stress: nine forms to tell apart
items.core_explanation_md:
| Form | What is happening | Bank example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Role stagnation** | After promotion the person has not outgrown the old role and cannot take charge of the new one | A clerk of fifteen years promoted to junior officer |
| **Inter-role distance** | Conflict between **different roles** the person holds | Manager vs husband and father |
| **Role ambiguity** | Unclear expectations: lack of information or cues | New post of DGM heading a new computerisation department |
| **Role expectation conflict** | Conflicting demands from boss, subordinates, peers, customers | Not sure whom to satisfy |
| **Role overload** | Demands exceed personal resources | Branch accountant at the opening of a new branch |
| **Role erosion** | Responsibility reduced; feeling under-used | A new GM post takes planning from the existing GM |
| **Resource inadequacy** | Needed information, people, material or facilities are missing | Branch without latest communication equipment |
| **Personal inadequacy** | The person lacks the **knowledge or skills** for the role | New role without training |
| **Role isolation** | Some roles in the set are far from the person; weak linkages | Field officer asked to act as accountant who cannot do it effectively |

**Ambiguity vs personal inadequacy:** in ambiguity the person has some knowledge of the role but is **unsure what is expected**; in personal inadequacy the person **lacks the skill** to do it.
items.expanded_explanation_md: HR has the duty to design roles with clarity of task and position, a vision, and decentralised control and decision-making, as technology, markets and products keep changing.

self_check.prompt_text: A newly appointed manager knows the job but is unsure what the CEO and the union each expect. Which role stress?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Role ambiguity (or role expectation conflict if the expectations also clash).

items.title: Employee feedback: why and how it is gathered
items.core_explanation_md:
Employee satisfaction is a measure of how well an organisation is doing, so progressive organisations ask for feedback regularly. Feedback is an **exchange of information** about teamwork, skills and performance, used to **refine personnel and HRD policies**.

| Formal | Informal |
| --- | --- |
| Well-designed **questionnaires** | Discussions with **employee representatives** |
| **Psychological instruments** | **Observation** of employee behaviour by managers and superiors |
| **Suggestion schemes** | Information from **appraisal interviews** |
| | **Exit interviews**, especially of people who leave unexpectedly |

A research example reported by the courseware (Schuster, 1982, the Human Resource Index): in a survey of several thousand employees in 28 organisations on 15 factors, employees were **least satisfied** with their opportunity to take part in decisions and with information about business objectives and plans, and relatively dissatisfied with **reward systems and how rewards are distributed**.

The real value: survey data help **diagnose** problems and open **two-way communication**, which starts organisational development.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Exit interviews matter because people who leave unexpectedly often give the plainest account of what is wrong.

self_check.prompt_text: Give two informal sources of employee feedback.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Any two of: discussions with employee representatives, observation by managers, appraisal interviews, exit interviews.

items.title: Climate surveys: nine things they measure
items.core_explanation_md:
A **climate survey** measures employees' perceptions of the prevailing climate. Scores are usually analysed **department by department**, so units can be compared. The HRD department coordinates it (design, administration, tabulation, presentation), line managers help, and results go to **top management** and department heads.

| Dimension | What employees feel |
| --- | --- |
| **Structure** | Constraints of rules, procedures, communication channels, delegation |
| **Responsibility** | Being their own boss; clarity of role |
| **Reward** | Being rewarded for a job well done; reward and punishment; pay and promotion |
| **Risk** | Challenge in the job; is calculated risk-taking encouraged, or is playing safe? |
| **Warmth** | Fellowship in the work group |
| **Support** | Helpfulness of managers and colleagues, from above and below |
| **Standards** | Importance of goals and performance standards |
| **Conflict** | Whether differing views are heard and conflict resolved |
| **Identity** | Belonging to the organisation and being valued |

Repeat the survey at reasonable intervals to see **trends**, using standard or custom instruments.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Because the content varies with the organisation, the nine dimensions are typical, not fixed.

self_check.prompt_text: Which dimension asks whether calculated risk-taking is encouraged?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Risk.

items.title: What a climate tells you, and cautions about surveys
items.core_explanation_md:
| Unfavourable climate | Favourable climate |
| --- | --- |
| Using job time to confer with peers in order to cope | Open problem solving |
| High stress | Loyalty |
| Looking for another job; considering reporting sick | Cooperation among peers and across groups |
| Reduced communication with superiors | Enhanced motivation and satisfaction |
| Considerable job dissatisfaction | **High-quality customer service** |

Top management, with the help of HRD, should have a **conscious strategy** to create and maintain a favourable climate.

**Cautions:**

- Take **expert help** to design the questionnaire, choose respondents and interpret the results.

- **Communicate the results** to employees (a summary is fine); otherwise confusion follows.

items.title: Total rewards: more than pay
items.core_explanation_md:
People take a job first to meet basic needs, but pay alone does not keep them. Compensation must be **reasonable and justifiable** and tied to a **reward system for better performance**. Pay out of line with the work and the industry attracts poor quality or high turnover; pay that is too high can also backfire.

**Total rewards** are the full combination of **monetary and non-monetary** investments an employer makes to attract, retain and engage people. Three categories:

| Category | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| **Pay** (foundational) | Base salary, healthcare, retirement, insurance |
| **Benefits / performance-based** | Short- and long-term incentives, profit sharing, recognition |
| **Intangible: career and environment** | Career development, mentoring, talent mobility, well-being, flexibility |

The courseware also lists **six elements**: compensation, benefits, work-life effectiveness, recognition, performance management, talent development. Many programmes fail because they are **poorly delivered, not poorly designed**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware gives two overlapping lists (five pillars: compensation, benefits, flexibility, performance recognition, career development; and the six elements). Learn both as listed.

self_check.prompt_text: Name the six elements of total rewards.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Compensation, benefits, work-life effectiveness, recognition, performance management, talent development.

items.title: Reward strategy and what makes a component a "total reward"
items.core_explanation_md:
**Reward strategy** (Armstrong and Murlis) sets the **direction** for reward innovations so that they support the business strategy, how they should be **integrated**, and the **priority and pace** of initiatives. It sits under the HR strategy, which sits under the business strategy, aims and values.

To write a purpose statement for each programme, answer three questions:

1. Why does the programme exist?
2. Why is it meaningful to employees?
3. How does it give the organisation a competitive advantage?

Two tests for a component to count as a **total reward**:

- **Programme**: a specific programme the company invests in and manages.
- **Value**: a specific value ascribed to it in the eyes of employees.

The courseware illustrates with company philosophies: a technology firm that pays competitively and offers perks to attract the best talent; a retailer that stresses egalitarianism and fairness in its pay structure; and a hotel group whose recognition system rewards compliments from guests and colleagues, noting that **timing of recognition is often more important than the reward itself** and that gratitude must come from **immediate supervisors**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: These company statements are the courseware's illustrations; the principle to remember is that reward design starts from purpose and business strategy.

self_check.prompt_text: What two tests must a component meet to count as part of total rewards?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It must be a specific programme the company invests in and manages, and it must have specific value in the eyes of employees.

items.title: Compensation terms and what decides the level of pay
items.core_explanation_md:
**Compensation** is money or remuneration for work plus the benefits an organisation provides (if quantifiable in money): wages or salary, bonus, allowances, accident and health insurance, the employer's contribution to retirement funds, accommodation.

| Job group | Usual word for the pay |
| --- | --- |
| Managerial (top, middle, junior) | **Remuneration** |
| Supervisory | **Salary** |
| Clerical or administrative | **Salary** |
| Unskilled, semi-skilled, highly skilled | **Wages** |

The three words are often used interchangeably. Pay may go to an **individual**, a **team**, or be **fixed monthly plus a variable part** linked to performance.

**What decides the level (the compensation base):**

| Factor | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| **Company objectives** | A firm that aims to be the highest pay master |
| **Market situation** | Scarce skills (forex, treasury, risk management in banking); an internal-growth policy lessens market dependence |
| **Internal factors** | Capacity to pay, union bargaining power, attraction and retention pressure |
| **External factors** | Labour laws, Companies Act on managers' remuneration, wage concepts, surveys, arbitrations, pay commissions |
items.expanded_explanation_md: Pay for scarce skills rises because supply is short: this is why banks pay a premium for treasury and risk specialists.

self_check.prompt_text: Which word does the courseware use for the pay of unskilled and skilled workers?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Wages.

items.title: Wage concepts, strategy alignment and the Labour Codes
items.core_explanation_md:
The **Committee on Fair Wages** distinguished four wage concepts:

| Concept | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Minimum wage** | Sustains the worker |
| **Living wage** | Also meets social needs and insurance cover |
| **Fair wage** | Between the minimum and what the organisation can pay; reflects productivity, prevailing rates and the economy |
| **Need-based minimum wage** | Meets the minimum human needs of the worker |

A good compensation package covers adequacy, societal considerations, supply and demand, fairness, **equal pay for equal work** and job evaluation.

**Pay should follow strategy:**

| Strategy | Compensation system |
| --- | --- |
| **Innovative** | Reward innovation; market-based, flexible pay |
| **Cost cutting** | Focus on competitors' labour cost; more variable pay; emphasise productivity |
| **Customer focused** | Customer satisfaction incentives; value jobs and skills by customer contact |

**Legal frame (as the courseware reports it):** the Central Government amalgamated 29 labour laws into four **Labour Codes**: Wages (2019), Social Security (2020), Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions (2020) and Industrial Relations (2020). Between them they require wages at regular intervals, prohibit unauthorised deductions, define minimum wages, provide for bonus and for equal remuneration for equal jobs to men and women.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware gives no date from which the Codes apply and this course has not checked it; treat the statement as the courseware's description of the reform, and check current commencement before relying on it.

self_check.prompt_text: Which wage concept lies between the minimum wage and the capacity to pay?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The fair wage.

items.title: Job evaluation: four methods compared
items.core_explanation_md:
**Job evaluation** assesses the **relative worth of jobs** by content and complexity, to set pay rates, link pay to the job's requirements, create differentials for skill, effort and hazard, and build a pay structure. It rests on job analysis, description and specification.

| Method | How | Strength | Weakness |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Ranking** (job comparison; non-quantitative) | Compare whole jobs and rank them | Easy, cheapest | Subjective; weak for big organisations |
| **Grading** (job classification; non-quantitative) | Define grades; place jobs by matching descriptions | Less subjective; acceptable | Jobs in one grade may differ; over- or under-rating |
| **Factor comparison** (quantitative) | Rank key jobs on ~5 constant factors; build the pay as a sum | Consistent, less subjective | Most complex and expensive |
| **Point rating** (quantitative) | Score factors and sub-factors by degree x weight; add up | Most widely used; less subjective | Complex, time-consuming |

In banks, the cadre (such as General Manager as a top managerial cadre) is a form of **grading**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Jobs with similar point totals go into the same pay grade; the total is an index of the job's relative significance.

self_check.prompt_text: Which job evaluation method is the most widely used?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Point rating.

items.title: Factor comparison, point rating and compa-ratio
items.core_explanation_md:
**Factor comparison.** For a new job, decide for each factor (skill, mental requirements, physical requirements, working conditions, responsibility) which **key job** it resembles, take that key job's money amount for that factor, and add the amounts. The courseware's toolmaker: 5 + 10 + 12 + 24 + 3 = **Rs 54**.

**Point rating.** Points = **degree x weight** for each sub-factor; add them up. Receptionist: education 1 x 25 + technical skill 1 x 25 + scope of control 1 x 10 + impact 2 x 20 + problem solving 1 x 10 + task complexity 1 x 10 = **120 points**.

**Compa-ratio** = actual salary / midpoint of the pay range x 100. At 100 per cent a person is paid what a competent performer would be paid. It guides pay raises, promotion and merit pay. The five zones:

| Compa-ratio | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| 80 to 87 | New, inexperienced or unsatisfactory |
| 88 to 95 | Gaining experience, not yet fully competent |
| 96 to 103 | Fully competent |
| 104 to 111 | Consistently above the job definition |
| 112 to 120 | Universally recognised as outstanding |
items.expanded_explanation_md: The compa-ratio should ideally match performance: a high performer sitting in a low zone is under-paid, which is a retention risk.

self_check.prompt_text: Salary Rs 26,000 and range midpoint Rs 24,000. What is the compa-ratio, and which zone?
self_check.expected_takeaway: 26/24 x 100 = 108.3 per cent: the zone of consistently above the job definition (104 to 111).

items.title: Fixed, variable and mixed pay, and the shape of a pay structure
items.core_explanation_md:
| | **Fixed** | **Totally variable** | **Mixed** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Based on | Job analysis, market, collective bargaining | Performance alone (output and quality) | Fixed base **plus** performance pay |
| Good | Assured payment | Strong motivation | Combines both |
| Weak | Low motivation; high performers become mediocre | **Undue pressure**; pay can fall for reasons outside control; hard to measure in services | Needs a sound appraisal system |

Variable and mixed pay **presuppose a well-established performance appraisal system**. They are followed in most private sector organisations, including new private sector and foreign banks, where the variable part is kept confidential.

**Pay structure.** Traditional: basic pay, **dearness allowance** linked to the consumer price index, house rent allowance, city compensatory allowance, conveyance. **Flexible ("cafeteria" or "menu")**: the employee decides how much goes under each head within the total, to use permissible tax benefits. **Cost to company** also includes leave fare concession, leave encashment, medical benefits.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Choosing fixed or variable pay is a trade-off between security and motivation; service jobs, where output is hard to measure, tend to suit mixed pay.

self_check.prompt_text: Which type of pay assures a fixed amount and adds performance-linked pay on top?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Mixed compensation.

items.title: Designing a pay structure and pay in Indian banks
items.core_explanation_md:
**Ten steps** (courseware) to build a compensation structure:

1. Write job descriptions.
2. Calculate **job evaluation points** with a rationale.
3. Consider outliers.
4. Fit a **market pay line**: market base pay (Y) against points (X) for benchmark jobs.
5. Check **R squared**: is the line good enough?
6. Compute predicted base pay.
7. **Adjust** if the firm wants to lead the market (for example 3 per cent above).
8. Form **pay grades** by combining comparable jobs.
9. Set the **pay range** (minimum, maximum) for each grade.
10. Check business sense, consistency with strategy and effects on retention and recruiting.

**Pay in Indian banks (as the courseware reports; check current settlements):** salaries were first at banks' discretion; disputes went to tribunals (Sastry and Desai Awards); since **1966 the wages of workmen are settled by Bipartite Settlements** between the **Indian Banks' Association** and workmen's unions, binding on member banks for a **five-year** period. In 2005 boards got some autonomy to sanction differential pay within scales. The **IXth Bipartite Settlement (11 November 2020)** introduced a **Performance Linked Incentive (PLI)**, a number of days of basic plus dearness allowance depending on growth in operating profit, payable to banks with a net profit, from FY 2020-21.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Later settlements may have changed the details; the courseware's PLI matrix is not taught here as current. Learn the mechanism: bipartite, IBA and unions, five years, binding on members.

self_check.prompt_text: Between whom are the Bipartite Settlements made, and for how long do they run?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Between the Indian Banks' Association (for banks) and workmen's unions; at present for five years (as the courseware reports).

items.title: Why appraise, and what appraisal is
items.core_explanation_md:
A bank cannot decide whether to appraise its people: someone will judge their performance, formally or not. The choice is the **method** (Flippo, as quoted):

1. casual, unsystematic, haphazard appraisal;
2. traditional, systematic measurement of characteristics and contribution;
3. mutual goal setting: **Management by Objectives (MBO)**.

**Performance appraisal** is a systematic evaluation of the work employees perform, comparing actual performance and personality against **predefined standards** (work knowledge, work performance, attitude, leadership, team behaviour, consistency, decision-making, skills). It is also called annual review or performance evaluation.

Definitions the courseware reports: **Heyel** (evaluating performance and qualifications against job requirements for administration: placement, promotion, rewards, differential treatment) and **Monappa and Saiyadain** (a systematic evaluation by supervisors familiar with the performance, because employers want to know about it and employees want to know their position).

Uses for the organisation: review performance, take **corrective steps** (training, interventions, placement), **reward** good performance and lift it higher. A very small firm can appraise informally; as it grows, records of achievements and failures make a systematic system necessary.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The purpose of HRD is to create an atmosphere in which people give their best; measuring what they contributed is part of that.

self_check.prompt_text: What are the three choices of appraisal approach that Flippo describes?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Casual, unsystematic and haphazard appraisal; traditional systematic measurement of characteristics and contribution; mutual goal setting, that is MBO.

items.title: Objectives and uses of appraisal
items.core_explanation_md:
McGregor's three needs an appraisal can serve:

| Need | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| **Judgemental** | Salary increases, transfers, promotions |
| **Developmental** | Telling the employee how he is doing; changes in skills, attitudes, behaviour |
| **Counselling** | Feedback and understanding the causes of poor performance (often seen as part of the developmental need) |

**Specific objectives** (courseware): keep an **inventory of skills** and identify **training needs**; **motivate** high performers; **counsel** those below standard and agree an action plan; set **performance-linked increments** and give data for promotions and transfers; support individual and group development by sharing observed performance and helping people reach benchmarks.

**Uses:** rates everyone on **the same scales**, so they are comparable; informs **promotion, pay, transfer and training** decisions; shows **weaknesses** so corrective action can start; improves **supervision** (the supervisor becomes a keen observer); and, with openness and trust, improves **supervisor-employee relations**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: In practice employees often criticise the system because it falls short of one or other of these objectives, which is why design and delivery matter.

self_check.prompt_text: Which of McGregor's three needs relates to salary increases, transfers and promotions?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The judgemental need.

items.title: The six steps of the appraisal process
items.core_explanation_md:
1. **Set performance standards** in advance: clear, realistic and measurable, with line managers involved.
2. **Communicate** the standards to employees.
3. **Measure performance**: department data, personal observation, and feedback from the appraisee.
4. **Compare** performance with the benchmark and note the deviations and their reasons.
5. **Discuss** the result with the employee: stress strengths and counsel on weak points.
6. **Initiate corrective measures** and act on good performance: increments, promotions, training.

Few organisations follow all six seriously. Setting standards is genuinely hard where jobs consist of steps that cannot easily be quantified. If the stages are neglected, the tool **loses credibility** and employees **lose faith** in the system.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Notice the dependency: you cannot fairly compare performance with a benchmark that was never set or never communicated.

self_check.prompt_text: Which step comes immediately after performance is measured?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Comparing it with the established standard or benchmark and noting deviations and reasons.

items.title: Traditional appraisal methods compared
items.core_explanation_md:
Methods fall into **traditional** (rate personality traits) and **modern** (stress results and job achievement). Traditional methods:

| Method | How it works | Main drawback |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Free form essay** | Open-ended written assessment | Subjective; hard to compare; used mainly for top management |
| **Straight ranking** | Rank by merit; oldest and simplest | Hard to compare people with different behaviour traits |
| **Comparison** (paired comparison) | Compare on selected factors; pairs two at a time and count preferences | Burdensome with large numbers |
| **Grading** | Grade on features such as analytical ability: A outstanding, B very good, C average, D below average | Widely used; scale choices matter |
| **Graphic / linear rating scale** | Rate characteristics and contribution (quality and quantity, weighted) on a continuous scale | Subjective; assumes every trait equally important for all jobs |
| **Forced choice / forced distribution** | The superior must choose descriptive statements, or place employees on a set distribution | Meant to minimise bias, forces choices |
| **Group appraisal** | A group (immediate supervisor plus three or four others) rates the employee | Thorough, least bias; time consuming and may become a ritual |
items.expanded_explanation_md: Forced distribution and forced choice reduce leniency and central tendency by design, at the cost of rating some people lower than they deserve.

self_check.prompt_text: Which traditional method is the oldest and simplest?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Straight ranking.

items.title: Management by Objectives (MBO)
items.core_explanation_md:
MBO tries to **minimise external control** and raise motivation through **joint goal setting** and participation in decisions that affect the employee. It is **result-oriented**: goal achievement counts more than the method.

**Process:**

1. Set organisational goals as **measurable** targets: realistic and achievable, though challenging.
2. Set short-term performance goals **jointly** by employee and superior.
3. Hold **frequent one-to-one reviews**.
4. Share **feedback** in these meetings: goals can be altered if required, and the employee knows where he stands.

| Advantages | Disadvantages |
| --- | --- |
| Participative goal setting | Concentrates on **results, not process** |
| Higher motivation | May create **unhealthy competition** |
| An atmosphere of healthy competition | May create **conflict** in setting goals |
| An **objective** appraisal method | Sometimes **soft targets** are set to show higher achievement |
| Early identification of problems | |
| Identifies training and development needs | |
items.expanded_explanation_md: In banks, goal setting is easiest for a branch manager, whose business parameters can be expressed in numbers; it is harder for roles whose work is qualitative.

self_check.prompt_text: Name one advantage and one disadvantage of MBO.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Advantage: participative goal setting (or objective appraisal). Disadvantage: it focuses on results rather than process, or may encourage unhealthy competition or soft targets.

items.title: Human asset accounting and BARS
items.core_explanation_md:
**Human asset accounting** treats people as **human capital** and attaches a money estimate to the organisation's personnel and its goodwill. If a trained, experienced employee leaves, the human asset value falls; if a skilled new employee joins, it rises. The value is assessed periodically from two variables: the **key causal variable** (management policies, strategies, skills) and the **intervening variable** (loyalty, attitudes, motivation, interaction). It is **not** a method of appraising an individual; at best it measures the human performance of the **organisation as a whole**.

**Behaviourally Anchored Rating Scales (BARS):** describe the job through **critical incidents** of effective and ineffective performance and use them as **behavioural anchors** on a rating scale. Reasonably objective but very time consuming. Five steps:

1. Identify effective and ineffective job behaviours.
2. Convert them into performance dimensions.
3. Job experts evaluate the dimensions against the job description and incidents.
4. Experts rate how effectively or ineffectively each incident represents performance on a dimension.
5. Use a subset of the incidents as behavioural anchors for each dimension.
items.expanded_explanation_md: BARS evaluates performance in terms of critical employee behaviours, which makes ratings more specific than a plain trait scale.

self_check.prompt_text: Is human asset accounting a method for appraising an individual employee?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No: it measures the human asset value of the organisation as a whole.

items.title: 360-degree and 720-degree appraisal, and the usual bank method
items.core_explanation_md:
**360-degree appraisal:** the employee is at the **centre** and is rated by people affected by the performance and familiar with it: **seniors, peers, subordinates, suppliers, customers** and other stakeholders, plus **self-assessment**. It gives all-round feedback and, being multi-rater, is likely to **minimise human bias**.

**The usual method in banks** (the courseware's description) has three parts:

1. **Self-appraisal** by the appraisee (a chance to assess oneself dispassionately).
2. **Appraisal by the reporting authority**, usually with an appraisal interview and goal setting.
3. **Review by the superior of the reporting authority**, to reduce subjectivity or bias.

It may combine descriptive and scale ratings against set goals. In the private sector appraisal is taken more seriously because financial rewards are linked to it.

**720-degree appraisal** (courseware): a 360-degree appraisal **done twice**. After the first, targets are set; after a short interval, feedback and guidance are given and a **second 360-degree** appraisal is compared with the first, giving a **pre- and post-round of feedback**. It is a double check that guides the employee to achieve targets.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The 720-degree label is the courseware's way of describing a repeated 360-degree cycle with feedback in between; it is not a different set of raters.

self_check.prompt_text: Who may rate an employee in a 360-degree appraisal?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Seniors, colleagues, subordinates, suppliers, customers and other stakeholders, and the employee through self-assessment.

items.title: Potential appraisal and the confidential report
items.core_explanation_md:
Appraisal looks at **present performance** against job benchmarks. It says little about **potential** for a higher job, because the higher job may need quite different attributes: an excellent salesman need not be an excellent sales manager. Promoting on appraisal alone is a **judgemental prediction**. So **potential appraisal** is used **with** performance appraisal (for example through a Potential Appraisal Report), and the **assessment centre** method helps.

| Confidential report (old) | Open appraisal (new) |
| --- | --- |
| Annual report sent to head office | Employee involved in goal setting |
| Surrounded by mystery; no transparency | Self-appraisal and regular feedback |
| **No feedback** to the employee | Joint corrective steps |
| Gives the superior power over the career | Developmental in intent |

The courseware concludes that the old system's disadvantages outweigh its positive features and that organisations are moving to open, transparent systems.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The classic mistake: promote the best salesman to sales manager because of top appraisal scores, and lose a good salesman while gaining a poor manager.

self_check.prompt_text: Why is performance appraisal alone not enough to decide a promotion?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It shows present performance, not whether the person has the attributes and skills for the higher post; potential appraisal is needed too.

items.title: Appraisal errors and the marks of a good system
items.core_explanation_md:
**Errors the courseware defines:**

| Error | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Halo effect** | One trait influences the whole assessment, so the person is rated consistently high or low |
| **Leniency / strictness** | The superior's own tendency to rate everyone high or low |
| **Central tendency** | Giving everyone **average** ratings without evaluating each aspect carefully |
| **Comparing with oneself** | People who resemble the rater are rated high |

The courseware also names thirteen common errors in a list: halo, horn, central tendency, strict rating, lenient rating, status, spillover, initial impression, latest impression (recency), same as me, different from me, performance factor order, sympathy. (The horn effect is the opposite of the halo: one weak trait drags the whole rating down. Recency means the latest events weigh too much. The others are named without definition in the courseware.)

**A good system is:** objective, transparent, gives timely feedback, allows self-appraisal, identifies potential and needs, discriminates between high and low performers, is seen as enhancing potential, and finds the impediments to low performance.

**Merits:** shows concern for performance and builds openness and trust; gives feedback so corrective steps are taken in time; raises motivation if implemented properly.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Appraising is an art: avoid personal liking or disliking, and learn to distinguish good from not-so-good performers.

self_check.prompt_text: A manager rates an employee high on every trait because of one outstanding skill. Which error?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The halo effect.

items.title: Performance review, preparation and the appraisal interview
items.core_explanation_md:
**Performance review** is the superior's appraisal of the employee for a period. Reviewing at **frequent intervals**, giving instant feedback and correcting course is part of **performance management**, which runs through the year, not only at year-end.

**Preparation by the superior:** gather the previous year's **goals**, reports and statements, **mid-term reviews** and an idea of how the organisation or industry is doing; form only a **preliminary** impression and **do not treat it as final**: hold an appraisal interview to hear the appraisee's view.

**The appraisal interview** gets information and clarification, identifies **development** areas with training measures, agrees **annual targets** and gives feedback on strengths, weaknesses and expectations.

**Precautions:**

- Venue: the **appraisee's place or a neutral place**, not the appraiser's room.
- Timing: free from disturbance.
- **Do not get personal**: compare performance with a standard, not with other people.
- **Value the employee's opinion**; encourage him to talk.
- **Do not tiptoe around**: say clearly what is right and wrong, and how to improve.
- Be a **listener** and an encouraging senior colleague; avoid judgemental remarks.
- Give feedback at the appropriate time.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A reviewer who fills in the form from the file alone, without an interview, risks missing the appraisee's side of events.

self_check.prompt_text: Where should the appraisal interview preferably take place?
self_check.expected_takeaway: At the appraisee's place or a neutral place, not the appraiser's own room.

items.title: Giving feedback: do's and don'ts
items.core_explanation_md:
Feedback should be **objective**, help the employee reach the right level next time, be **suggestive rather than judgemental**, focus on **training and development needs**, take a **problem-solving, not fault-finding** approach, and keep sight of its aim: to **improve performance**, not to criticise.

| Do | Don't |
| --- | --- |
| Let the employee do **most of the talking** | Hold the meeting when you cannot give **undisturbed time** |
| Encourage him to describe **success and failure** | Ramble without a **clear message** |
| Create an atmosphere where he **opens up** | Use **highly charged** language, positive or negative |
| Use **clear and actionable** language | Allow **disturbance** once it starts |
| Ask **relevant questions** | Take a **judgemental** role without reasons or evidence |
| **Praise** achievements | **Criticise** him for failures or for not appreciating achievements |
| Say **honestly** where he could have done better | |
| Ask **what help** he expects and give it | |
items.expanded_explanation_md: Trust is reinforced when a sincere attempt is made to help: the interview is a development tool, not an examination.

self_check.prompt_text: Name two "don'ts" of an appraisal feedback meeting.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Any two of: meeting without undisturbed time, rambling, charged language, allowing disturbance, a judgemental stance without evidence, criticising for failures.

items.title: Counselling a low performer
items.core_explanation_md:
**Counselling** means advising the employee about performance. It comes **after** the appraisal interview and feedback, when the superior concludes that performance is **far below** expected and needs **immediate, major** corrective action. It is defined as using a set of skills to help another person take **responsibility** for and manage his own work-related decisions.

**Three stages:**

1. **Recognise** the problem or issue.
2. **Help the employee realise** the problem.
3. **Manage** the problem.

**Skills:**

- State the **purpose** at the start.
- Be **specific and descriptive**, about performance, not about the person.
- **Criticise behaviour, not the person**, and do so without crippling.
- Offer **workable solutions** and act where the appraisee can start to improve.
- Avoid **prejudice**; weigh the employee's version objectively.
- **Successful counselling is effective listening.**

Clear key result areas lower the chance of falling short through **ambiguity**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: It is a human tendency to react negatively to feedback and counselling, so the counsellor should expect it and not take it personally.

self_check.prompt_text: What are the three stages of the counselling process?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Recognising the problem, helping the employee realise it, and managing it.

items.title: Managing average performers
items.core_explanation_md:
Every organisation has many **average performers**. They lend stability through loyalty, but their motivation is often low.

**What the courseware recommends:** try **rotation**, **transfer**, classroom training and **skill upgradation**. If these fail, handle with care and **humanely**; the courseware notes that organisations in the Indian culture rarely remove people just for being average, although mergers and competition put them at risk. It observes that in Indian banks many average performers stay on moderate performance because of **job security** and an **ineffective reward and punishment system**.

**Six strategies:**

| Strategy | Idea |
| --- | --- |
| Understand how they define success | Outside interests and what sparks enthusiasm |
| Find out how they think they are doing | They may not know they are only average |
| Assess skills; **change the job role** | Lateral moves can spur them |
| **Show appreciation** | Praise in public, criticise in private |
| **Set high expectations** | Move the bar a little each time |
| **Motivate through counselling** | Motivation is an emotional need; counselling removes hurdles |
items.expanded_explanation_md: If the cause of average performance is attitude, counselling can address it; if it is a skill gap, training or a role change fits better.

self_check.prompt_text: Which rule does the courseware attach to showing appreciation to average performers?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Appreciate in public and criticise (or depreciate) in private.

items.title: Competency: knowledge, skill and attitude
items.core_explanation_md:
A **competency** is a **knowledge, skill or attitude (KSA)**; in the courseware's words, a set of demonstrable characteristics and skills that enable and improve the efficiency of performing a job.

Definitions it quotes:

| Source | Core idea |
| --- | --- |
| Spencer and Spencer (1993) | An **underlying characteristic** related to effective or superior performance |
| Lucia and Lepsinger (1999) | A **cluster** of knowledge, skills and attitude that affects a major part of the job, **correlates with performance**, can be **measured against standards** and **improved by training** |
| Parry (1996) | Interrelated KSA of a job role that associates with performance, can be measured and **reinforced through training** |

Two things to separate: **competency** is **what an employee can do** (ability); **performance** is **what the employee actually does**. That is why competency links to performance planning: it tells you what to develop and what to expect.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A person can have the competency and still perform poorly if motivation, resources or role clarity are missing.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the difference between competency and performance?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Competency is what an employee can do or has the ability to do; performance is what the employee actually does.

items.title: Competence versus competency
items.core_explanation_md:
The courseware, summarising a literature review, separates two approaches:

| | **Competence** (task-oriented, functional) | **Competency** (person-oriented, behavioural) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Focus | **Results or outcomes** | The person's **behaviour and attitudes** |
| Describes | Work and tasks, job outputs | **Traits and attributes** of the person |
| Made of | Skills, knowledge and attitudes needed for a **particular job** | Underlying attributes for **superior** performance |
| Transferable? | **Not** easily: specific to a job | **Easily** transferable between people |
| Assessed by | Performance on a particular job | Behaviours and attitudes |
| Orientation | Task | People |

They complement each other: **being competent** means achieving what the job demands; **having competencies** means showing the essential behaviours for effective work performance.
items.expanded_explanation_md: In everyday use the two words are often mixed up; exam questions usually test the contrast between result-focused competence and behaviour-focused competency.

self_check.expected_takeaway: Competency.
