items.title: Types, descriptions, levels and the dictionary of competencies
items.core_explanation_md:
**Types:** **technical competency** (hard skills: processes and procedures that turn inputs into outputs; easier to identify and describe) and **behavioural competency** (soft skills: listening, initiative, problem solving, interpersonal skills, leadership; harder to observe). Most tasks need both.

**Competency description:** the list of competencies needed for each position. For each competency, give a **definition** and **behaviour indicators** that observers can look for. Example: adaptability, defined as changing style or approach when needed, shown by adapting to change quickly, suggesting ways to make changes work, and being willing to learn new methods. Prepare it **after** a systematic job analysis.

**Competency levels:** the same competency is needed at different proficiency.

| Level | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **At entry** | The standard expected of a new entrant, who may still be learning |
| **Fully effective** | What experienced employees perform at the expected standard |
| **Stretch / mastery** | Employees who have mastered the role; others seek their advice |

**Competency dictionary (catalogue):** all general competencies with definitions covering all job families, including those **core to all jobs** (teamwork, adaptability, communication) and those for **specific functions** (IT skills, financial administration).
items.expanded_explanation_md: The behaviour indicators are what make a soft skill observable and assessable.

self_check.prompt_text: Which competency level describes employees who have mastered the role and are sought out for advice?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The stretch or mastery level.

items.title: Competency mapping: what it is, where it applies, how it is done
items.core_explanation_md:
**Competency mapping** is the systematic process of identifying the **knowledge, skill, attitude and behaviour** needed for success in a given job, and using it for **job evaluation, recruitment, training and development, performance management, succession planning, appraisal and identifying training needs**. It also assesses strengths and weaknesses of a person or organisation in areas such as teamwork, leadership and decision making.

**Five layers:**

| Layer | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| **Company** | Values and core competencies |
| **Function** | Generic competencies for everyone in a function (HR, finance) |
| **Department** | More specific than the function level |
| **Job** | Linked to generic job roles |
| **Position** | Very specific, for the unique position (product knowledge, domain experience) |

**Why it matters:** for the **individual** it spells out the performance level required; for the **organisation** it is the basis of performance management and keeps a list of competencies for every role for recruitment, promotion, placement and training.

**Two approaches:**

| Approach | Steps |
| --- | --- |
| **Post performance-based** (uses BEI: the best predictor of future behaviour is past behaviour) | Identify the position; identify outstanding, below-average and average performers; interview them with BEI; list competencies **needed** (from outstanding) and **not needed** (from below-average or average) |
| **Job-focused** (position information questionnaire) | Understand the purpose of the job; incumbents list job tasks; map each accountability or major task to the job |
items.expanded_explanation_md: The post performance-based approach starts with people (the best performers) and works back to competencies; the job-focused approach starts with the job and works forward.

items.title: What an assessment centre is and where it came from
items.core_explanation_md:
An **assessment centre** is a **variety of testing techniques**, run under **standardised conditions**, that lets candidates demonstrate the skills and abilities most essential for success in a given job. It is a **method**, not a place: candidates take part in **exercises that resemble actual work situations** while **several assessors** observe.

**Purposes:** measure **potential** for a higher managerial position; assess **training and development needs**; select **campus recruits or fresh students**; identify **future leaders**.

**It generally measures:** interpersonal skills, leadership, organising and planning, problem solving, stress tolerance, motivational orientation and communication.

**Limits:** time consuming; good performers may dislike being examined; needs **highly trained observers**; the objectives must be clearly stated. It can be used with appraisal for career progression decisions, and today mainly for **supervisory and management** positions.

**Origins** (courseware): work simulations used by the OSS in the Second World War to identify potential agents; earlier German military and British War Office Selection Board practice; research at AT and T and, from 1958, the Bell System, which became the classical model.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The history is the courseware's account; the part worth remembering for use is that the method judges behaviour in simulations, not paper credentials.

self_check.prompt_text: Name two purposes of an assessment centre.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Any two of: measuring potential for a higher managerial position, assessing training and development needs, selecting campus recruits, identifying future leaders.

items.title: Seven essential elements of an assessment centre
items.core_explanation_md:
For a technique to count as an assessment centre, the courseware (citing a 1979 task force) says seven conditions must be met:

| # | Element | What it means |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | **Multiple assessment techniques** | At least one must be a **simulation** (in-basket, group discussion, fact finding) |
| 2 | **Multiple assessors** | About **3 to 4 participants per assessor**; each person rated by more than one assessor; assessors trained and briefed |
| 3 | **Pooling of information** | Judgements rest on **pooled** information; wide variations resolved by discussion; critical incidents recorded |
| 4 | **Time of observation** | Overall assessment made **separately** from observation, after compiling all the data |
| 5 | **Design of exercises** | Reliable and valid; off-the-shelf tools validated and customised |
| 6 | **Dimensions evaluated** | Determined by **thorough analysis of relevant job behaviours** |
| 7 | **Tools and exercises** | Designed to give the information used to evaluate those dimensions |

items.title: Planning and running an assessment centre, and the assessors
items.core_explanation_md:
**Planning (steps):**

1. State the **purpose** (recruitment, promotion, placement, training or incentive).
2. Identify the **position** and the **target group**.
3. List the **critical competencies** to be assessed, based on purpose and position (the **most critical** step).
4. Choose the **tools and exercises**; bought or made tools must be tested and **validated**.
5. Finalise the **criteria and procedure** for assessment.
6. **Train the assessors**, even experienced ones.
7. Put all instructions in an **assessment manual**.

**Conducting:** make candidates comfortable, **brief** them on the purpose, give **clear instructions** for each activity, evaluate against the criteria, arrange **feedback and counselling** if part of the objective, and make the reports available to management.

**Assessors:** trained **external experts**, or trained line managers. HR officials usually act as **facilitators** and **avoid** assessing, to avoid role conflict. Assessors must know the job, share an understanding of purpose and dimensions, and be able to **observe behaviour, record accurately, report clearly, suspend judgment and give constructive feedback**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Decisions after an assessment centre can shape careers, so the tools, the criteria and the assessors' training must be sound before the day.

self_check.expected_takeaway: Preparing the list of critical competencies to be assessed, based on the purpose and position.

items.title: The behavioural event interview (BEI)
items.core_explanation_md:
**BEI** is a **structured interview** that collects information about **past behaviour**, on the premise that the **best predictor of future behaviour is past behaviour**. It asks open-ended questions in which the interviewee describes in detail past experiences that show how he performed. It is the heart of the **job competency assessment** process and its data are the richest source of competency data. **Principle:** what people *say* about their motives and skills is not credible; only what they *actually did* is, so the interviewer gets people to describe how they **behaved in specific incidents**.

**Five steps:**

1. **Introduction and explanation**: build trust and goodwill; put the interviewee at ease.
2. **Job description**: most important tasks, responsibilities, desired output.
3. **Behavioural events** (the bulk of the time): complete stories of critical incidents, gathered with the **STAR** technique: **S**ituation, **T**ask, **A**ction, **R**esult.
4. **Characteristics needed to do the job**: knowledge, skills, abilities the interviewee thinks are needed.
5. **Conclusion and summary**: thank, ask what may have been overlooked, and summarise in a set format.

**Limitations:** it depends on the **respondent's recall** (only what is remembered or chosen is given, possibly self-serving); it gets at actions, thoughts and feelings but not the **knowledge** behind them, so it is a weak source of **specialised knowledge**; and interpretation depends on the **interviewer**, who may not be an expert, leaving room for guesswork.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The Potential Appraisal Report in the courseware's annexure rates ten attributes: functional knowledge, managing skills, initiative, decision making, flexibility, self-managing skills, communication, achievement orientation, entrepreneurial skills and innovation.

self_check.prompt_text: What does STAR stand for in a BEI?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Situation, Task, Action and Result.

items.title: What conflict is, and why banks must manage it
items.core_explanation_md:
**Conflict** is a sharp disagreement or opposition of interests or ideas. It arises whenever people have different **values, opinions, needs and interests** and cannot find a middle way. The courseware defines it as a clash between individuals arising from differences in **thought process, attitudes, understanding, interests, requirements and even perceptions** (McLean: the struggle associated with the perception of opposing goals, desires, demands, wants or needs).

It shows as insults, non-cooperation, bullying and anger. Causes run from **personality clashes** to **misunderstood communication** to **organisational mismanagement**. Costs: disrupted work, lower productivity, absenteeism, turnover, even termination; stress can be both a cause and an effect.

**Banks and conflict:** because banks are **custodians of public money**, the courseware says conflict management should be assigned to executives with the right skill and strategy, and an executive's handling of conflict should appear among **key performance indicators** in appraisal. The employer's main tool is a **culture of fairness, trust and mutual respect**.

Key point: conflict is a **normal** part of any relationship. The aim is not to fear or avoid it but to **resolve it in a healthy way**; how it is handled can strengthen or destroy a relationship.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Respectfully handled, conflict clears up doubts and misconceptions and can strengthen the bond between people; early identification makes resolution easier.

self_check.prompt_text: Why does the courseware say conflict handling should be a key performance indicator for executives in banks?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Conflict is more harmful in service organisations such as banks, which hold public money, so handling it well should be assessed in appraisal.

items.title: Conflict at the workplace: its characteristics
items.core_explanation_md:
At work, conflict **lowers morale**, raises **absenteeism** and cuts productivity. People usually respond by **flight or fight**, and either way they feel dissatisfied because nothing is resolved. (The courseware says managers spend at least a quarter of their time on conflicts; this figure is not verified.)

Hocker and Wilmot's principles (as reported): conflict is **universal**, linked to **incompatible goals, scarce resources and interference**, is **not a sign of a poor relationship**, **cannot be avoided**, **cannot always be resolved** and is **not always bad**.

| Characteristic | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Involves **opposition** | It exists only where there is disagreement between parties |
| More than disagreement | One or both parties perceive a **threat**, real or imagined |
| Rests on **perception** | Responses reflect experience, culture, values and beliefs, not an objective review of facts |
| **Inevitable** | Diverse people with different views and work styles |
| **An opportunity for growth** | Once resolved it builds trust and confidence in the relationship |

It can also be seen as a **process**: it begins when one party perceives the other as opposing its interests and ends with competing, collaborating, compromising or avoiding.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Because response rests on perception, two people can see the same event as a minor difference or as a serious threat.

self_check.expected_takeaway: One or both parties perceive a threat, real or imagined.

items.title: Task, relationship and value conflict
items.core_explanation_md:
| | **Task** | **Relationship** | **Value** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| About | Work details and goals: duties, assignments, resources, procedures, policy, interpretation of facts | **Personal** issues, not work: personality, style, taste, working style | Fundamental differences in **life experience, culture, identity, values and beliefs** (politics, religion, ethics, norms) |
| Difficulty | **Easiest** to solve | Often the **hardest** to defuse; can be long lasting; hurts commitment, productivity, trust | Heightens **defensiveness, distrust, alienation** |
| Resolve by | **Collaborative problem solving**; solutions found jointly, not imposed; active listening | **Listening** to the other's point of view; **empathy** and interest | Move from **demonising** towards **mutual understanding and respect through dialogue**; understanding the other's view needs no sympathy, only accurate description |

Task conflict can even be **useful**: it prompts good discussion and can streamline productivity channels.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A task conflict that is left alone can drift into a relationship conflict when people start to blame each other, which is why it is best handled early.

items.title: Conflict within an individual: goal, frustration and role conflict
items.core_explanation_md:
**Intra-individual** (intra-personal) conflict arises when a person's objectives differ from the company's vision, from frustration, from roles that demand equal attention, and from goals with positive and negative features.

**Goal conflict** (attaining one goal excludes another):

| Form | Choice between |
| --- | --- |
| **Approach-approach** | Two or more **positive**, mutually exclusive goals |
| **Approach-avoidance** | A single goal with **both** positive and negative features |
| **Avoidance-avoidance** | Two or more **negative**, mutually exclusive goals |

**Frustration:** a motivated drive is **blocked** before the goal is reached, by external barriers (non-social such as power failures or transport breakdown; or social) or internal ones (limitations, lack of skill; more lasting). Four defences: **aggression** (attack the barrier), **withdrawal** (back away), **fixation** (keep trying to break through), **compromise** (find a new goal).

**Role conflict:** playing several roles at once with too little time or resources.

| Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Person-role** | Between the person's personality and the role's expectations |
| **Intra-role** | Contradictory expectations about how **one** role should be played |
| **Inter-role** | Differing requirements of **two or more** roles played at the same time |
items.expanded_explanation_md: An officer offered a promotion that means moving away from family faces an approach-avoidance conflict: the post attracts, the relocation repels.

items.title: Why conflicts arise at work
items.core_explanation_md:
Behind most conflicts lie **misunderstandings, poor communication and disagreement**, often with a deep personal need underneath (to feel safe, respected or valued). **Ego** turns conflict into **win-lose**, and the "losers" resist and retaliate.

| Cause | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| **Resistance to change** | Fear of the unknown; for example early computerisation in banks |
| **Work habits** | For example being over-diligent and rechecking files |
| **Poor communication** | Different styles; silence drives conflict underground |
| **Personality clashes** | Differences in attitudes, values, goals and perceptions |
| **Poor performance** | Not addressed; training needed |
| **Poor supervision** | Incompetent or biased supervisors who hear one side |
| **Economics** | Insufficient remuneration |
| **Stress; weak leadership; poor structure; no teamwork** | Working conditions, less qualified leader, unclear organisation |
| **Status; power struggle** | A "wrong" person promoted; everyone wants to lead |
| **Incongruence** | Required to do something against one's liking or interests |
| **Lack of transparency** | At management level |
items.expanded_explanation_md: Management should guide employees through change by explaining the reasons behind it and what it means for them.

items.title: The five phases of a conflict
items.core_explanation_md:
| Phase | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| 1. **Prelude** | The background factors: lack of coordination, differing interests, cultural, religious or educational dissimilarity |
| 2. **Triggering** | An **event** sets the conflict off (no conflict arises on its own) |
| 3. **Initiation** | The conflict has begun: heated arguments, abuse, verbal disagreement are warning signs |
| 4. **Differentiation** | The parties **voice their differences** and the reasons are raised |
| 5. **Resolution** | Options are explored; people reconcile and compromise to some extent |

The earlier a conflict is spotted, the easier to resolve. The courseware's advice: talk and discuss rather than continue the fight.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Spotting the prelude factors (such as poor coordination between two teams) allows a manager to act before a trigger occurs.

items.title: Resolving conflict: listen, talk, resolve; and the Thomas-Kilmann styles
items.core_explanation_md:
Resolved in a healthy way, conflict **builds understanding and trust**; constructively resolved, it can turn a destructive situation into **growth, creativity and better performance**. The courseware's easiest formula: **Listen, Talk, Resolve**. The Helpguide.org team adds: listen for what is **felt** as well as said; make **resolution** the priority rather than winning or being right; **focus on the present**; **pick your battles**; **be willing to forgive**; **agree to disagree**.

**Thomas-Kilmann model:** five approaches on two dimensions, **assertiveness** (satisfying your own needs) and **cooperativeness** (satisfying the other's):

| Approach | Meaning | Assertiveness / cooperativeness |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Avoiding** | Ignore or sidestep the conflict | Low / low |
| **Accommodating** | Satisfy the other's concerns at your own expense | Low / high |
| **Competing** | Satisfy your desires at the others' expense | High / low |
| **Collaborating** | A solution that fully satisfies all parties | High / high |
| **Compromising** | A partial satisfaction for all | Medium / medium |
items.expanded_explanation_md: Collaborating takes the most time but gives the best result when the issue matters to both sides; avoiding is sensible only when the issue is trivial or the timing is wrong.

self_check.prompt_text: Which Thomas-Kilmann approach tries to satisfy the manager's own desires at the expense of the other parties?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Competing.

items.title: The five-step resolution process for a manager
items.core_explanation_md:
1. **Find the source**: ask questions ("Why are you so upset?", "How did this begin?") and give **both** parties a chance to tell their story; acknowledge what you hear.
2. **Look beyond**: the cause is often the person's point of view, or a minor old issue grown with stress; probe beyond the triggering incident.
3. **Take suggestions** from each party on how things could change; steer away from **finger-pointing** and towards solutions.
4. **Identify acceptable solutions**: point out the merits of ideas from each perspective and for the organisation, and suggest the need for **cooperation**.
5. **Final agreement**: get both parties to accept one alternative; aim for a **mutually accepted** agreement, sometimes written with actions and timeframes.

It works between **groups** as well as individuals.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Impartiality matters: listening to both sides shows the manager is not taking one.

self_check.prompt_text: What should a manager do first when two staff are in conflict?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Find out the source of the conflict by asking questions and giving both parties a chance to tell their side.

items.title: Managing conflict: styles and what a manager can do
items.core_explanation_md:
In most conflicts **neither party is simply right**: different perceptions collide. Conflict management aims at **minimising affective conflict** (about feelings and relationships) at all levels and keeping a **moderate amount of substantive conflict** (about the work).

**Styles** the courseware names:

| Author | Styles |
| --- | --- |
| **Follett** | Domination, compromise, **integration** (open exchange to find a solution acceptable to both) |
| **Blake and Mouton** | Forcing, withdrawing, smoothing, compromising, problem solving |

No style fits every situation.

**Do not** avoid a conflict hoping it will go away. Ask participants to describe the **specific actions** they want from the other party; consider a **third party** (a non-direct superior with access to the situation).

**Preventive actions:** regular review of **job descriptions**; **rapport** with subordinates; regular **reports**; **training** in communication, conflict management and delegation; **mutual development of procedures**; regular **meetings**; a **suggestion box**.

**Policy elements:** acknowledge the problem; let people express feelings; define the problem; find the **underlying need**; find **common ground**, however small; find solutions that satisfy needs (silence may be passive resistance); **follow up**; and if unresolved, use an **outside facilitator** or treat it as a **performance issue**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Looking for needs rather than solutions is described as a powerful tool: once you know why each party wants what it wants, there is more room to find a solution both can live with.

self_check.prompt_text: What should a manager do if an unresolved conflict disrupts a department?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Bring in an outside facilitator or expert, or treat it as a performance issue for coaching, appraisal or disciplinary action.

items.title: Negotiation for resolving conflicts
items.core_explanation_md:
**Negotiation** is communication aimed at an agreement that addresses the concerns of parties who want **different outcomes**. It helps when two people share an objective but disagree on how to reach it. **Conflict resolution** means meeting at least some of each side's needs and interests; it may need both **power-based** and **interest-based** approaches, but force and intimidation **add to the grounds for future conflict**.

Common situations: **conflicts between employees** (a main duty of supervisors), **compensation**, **disputes with the public** (a dissatisfied customer) and **disagreements in collaboration** (limited resources, approach to a client).

**Eleven skills and strategies:**

1. Effective communication (polite, specific, no shouting)
2. Listening (repeat back, reaffirm, eye contact)
3. Discussion (open, invite all involved)
4. Patience
5. Impartiality
6. Never criticise (guide the other person)
7. Positive attitude (no blame game, no backbiting)
8. **Address the conflict, not the person**
9. **Find shared interests**
10. **Set an objective**
11. Know your **BATNA** (Best Alternative to a Negotiated Agreement), and the other side's

**Golden rule:** aim for **win-win**. Win-lose and lose-lose outcomes do not resolve the conflict.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Knowing your BATNA tells you when to walk away: you will not accept a deal worse than your best alternative.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the "golden rule" of negotiation in the courseware?
self_check.expected_takeaway: To attain a win-win situation in which both parties feel they achieved something worthwhile.

items.title: IT and HRM: a two-way dependence
items.core_explanation_md:
In the information age, success belongs to those who can **access data, turn it into information, and draw knowledge and wisdom from it**. **Information technology** is the **merging of communication and computer technology**.

HRM carries a **dual responsibility**:

| Responsibility | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| **Change mind-sets** | As part of strategic HRM, bring about the transformation of beliefs and attitudes that new technology demands across the organisation |
| **Use IT in HR itself** | For day-to-day and policy decisions, through a comprehensive **HRIS** |

The two depend on each other: IT projects have **suffered** where HR handling was poor, and HR initiatives **could not be implemented** effectively without technology change.

Likely effects of technology, as the courseware sees them: work may move away from a single office (multiple workstations, mainly at homes); organisations become **flatter and leaner**; workers become knowledge workers, more individualistic. IT **has not reduced the importance of HR**: quantity of staff needed may fall, but pressure on **quality** rises. It also **releases excess staff** and makes some branches surplus, to be managed through HR strategy including an **exit policy**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware observes that in Indian banks technology has mainly been applied to core banking operations and not yet to the desired extent in HR management and development.

self_check.prompt_text: What are the two responsibilities of HRM in the face of information technology?
self_check.expected_takeaway: To bring about the change in mind-set that technology demands, and to apply IT in the HR function itself, through a human resource information system.

items.title: Why HR needs IT: the case for a shared database
items.core_explanation_md:
**ICT** (information and communication technologies) is the umbrella for technologies combined with the internet, social media, mobile communication and computers. Its effect on HR is mainly in **how information is collected, stored, used and disseminated**. Benefits: lower administrative expense, higher productivity, better decisions and customer service.

The courseware's observations on why HR needs a database:

1. Many functionaries inside and outside HR use the **same basic employee information**: a **shared database** avoids duplicate collection.
2. The employee record is **broad-based** (experience, training, competencies, skills, performance, expectations, as well as pay, leave and increments), so it is large.
3. Different people can **update parts** from different locations.
4. Decisions should be **embedded in the data** for objectivity and consistency (for example choosing the right person for a training).
5. **Policy review** needs analysis of whether practices work and whether there is **bias**.
6. **Statutory requirements** call for such a database.

The answer: a computer-based **HRIS**, with security measures for **confidentiality, integrity, availability and access control**. The aim of automation is to help managers work faster and focus on managing the workforce.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The HR department itself has to become a learning set-up, with self-introspection and openness to new systems, to lead the organisation in this change.

self_check.prompt_text: Name the four security properties the courseware says an HRIS must protect.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Confidentiality, integrity, availability and access control.

items.title: HR data and database management
items.core_explanation_md:
HR teams sit on a **"data gold mine"** (Bernard Marr, as quoted): recruitment, career progression, training, absenteeism, productivity, development review, competency and satisfaction data. Used well it improves decisions, makes employees happier and optimises processes.

**What an HR database holds:** employee details, manager information, holiday and absenteeism data, rotas, clock-in and clock-out times, timesheets and expenses. **Secure** databases let each user see **only the data that applies to their role**; employee self-service lets staff update their own information and so reduces the HR team's burden.

**Maintaining the database:**

| Matter | Practice |
| --- | --- |
| **Static data** | Entered **once** in a master file (name, date of birth, date of joining) |
| **Dynamic data** | Upgraded often (placement, training) |
| **Partial access** | Several people can work on different sections at once |
| **Confidentiality** | Parts such as appraisal data restricted by permissions in software |
| **Analysis** | By age, gender, region, level; helps placement, career planning and reviews |

Tools mentioned: **DSS, expert systems, SQL, AI, data warehouse and data mining**. The database is kept "active" so it prompts the decision-maker to use it.
items.expanded_explanation_md: HR people need not be data scientists, but they should understand how data is stored, retrieved, merged, analysed and reported so they can be effective users of data.

items.title: HRIS: what it is, why it is needed and what it holds
items.core_explanation_md:
A **Human Resource Information System (HRIS)** is a systematic way of storing data on each employee to aid **planning, decision making and the submission of returns and reports** to external agencies. It is integrated systems to **gather, store and analyse** information on an organisation's human resources, merging HRM with information technology.

**Why needed:** decisions on **posting, training, compensation, rotation, promotion and appraisal** depend on each person's competence and background. Computer-based data makes such decisions **objective**, and when criteria are known they are perceived as **unbiased and fair**.

**Advantages (courseware):** realistic HR policies and schemes; timely, accurate decisions on promotion, transfer, provident fund, retirement, gratuity, leave travel and leave encashment; easy **returns to statutory agencies**; data converted into **information and knowledge**; more accurate **real-time reports**; re-engineered HR processes; faster HR service to employees; a **single integrated database** that connects units. By automating routine tasks and passing some to line managers, HRIS frees HR for **leadership development and talent management**.

**Typical contents:** bio-data, qualifications, organisational history (placements, promotions, training, competencies, appraisal), salary and allowances. **Components** in the courseware's figure: employee portal at the centre; benefit management; demographics and compensation; time and attendance; applicant tracking; performance management; workflows and communication; reporting.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware names lack of management commitment as the major barrier to HRIS and high cost as the major limitation, but says the benefits are greater.

self_check.prompt_text: Why can an HRIS make HR decisions seem fairer?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Because decisions rest on computer-based data and known criteria, so they are objective and perceived as unbiased.

items.title: HRMS versus HRIS: what each does and when a company needs one
items.core_explanation_md:
A **Human Resource Management System (HRMS)** combines systems and processes that connect HR and IT through **HR software**. It can handle **recruitment and onboarding, payroll, leave approval, attendance, performance reviews, benefits, learning management, succession planning, employee self-service, scheduling and analytics**. Automating repetitive tasks lets HR focus on **culture and retention**.

| | **HRIS** | **HRMS** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mainly tracks | **Numerical** data and employee information | All of that **plus non-quantitative** information |
| Core tasks | Reporting, training, recruiting, compensation, benefits administration, data tracking, workflow automation, accounting | Also onboarding, employee satisfaction, job performance, analytics, profitability |
| Relation | A **type of** HRMS | The more robust system (IT and HR) |

The courseware notes the terms are often used as synonyms and that rebranding has blurred the difference.

**Benefits:** employees do some clerical tasks themselves; **built-in security**, with authentication limiting access; customisable workflow; automated reminders; less bureaucracy.

**Signs a company needs one:** HR is overworked; money lost on HR data or **compliance errors**; offices spread across locations without a unifying platform; no way to monitor **turnover** or control unengaged staff; employees have no opportunity to manage their own appraisal.

**Choosing one:** understand features and compliance needs; compare vendors; research your needs; check user experience; assess the vendor as a whole.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Systems are not "one size fits all": each organisation differs, so the choice must follow the organisation's own needs.

self_check.prompt_text: Name two signs that a company could benefit from an HRMS.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Any two of: an overworked HR department; losses from HR data or compliance errors; offices without a unifying platform; no way to monitor turnover; employees unable to manage their own appraisal.

items.title: e-HRM: three tiers and five activities
items.core_explanation_md:
**e-HRM** is the planning, implementation and application of IT to **network and support** HR activities: the integration of all HR systems using **web technologies**. In essence it **devolves HR operations to managers and employees**, typically through an **intranet** or other web channels. Strohmeier (2007): IT for networking and supporting at least two actors in their shared performance of HR activities.

**Three tiers:**

| Tier | Concern | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Operational** | Administrative functions | Payroll, personal data |
| **Relational** (social) | Supporting business processes and relationships | Training, recruitment, selection; sharing data with managers; virtual relationships |
| **Transformational** | Strategic HR | Knowledge management, strategic re-orientation |

**Five main online activities:**

| Activity | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| **e-Recruitment** | Hiring through the company website or recruitment websites |
| **e-Selection** | Online selection that follows the procedure at lower cost and time |
| **e-Performance management** | Web-based evaluation: monitoring tools, reviews and feedback through a portal |
| **e-Learning** | Training through the internet or intranet, irrespective of location |
| **e-Compensation** | Online gathering, storing, analysing and distributing compensation data, available at any time |

Result: records of employees in different locations are stored together and candidates can be hired from anywhere.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Because e-HRM devolves tasks to employees and managers, it lets HR departments act as strategic partners with better efficiency and cost effectiveness.

self_check.prompt_text: Which tier of e-HRM covers payroll and personal data?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Operational e-HRM.

items.title: HR research: four approaches and what it studies
items.core_explanation_md:
**HR research** evaluates HR practices and performance, using a systematic, scientific process of collecting information, analysing it and drawing conclusions for decisions. It can be **academic** (adds to the body of knowledge) or **applied** (used to assess HR performance). **Four applied approaches:**

| Approach | How it works |
| --- | --- |
| **Statistical** | Set statistical standards from existing records; even the smallest errors show |
| **Comparative** | Compare your organisation with another to find areas of poor performance |
| **Outside authority** | Use a consultant's expertise or published research as the standard |
| **Compliance** | Use samples from the HRIS to find **deviations from laws and company policy** |

**What HR research studies:** trends in recruitment, promotion, training and appraisal systems; the **pulse of the workforce** (motivation, commitment, expectations, frustration); biases in selection (compare the applicant population with those selected); profile of new entrants against existing staff; education, gender and regional representation; best practices elsewhere.

**Climate and job satisfaction surveys** give data for action, and in strategic HRM research is **integral**: regular opinion surveys, benchmarking and climate studies keep HR sensitive to the internal environment.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A simple analysis can sometimes throw up a problem and show that a policy needs revising.

self_check.prompt_text: Which applied research approach uses HRIS samples to look for deviations from laws and company policy?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The compliance approach.

items.title: Knowledge management: five components, eight steps, benefits
items.core_explanation_md:
**Knowledge management (KM)** is the process of **creating, identifying, storing, distributing and pooling** an organisation's knowledge and structuring it for effective use; in particular, **capturing the tacit knowledge** of people for future use. Knowledge workers must be continually **re-skilled**. In banks the issue is sharpened by competent employees leaving for other banks. An organisation using KM as strategy must first **identify its knowledge workers** (creators, handlers, processors).

**Five core components to assess:**

| Component | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **People** | Individuals' ability to influence others with their knowledge |
| **Processes** | Best practices and governance for identifying, managing and sharing knowledge |
| **Technology** | Tools and automation that enable KM |
| **Structure** | Organisation that encourages cross-discipline awareness |
| **Culture** | A knowledge-sharing, knowledge-driven culture |

**Eight implementation steps:** 1 establish objectives; 2 prepare for **change** (KM is a culture change: rewarding only individual performance breeds "knowledge is power"); 3 define a high-level process; 4 define technology needs; 5 assess present KM status; 6 draw an implementation plan; 7 implement (celebrate short-term wins); 8 **monitor and measure** (baseline and balanced scorecard).

**Benefits (courseware):** lower costs; improved decision-making; easy to find information; tracking ideas and documents; **preventing brain drain**; **learning from mistakes**; faster delivery to clients; growth and innovation; standardised processes; better service to employees and customers.
items.expanded_explanation_md: KM is more than technology: tools matter, but without a sharing culture and rewards that support it, knowledge stays with individuals.

self_check.prompt_text: Name the five core components of knowledge management to be assessed.
self_check.expected_takeaway: People, processes, technology, structure and culture.

items.title: Technology in training: VILT, e-learning, AR and VR
items.core_explanation_md:
Technology lets training be **tailored to individuals**, mass-produced cheaply, and taken at the learner's **chosen time, place and form**, including **distance learning**. Options include interactive multimedia, video conferencing, computer simulation and virtual reality.

| Type | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| **VILT** (virtual instructor-led training) | Instructor-led training converted to online delivery, live or pre-recorded, with real-time interaction |
| **e-Learning** | Learning with electronic resources on any digital device, mostly on **LMS portals**: web-based, mobile, gamified, interactive |
| **AR** (augmented reality) | Digital content superimposed on the real environment through a device camera: 360-degree views of heavy equipment, realistic onboarding |
| **VR** (virtual reality) | Immersive simulated environment through a headset: safe hands-on practice, able to simulate **dangerous or risky** places |

The courseware says **e-learning is the commonly used method in banks**, reaching many employees on time.

| Advantages of e-learning | Disadvantages |
| --- | --- |
| Convenient time and place; privacy | Relatively **inflexible** (pre-produced programme) |
| Own pace | Needs **self-discipline** and commitment |
| Interaction with immediate feedback | May cause a **sense of isolation** |
| Can simulate real life | No **personal reinforcement**, so motivational effects are lost |
| Can be cost-effective | Hardware and software can be **costly** |
items.expanded_explanation_md: Different training programmes need different approaches: soft skills may be delivered through web-based training combined with instructor-led sessions.

self_check.prompt_text: Name two disadvantages of e-learning.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Any two of: inflexible pre-produced content, need for self-discipline, isolation, lack of personal reinforcement, cost of hardware and software.

items.title: HR analytics, business intelligence and big data
items.core_explanation_md:
**HR analytics** (also workforce, people or talent analytics) is the **collection and application of talent data** to improve critical talent and business outcomes. It is part of **business analytics**, which uses huge data and modern statistical methods.

**HR metrics are not HR analytics:** metrics (such as turnover rates and sick days) describe what is; analytics lets HR gauge **engagement and skills**, interpret data, spot trends and act early. The goal: insights for managing people so goals are met, by deciding **what data to capture** and **modelling and predicting** outcomes for the best **return on investment in human capital**.

| Business intelligence (BI) | Analytics |
| --- | --- |
| Querying, reporting, OLAP, alerts | **Why** is it happening? |
| What happened? How many? How often? Where is the problem? | **What if** trends continue? What **will happen**? What is the **best that can happen**? |

**Big data** is data whose size or type is beyond traditional relational databases to capture and process with low latency. Gartner's **Doug Laney** set out the **3Vs**:

| V | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Volume** | The amount of data |
| **Variety** | The number of types of data |
| **Velocity** | The speed of data processing |

Sources include sensors, devices, video and audio, log files, transactional applications, the web, social media, AI and the Internet of Things. **Benefits of big data analytics:** faster, better decisions; cost reduction and efficiency; and a data-driven approach to new products and services.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware notes that the R language is useful for unstructured data and that open-source tools such as Hadoop and Spark handle volume cost-effectively; no particular product is required for the concepts.

self_check.prompt_text: What are the 3Vs of big data?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Volume, variety and velocity.

items.title: Why credit matters, and where Indian credit came from
items.core_explanation_md:
**Credit is leverage.** It lets an entrepreneur start a project bigger than her own savings allow, and a consumer buy before earning. The extra demand pushes producers to produce more, so cheap, adequate credit lifts the economy onto a higher growth path.

**The flip side:** supply takes time to catch up with demand. Too much credit, above all for **non-productive** uses, puts **inflationary pressure** on the economy. So the RBI uses monetary tools (Bank rate, CRR, SLR) to strike a balance between growth and inflation.

**Background in India** (the courseware's account):

| Period | Credit picture |
| --- | --- |
| Earlier | **Private moneylenders** met individuals' needs; rural indebtedness and landlessness followed, worsened by financial illiteracy |
| Before **1969** | Credit flowed mainly to big business houses, often connected to the banks' ownership or management |
| After the 1969 **nationalisation** | The RBI directed credit to neglected sectors; the **priority sector** concept became part of banking |
items.expanded_explanation_md: The balance between growth and inflation is the core idea: credit for production adds supply, credit for speculation or consumption alone mostly adds demand.

self_check.prompt_text: Why can excessive credit for non-productive purposes be harmful?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It raises demand without creating matching supply, adding inflationary pressure.

items.title: The six principles of credit
items.core_explanation_md:
Bankers have evolved six unwritten principles that shape every loan policy:

| Principle | The question it asks |
| --- | --- |
| **Safety of funds** | Will the money come back? (the depositors' money) |
| **Purpose** | What will it be used for, and is that sound and permitted? |
| **Profitability** | Does the bank earn enough on it? |
| **Liquidity** | Can the loan be repaid when needed, matching the bank's own funding? |
| **Security** | If repayment fails, what can the bank fall back on? |
| **Risk spread** | Is the portfolio spread so that one failure does not hurt? |

Safety comes first because a bank lends other people's money.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The principles pull against each other: a very safe loan earns little, and a profitable one is often riskier. Loan policy is the balance.

self_check.prompt_text: Name the six principles of credit.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Safety of funds, purpose, profitability, liquidity, security and risk spread.

items.title: Who can borrow, and which law governs them
items.core_explanation_md:
A borrower may be an individual, sole proprietor, HUF, one person company, partnership, LLP, joint venture through an SPV, private or public company, statutory corporation, trust, REIT, co-operative society, club or association, local authority, institution or government department. **The law that governs the borrower decides who can sign, what the borrower can pledge and how it can be sued.**

| Borrower | Governing law (courseware) |
| --- | --- |
| Individual | Indian Contract Act 1872 |
| Partnership firm | Indian Partnership Act 1932 |
| LLP | Limited Liability Partnership Act 2008 |
| Hindu Undivided Family | Hindu Succession Act 1956 |
| Company | Companies Act 2013 |
| Statutory corporation | The Act that created it |
| Trust / REIT | Indian Trusts Act 1882 (and state public trusts Acts) |
| Co-operative society | Co-operative Societies Act 1912, Multi-State Co-operative Societies Act 2002, or state Acts |
| Club / association | Societies Registration Act, or the law it is registered under |
items.expanded_explanation_md: This is why a bank checks the constitution of every borrower before documentation: a partnership firm and a company need different documents and authorities.

self_check.prompt_text: Which Act governs partnership firms, according to the courseware?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The Indian Partnership Act 1932.

items.title: Fund-based and non-fund-based credit
items.core_explanation_md:
| | **Fund-based** | **Non-fund-based** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Money moves from bank to borrower? | **Yes**, actual transfer | **No**, only a commitment |
| Examples | Cash credit, overdraft, loans, term loans | **Guarantees**, letters of credit, co-acceptance of bills, forward contracts, derivatives |
| Risk | Credit risk on the money lent | **Contingent**: may turn into fund-based |

**Why a guarantee is still credit:** a bank guarantee for a contractor in favour of a government department needs no cash now. If the beneficiary **invokes** it, the bank pays and the customer must repay the bank. A non-fund-based facility therefore always carries a chance of becoming fund-based.

**Other ways to classify credit:**

- by **period**: short-term or long-term (term loan);
- by **purpose**: working capital, fixed asset or project finance, export finance, crop loan;
- by **customer**: corporate, MSME, retail, agriculture, international, institutional;
- by **currency**: rupee credit or foreign currency credit.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Banks therefore assess and limit non-fund-based exposure like any other credit exposure, and often include it in a borrower's total exposure.

self_check.prompt_text: Why can a bank guarantee turn into fund-based credit?
self_check.expected_takeaway: If the beneficiary invokes the guarantee the bank must pay, and the customer then owes the bank that amount.

items.title: The bank's loan policy
items.core_explanation_md:
Every credit proposal must be sanctioned **within the framework of the bank's loan policy**. The policy is shaped by market conditions, competitors' policies, the bank's own SWOT analysis and RBI guidelines.

**What a loan policy normally lays down:**

1. **Exposure limits** for a single counterparty and for groups of connected counterparties.
2. **Sector exposure limits** (real estate, capital market, steel, cement, software and so on) set on the bank's **perception of risk**. If perception of a sector worsens, the limit is cut, fresh sanctions are curtailed, and the bank may plan to **exit** some existing accounts.
3. **Thrust areas** and **low priority areas**.
4. **Discretionary powers** at each level for sanctions, and for allowing excess drawings or ad hoc limits.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The sector limits are a live tool: they move as the bank's view of each sector changes.

self_check.prompt_text: What does a bank do to its sector exposure limit when its view of that sector turns negative?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It reduces the limit, curtails fresh sanctions to that sector, and may plan exits from existing accounts.

items.title: Credit appraisal: the questions and the evidence
items.core_explanation_md:
Appraisal answers seven questions:

1. Is the borrower **trustworthy**?
2. What will she do with the money: is the project **viable** and what are the **risks**?
3. How **much** should be given?
4. What **repayment terms** and **interest rate**?
5. What **covenants** will allow effective monitoring?
6. Is **collateral or a personal guarantee** needed?
7. How is the **charge created**, and which **documents** will let the bank enforce its claim in court?

**Evidence used** (some or all, depending on the case):

| Evidence | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| **Background, credit history, market reports** | Trustworthiness |
| **Financial track record** | From financial statements; where none exist (most individuals), net worth and repayment capacity from assets, liabilities and income |
| **Techno-economic feasibility** | A detailed project report by a competent agency for industrial projects; otherwise judgement from past record, finances, income and expenditure |
| **Securities available** | Their value and **realisability** |

The effort depends on the amount, duration, purpose, borrower category, risks, security and RBI guidelines: a small crop or vehicle loan is appraised very differently from an industrial project.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Realisability matters as much as value: security that cannot be sold quickly or at a fair price protects little.

self_check.prompt_text: Where an individual has no financial statements, how does the courseware say repayment capacity is judged?
self_check.expected_takeaway: From the net worth and repayment capacity worked out from assets, liabilities and sources of income.

items.title: After sanction: delivery, monitoring, rectification, restructuring, refinance
items.core_explanation_md:
| Stage | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| **Delivery** | Documentation, **charge creation**, method of delivery (loan or cash credit), disbursal of a term loan |
| **Control and monitoring** | End use of funds and safety of funds; helps the borrower too; **delay in acting** on a deviation cuts recovery |
| **Credit risk management** | Policies to **identify, measure and control** credit risk within acceptable limits |
| **Rectification** | First try to **regularise** the account |
| **Restructuring** | If rectification is beyond the borrower: longer repayment, reduced margin, pricing concessions, additional finance, so the enterprise becomes **viable again** |
| **Recovery** | If restructuring is not possible (no viability, no interest or contribution from the promoter) or in **wilful default** |
| **Refinance** | Matters when liquidity is tight (NABARD, SIDBI, RBI for some priority sector advances); the **risk stays with the bank** |

Default can arise from genuine business problems or from intentional (wilful) default; the response differs.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Refinance is a funding source, not a risk transfer, so it does not change whether a proposal should be sanctioned.

self_check.prompt_text: Does refinance remove the credit risk from the lending bank?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No: even if a bank gets refinance for eligible advances, the risk remains with the bank.

items.title: End use of funds: what banks must watch
items.core_explanation_md:
Banks must **ensure proper end use** and **monitor the flow of funds**. Drawals from cash credit or overdraft must be **strictly for the sanctioned purpose**. In particular, working capital must **not be diverted** to:

- buying **fixed assets**;
- investing in **associate companies or subsidiaries**;
- buying **shares, debentures or mutual fund units**, or other **capital market** investments.

**Tools banks use** (illustrative):

| Tool | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Scrutiny of progress reports and financial statements | Spot deviations early |
| Regular visits and inspection of charged securities | Physical check |
| Scrutiny of the borrower's books | Trace the flow |
| **Stock audits** (by exposure) | Verify stock |
| **Borrower certificates** of end use | If false, prompt action: **withdraw facilities**, legal recourse |
| **Separate mandate to the borrower's auditors** | For a certificate on diversion or siphoning |
| Internal audit and branch inspection | Examine diversion |
items.expanded_explanation_md: This is the courseware's description of the guidance; the current wording of the RBI direction was not checked.

self_check.prompt_text: Name two uses to which working capital finance must not be diverted.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Any two of: acquiring fixed assets, investing in associates or subsidiaries, buying shares or debentures, mutual fund units or other capital market investments.

items.title: Priority sector lending: categories, rules and targets
items.core_explanation_md:
The **RBI decides** which sectors are priority sectors and the **minimum share of credit** they must receive, monitors banks through periodic returns, and reviews them in forums such as the **Lead Bank Scheme**.

**Eight categories:** agriculture; micro, small and medium enterprises; export credit; education; housing; social infrastructure; renewable energy; others. **Weaker sections** is an overlapping category with its own target. A loan is classified in **only one** of the eight.

**Targets** (as a share of **ANBC** or **CEOBSE**, whichever is higher, on the corresponding date of the preceding year):

| Category | Domestic commercial banks (excl. RRBs, SFBs) and foreign banks with 20+ branches |
| --- | --- |
| **Total priority sector** | **40 per cent** |
| **Agriculture** | **18 per cent**: of which **14 per cent non-corporate farmers**, of which **10 per cent small and marginal farmers** |
| **Micro enterprises** | **7.5 per cent** |
| **Weaker sections** | **12 per cent** |

Other banks: foreign banks with fewer than 20 branches 40 per cent (up to 32 per cent export credit, at least 8 per cent other); RRBs and SFBs 75 per cent; urban co-operative banks 60 per cent. **District weights** apply to incremental credit: **125 per cent** where per capita credit is low and **90 per cent** where high.

**Common guidelines:** interest rates as per RBI directions; no loan-related or ad hoc service or inspection charges on priority sector loans up to Rs 50,000; records of receipt, sanction, rejection and disbursement; **acknowledgement** of applications with a Board-set time limit; approved purposes with **end use** monitored.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Eligibility limits for each category (loan amounts, farmer definitions and so on) are laid down in detail by RBI and have been amended; look them up in the current Directions rather than learning them from older text.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the total priority sector target for a domestic commercial bank, and what is the agriculture sub-target?
self_check.expected_takeaway: 40 per cent of ANBC or CEOBSE (whichever is higher) in total, and 18 per cent for agriculture.

items.title: MSME classification: investment and turnover together
items.core_explanation_md:
The courseware says enterprises are classified by **both** tests, with no difference between manufacturing and service units. To be in a class an enterprise must meet **both** the investment limit **and** the turnover limit.

| Class | Investment in plant and machinery or equipment | Annual turnover |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Micro** | up to Rs 2.5 crore | up to Rs 10 crore |
| **Small** | up to Rs 25 crore | up to Rs 100 crore |
| **Medium** | up to Rs 125 crore | up to Rs 500 crore |

If the investment fits micro but the turnover does not, the enterprise moves up to the class whose **both** limits it meets.

**Registration:** on the **Udyam** portal; for priority sector purposes banks go by the classification in the **Udyam Registration Certificate**. Retail and wholesale trade count as MSMEs for the limited purpose of priority sector lending. Informal micro enterprises with an **Udyam Assist** certificate are treated as micro enterprises.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The thresholds are the courseware's statement of a March 2025 notification; check the current notification before relying on them.

self_check.prompt_text: An enterprise has investment of Rs 2 crore and turnover of Rs 15 crore. Which class?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Small: its investment fits micro but its turnover exceeds the micro limit of Rs 10 crore, and both limits for small are met.

items.title: Credit exposure norms: limits as shares of Tier 1 capital
items.core_explanation_md:
To avoid **concentration** of credit the RBI has prescribed limits on exposure to a **single counterparty** and to a **group of connected counterparties**, as a share of the bank's **Tier 1 capital** (as the courseware states the 2019 Large Exposures Framework):

| Exposure to | Ceiling |
| --- | --- |
| A single counterparty | **20 per cent** of Tier 1 (Board may allow **5 per cent more** in exceptional cases) |
| A group of connected counterparties | **25 per cent** of Tier 1 |
| A single NBFC | **20 per cent** (no extra 5 per cent) |
| A group of connected NBFCs | **25 per cent** |

**Large exposure:** the sum of exposures to a counterparty or group that is **10 per cent or more** of Tier 1 capital.

**Connected counterparties:** two or more persons are connected if one **controls** the others, or if they are **economically interdependent** (trouble for one would cause trouble for another). Checking economic interdependence is mandatory once exposure to one counterparty exceeds **5 per cent** of Tier 1. Entities connected with the **sovereign** are exempt from being treated as a group.

**Look-through:** for securitisation and similar structures, if the bank's exposure is **0.25 per cent or less** of Tier 1 the structure itself may be treated as one counterparty; otherwise the underlying exposures go to an unknown client.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware's figures are used here as its account; the current RBI direction on credit concentration was not retrieved and may have changed.

self_check.prompt_text: What share of Tier 1 capital is the ceiling for exposure to a group of connected counterparties, as the courseware states it?
self_check.expected_takeaway: 25 per cent of Tier 1 capital.

items.title: Benchmarks for pricing advances
items.core_explanation_md:
RBI requires a **Board-approved interest rate policy**. The idea of benchmark pricing, as the courseware describes it:

| Loan type | Pricing reference |
| --- | --- |
| New floating rate personal or retail loans (housing, auto); MSE floating rate loans from 1 October 2019; medium enterprises from 1 April 2020 | **External Benchmark-based Lending Rate (EBLR)** |
| Rupee loans sanctioned and limits renewed from 1 April 2016 | **MCLR** (Marginal Cost of Funds based Lending Rate) unless the bank switches to EBLR |
| Foreign currency advances | A **market-determined external benchmark plus spread** |

Banks may offer fixed or floating rates; the courseware adds that fixed rates for tenor below 3 years may not be less than the benchmark for similar tenor.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware cites the 2016 Directions updated in 2023; those have since been consolidated into 2025 directions, so learn the benchmark idea and look up the current rules for any specific question.

self_check.prompt_text: Which benchmark is used for new floating rate retail loans?
self_check.expected_takeaway: An external benchmark, through the EBLR.

items.title: The rules of pricing a floating rate loan
items.core_explanation_md:
RBI requires every bank to have a **Board-approved interest rate policy**. The rules that run through the Directions:

- A floating rate loan is priced as **reference benchmark + spread**.
- The benchmark used is written into the **loan contract**.
- **No lending below the benchmark** for that maturity.
- Banks can offer **fixed or floating** rates on any category of advance.
- **Fixed rate loans of under three years** may not be priced below the benchmark rate for similar tenor.
- Interest is charged at **monthly rests** (some agricultural advances follow other rules) and **rounded to the nearest rupee**.
- Interest on **small value loans** such as personal loans must be **justifiable** against the bank's cost and a reasonable return.
items.expanded_explanation_md: This replaces the older 2016 text that the courseware reproduces; the structure is the same.

self_check.prompt_text: How is the lending rate on a floating rate loan arrived at?
self_check.expected_takeaway: By adding the components of spread to the reference benchmark rate written into the loan contract.

items.title: From Base Rate to MCLR
items.core_explanation_md:
| Benchmark | Applied to | Key feature |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **BPLR** | Older loans | Continues till repayment or renewal |
| **Base Rate** | Floating rate rupee loans sanctioned or renewed **1 July 2010 to 31 March 2016** | Elements **common to all borrowers**; **one** per bank; reviewed at least **quarterly** |
| **MCLR** | Floating rate rupee loans sanctioned or renewed **from 1 April 2016** | Internal benchmark built from the bank's **marginal** cost |

Existing borrowers on Base Rate or BPLR may **move to MCLR** on mutually acceptable terms, and the switch is **not a foreclosure**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The Base Rate was based on average or marginal cost; the MCLR moved to a marginal-cost basis so that policy rate changes pass through faster.

self_check.prompt_text: From which date are floating rate rupee loans priced with reference to MCLR?
self_check.expected_takeaway: 1 April 2016.

items.title: The four building blocks of MCLR
items.core_explanation_md:
| Component | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| **Marginal cost of funds** | Marginal cost of **borrowings** plus **return on net worth** |
| **Negative carry on CRR** | The cost of holding the mandatory CRR, which earns **nothing**: **CRR x marginal cost / (1 - CRR)** |
| **Operating costs** | All costs of providing the loan product incl. cost of raising funds; **excludes** costs recovered through separate service charges; set as a **percentage of the marginal cost of funds** |
| **Tenor premium** | Extra for longer commitments; **uniform** for all loans of a given residual tenor; covers the period to the next reset |

**MCLR = marginal cost + negative carry on CRR + operating costs + tenor premium.**

Why the CRR formula divides by (1 - CRR): for every rupee the bank raises, only (1 - CRR) can be lent, so the cost of the idle CRR portion is spread over the lendable amount.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Because the tenor premium differs by tenor, the bank gets a different MCLR for each maturity.

self_check.prompt_text: Which MCLR component is the same for all loans of a given residual tenor, whoever the borrower is?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The tenor premium.

items.title: Which tenor does the MCLR cover, and when is it published?
items.core_explanation_md:
The bank's funds (other than equity) are grouped into **maturity buckets**.

- If the **single largest bucket** is **more than 30 per cent**, the MCLR corresponds to **that bucket's tenor**.
- Otherwise, take buckets **in descending order of maturity** until their cumulative weight is **more than 30 per cent**, and use the **weighted average tenor** of those buckets.

**Illustration (from the Directions):** buckets of 15.1 (5 years and above), 11.8 (3 to under 5 years), 9.3 (2 to under 3 years) and so on. No bucket exceeds 30 per cent; the first two total 26.9, still under 30; adding the third gives **36.2**, so the MCLR corresponds to the **weighted average tenor of the first three buckets**.

**Publication:** the bank publishes **overnight, one-month, three-month, six-month and one-year** MCLR (longer maturities optional), reviewed **every month** on a **pre-announced date** with Board or delegated committee approval.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The idea is that the headline MCLR should reflect where most of the bank's funding really sits.

self_check.prompt_text: How often must a bank review and publish its MCLR?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Every month, on a pre-announced date.

items.title: Spread: what it holds and when it may change
items.core_explanation_md:
A bank needs a **Board-approved spread policy** saying how to fix each component, the **range** of spread for each borrower category or loan type, and who may decide pricing.

| | **Under MCLR** | **Under an external benchmark** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Components | **Business strategy** + **credit risk premium** (both **zero or positive**, never negative) | Bank is **free** to decide the spread |
| Raising spread on an existing borrower | Only for **deterioration in credit risk**, backed by a **full risk profile review** (not for consortium loans) | **Credit risk premium** may change only on a **substantial change** in credit assessment, as agreed in the contract |
| Other components (including operating cost) | n/a | May be altered **once in three years**; may be **reduced earlier** for retention, on justifiable, non-discriminatory grounds |

**Credit risk premium** reflects the loan's default risk, from a rating or scoring model, the customer relationship, expected losses and collaterals.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The rule protects the borrower: a bank cannot raise the spread merely because it would like more margin.

self_check.prompt_text: Can the spread components under MCLR be negative?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No: they must be zero or positive.

items.title: Reset of rates, switching, and the loans that are exempt
items.core_explanation_md:
**Reset under MCLR:** the bank may link reset dates to the **first disbursement** or to the **MCLR review date**. The MCLR on the date of first disbursement applies **until the next reset date**, whatever happens to the benchmark meanwhile. Reset periodicity is **one year or lower**, written into the contract, and matches the **tenor of the MCLR** the loan is linked to.

**Switching to an external benchmark:** existing loans continue till repayment or renewal. A floating rate term loan whose borrower may **prepay without charge** can switch **without charges or fees** (except reasonable administrative and legal costs), at the **rate a new loan of the same category, type, tenor and amount would get**. Others may move on **mutually acceptable terms**. A switch is **not a foreclosure**.

**Exempt from the benchmark rules:** government scheme loans at scheme rates; **working capital term loans and funded interest term loans** in a restructuring; refinance-scheme loans (to the extent of refinance); advances against **own deposits**, to **own employees** (including retired), to the **CEO or whole time directors**; loans linked to a market-determined external benchmark; and **fixed rate loans above three years**. Fixed rate loans of **up to three years** (except bill discounting and factoring) may not be below marginal cost + negative carry on CRR + operating cost + tenor premium.

**Foreign currency advances:** a market-determined external benchmark plus spread, under the Board policy.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The floor for short fixed rate loans means banks cannot lend fixed below their own cost-based benchmark.

self_check.prompt_text: Which kind of restructuring loan is exempt from the benchmark rules?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Working capital term loans and funded interest term loans granted as part of a rectification or restructuring package.

items.title: Building an MCLR and a lending rate
items.core_explanation_md: A bank has a marginal cost of funds of 8.00 per cent, a required CRR of 4 per cent, operating costs of 0.50 per cent and a tenor premium of 0.20 per cent for one year. worked_steps.description: Negative carry on CRR = CRR x marginal cost / (1 - CRR).
Add the four components.

items.title: Special mention accounts: early warning before an NPA
items.core_explanation_md:
RBI created a **special mention account (SMA)** class that sits **between standard and sub-standard** assets. The aim is **early identification of stress** so the bank can act (including rehabilitation or restructuring) before the account becomes an NPA.

| Category | Term loans: amount overdue (principal, interest or any other amount) | Revolving facilities such as cash credit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **SMA-0** | **1 to 30 days** | **None**: this category does not exist |
| **SMA-1** | **31 to 60 days** | Balance **continuously above the limit or drawing power** (whichever is lower) for **31 to 60 days** |
| **SMA-2** | **61 to 90 days** | The same excess for **61 to 90 days** |

An SMA is **not an NPA**, so **no provision** is needed for it, but irregularity and control reports must **state whether the account is an SMA and which category**.
items.expanded_explanation_md:
After 90 days the NPA tests in the next card apply, so SMA-2 is the last warning stage.

*Source note:* this card follows the courseware; the 2025 asset classification Directions do not contain the SMA bands, so the card is held at needs_review.

self_check.prompt_text: A term loan instalment has been overdue for 45 days. Which SMA category is it?
self_check.expected_takeaway: SMA-1 (31 to 60 days).

items.title: When an account becomes an NPA
items.core_explanation_md:
An **NPA** is an asset (including a leased asset) that has **ceased to generate income** for the bank. A bank must classify an advance as NPA if **any** of these holds:

| Facility | Trigger |
| --- | --- |
| **Term loan** | Interest or instalment overdue **more than 90 days** |
| **OD / CC** | Account stays **out of order** |
| **Working capital** | **Irregular drawings** for a continuous **90 days** |
| **Bills purchased / discounted** | Overdue **more than 90 days** |
| **Any limit** | Regular or ad hoc limit **not reviewed or renewed within 180 days** of the due date or ad hoc sanction |
| **Agriculture** | Overdue for **two crop seasons** (short duration crops) or **one crop season** (long duration crops) |
| **Securitisation liquidity facility** | Outstanding more than **90 days** |
| **Derivatives** | Overdue positive mark-to-market receivable unpaid for **90 days** |
| **Credit card** | Minimum amount due not paid in full within **90 days** of the due date |
items.expanded_explanation_md: Remember "90 days" as the common clock, and 180 days for unreviewed limits.

self_check.prompt_text: Which facility has a 180-day test rather than a 90-day test?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A credit limit not reviewed or renewed within 180 days of the due date or ad hoc sanction.

items.title: Out of order, borrower-wise classification and temporary deficiencies
items.core_explanation_md:
**Out of order** (cash credit or overdraft): the account is out of order if **any** of these holds:

1. the balance stays **above the limit or drawing power for 90 days**;
2. the balance is within the limit but there are **no credits for 90 days**;
3. the balance is within the limit but **credits do not cover the interest debited in the previous 90 days**.

**Borrower-wise, not facility-wise:** when one facility turns NPA, **all facilities** to that borrower (and the bank's investments in the borrower's securities) are treated as NPA.

**Record of recovery decides.** Temporary deficiencies do **not** by themselves make an NPA: inadequate drawing power on the latest stock statement, a temporary excess over the limit, stock statements not submitted, or limits not renewed on the due date.

The **availability of security** or the **net worth** of the borrower or guarantor is **not** a reason to avoid NPA classification.
items.expanded_explanation_md: There is one exception to the security rule, covered in the sub-standard, doubtful and loss card: where there is a potential threat to recovery from the value of security, the account can be classified doubtful or loss at once.

self_check.prompt_text: One of a borrower's three facilities has become an NPA. How are the other two classified?
self_check.expected_takeaway: As NPA too, because classification is borrower-wise.

items.title: Sub-standard, doubtful and loss assets
items.core_explanation_md:
| Category | Defining test | Nature |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Sub-standard** | NPA for **up to and including 12 months** | **Well defined credit weaknesses**; distinct possibility of loss if not corrected |
| **Doubtful** | Remained sub-standard for **12 months** | All sub-standard weaknesses **plus** full recovery is **highly questionable and improbable** |
| **Loss** | **Loss identified** by the bank, auditors or RBI inspection, **not yet written off wholly** | Loss assets should be **written off** |

**Straight to doubtful or loss.** Where recovery is under threat from security or fraud:

- realisable value of security **less than 50 per cent** of the value assessed at the last valuation or inspection: the NPA **may be classified doubtful** straight away;
- realisable value **less than 10 per cent of the outstanding**: security is ignored and the asset is classified **loss** straight away.

**Upgrade:** an NPA goes back to standard only when the **whole arrears of interest and principal** are paid.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Time moves an asset from sub-standard to doubtful; a collapse in security value can move it faster.

self_check.prompt_text: After how long in the sub-standard category does an asset become doubtful?
self_check.expected_takeaway: After twelve months.

items.title: Recognising income on standard assets and on NPAs
items.core_explanation_md:
| Account | Basis |
| --- | --- |
| **Standard** | **Accrual** basis |
| **Not standard** (including Government guaranteed) | **Actual receipt (cash)** basis |

**On becoming an NPA:** the interest already **accrued and credited to income** in past periods is **reversed** if not realised (including for bills and Government guaranteed accounts). Exception: capitalised interest for a **permitted moratorium period** need not be reversed.

**Interest actually recovered** in an NPA may be taken to income, **provided** the credit is **not out of fresh or additional facilities** granted to the same borrower (that would be evergreening).

**Appropriation:** without a clear agreement, the bank applies a **uniform and consistent** accounting principle to split recoveries between principal and interest.

**Exception:** interest on advances against **term deposits, NSCs, KVPs and life insurance policies** can be taken to income **on the due date** if the margin is adequate.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Why this matters: profit must not be inflated by interest that is only a book entry.

self_check.prompt_text: May interest on an NPA be taken to income if it was paid from a fresh loan to the same borrower?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No: only interest realised not out of fresh or additional facilities may be taken to income.

items.title: Provisioning on standard assets
items.core_explanation_md:
A bank makes a **general provision** on the **funded outstanding** of standard assets, on a **global loan portfolio basis**:

| Advances | Rate |
| --- | --- |
| Farm credit to agricultural activities, **individual housing loans** and **Small and Micro Enterprises** | **0.25 per cent** |
| **Commercial real estate (CRE)** | **1.00 per cent** |
| **CRE - residential housing (CRE-RH)** | **0.75 per cent** |
| All other loans and advances (including **Medium Enterprises**) | **0.40 per cent** |

(Teaser rate housing loans and restructured advances have their own stipulated treatment.)

- These provisions are **not** used to arrive at **net NPAs**.
- They are **not netted** from gross advances; they are shown as **contingent provisions against standard assets** under other liabilities and provisions.
- Borrowers with **unhedged foreign currency exposure** may need **extra** provision of **20 to 80 basis points** on the bank's total exposure to them, depending on likely loss as a share of EBID.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Note the courseware lists small and micro enterprises and farm credit at 0.25 per cent; the Directions also place individual housing loans in this group.

self_check.prompt_text: What standard asset provision applies to a loan to a Medium Enterprise?
self_check.expected_takeaway: 0.40 per cent.
