items.title: Starting a corporate insolvency resolution process and the moratorium
items.core_explanation_md:
**Threshold:** the Code applies where the **minimum default is Rs 1 lakh**; the Government may notify a **higher minimum, not above Rs 1 crore** (the courseware gives **Rs 1 crore**).

**Who can apply:** a **financial creditor** (alone or jointly), and, per the courseware, an **operational creditor** or the **corporate debtor**. **Default** means non-payment of **dues in full or part to any creditor**: a third party can start the process even when the bank's account is **standard**.

**Admission:** the Adjudicating Authority admits or rejects a financial creditor's application **within 14 days**, after giving **7 days** to correct defects (2026 amendment).

**Moratorium from the insolvency commencement date prohibits**

1. **Suits and execution** of judgments against the corporate debtor.
2. The corporate debtor **transferring, encumbering or disposing** of assets.
3. **Enforcing security interest**, including under the **SARFAESI Act**.
4. **Recovery of property** by an **owner or lessor**.

**Protected:** supply of **essential goods and services**, and supplies the **RP** treats as **critical** to run the business as a **going concern**.

**IRP:** named by the applicant; **takes over management** and runs the corporate debtor as a **going concern**; for an **operational creditor** application with no proposed IRP, the NCLT appoints one after **consulting IBBI within 14 days**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The moratorium protects assets while the plan is formed; it is why SARFAESI and DRT actions stop.

self_check.prompt_text: Name two actions barred by the moratorium.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Any two of: suits and execution of judgments, disposal of assets by the corporate debtor, enforcement of security interest including SARFAESI action, recovery of property by an owner or lessor.

items.title: The time limit for the process and withdrawal
items.core_explanation_md:
| Rule | Detail |
| --- | --- |
| **Basic period** | **180 days** from the **date of admission** of the application |
| **Extension** | The **RP** applies if the **CoC resolves with 66 per cent** of the voting share; the Authority may extend by up to **90 days**, and **only once** |
| **Overall maximum** | **330 days** from the insolvency commencement date, **including any extension** and the **time in legal proceedings** |

**Withdrawal (section 12A as substituted in 2026)**

- The **RP** applies to the Adjudicating Authority with the approval of **90 per cent** of the CoC voting share.
- **Not before** the **CoC is constituted**, and **not after the first invitation** for resolution plans.
- The Authority decides **within 30 days** of receiving the application.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The 330-day cap includes the time spent in litigation, so appeals cannot extend it.

self_check.prompt_text: What is the overall maximum duration of a CIRP including extension and legal proceedings?
self_check.expected_takeaway: 330 days from the insolvency commencement date.

items.title: Voting shares in the committee of creditors and CIRP timing
items.core_explanation_md: The financial debts of a corporate debtor are Rs 400 crore to Bank A, Rs 300 crore to Bank B, Rs 200 crore to Bank C and Rs 100 crore to Company D, which is a related party of the corporate debtor. The CIRP is admitted on day 1. Find the voting shares in the committee of creditors, whether Banks A and B together can approve a resolution plan, and the latest day by which the process must end if the Authority grants the single permitted extension.

worked_steps.description: The related party has no vote, so it is excluded from the voting total.
Bank A voting share.
Bank B voting share.
Banks A and B together against the 66 per cent needed.
worked_steps.intermediate_result: 77.78 per cent, so the plan can be approved

worked_steps.description: Basic period plus the one permitted extension of up to 90 days.
But the overall cap, including extension and legal proceedings, is 330 days from commencement.
worked_steps.formula_or_substitution: min(270, 330) for the process itself; legal time counts within 330

items.title: The committee of creditors: who is in it and how it votes
items.core_explanation_md:
After **collating claims**, the IRP forms the **committee of creditors (CoC)** of **all financial creditors**.

- A **related party** financial creditor has **no right of representation, participation or voting** (narrow exception for a **regulated** financial creditor that is related **only by debt-to-equity conversion** before commencement).
- **Consortium:** each financial creditor sits with **voting share by the debt owed to it**; with a single **trustee or agent**, each may **authorise the agent, represent itself, appoint an IP, or vote jointly**.
- A **dual creditor** is a financial creditor for its **financial debt** and an operational creditor for its **operational debt**.
- **First meeting** within **7 days** of constitution.

| Decision | Vote of voting share |
| --- | --- |
| Appoint or replace the **resolution professional** | **66 per cent** |
| **Extend** the process beyond 180 days | **66 per cent** |
| **Approve a resolution plan** | **66 per cent** |
| **Decide to liquidate** | **66 per cent** |
| **Withdraw** the application | **90 per cent** |

**Courseware (needs_review):** operational creditors take an **observer** role (voting only where there are **no financial creditors**); **quorum 33 per cent by value**; routine matters **51 per cent**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Because votes are by value of financial debt, large lenders such as banks dominate decisions.

self_check.prompt_text: What vote is needed to approve a resolution plan?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Not less than 66 per cent of the voting share of the financial creditors.

items.title: The model CIRP timeline (courseware)
items.core_explanation_md:
The courseware gives a **model timeline** from the IBBI regulations (amended up to 4 July 2025); **T** is the commencement date. **Held at needs_review**: the regulations were not retrieved.

| Day | Step |
| --- | --- |
| **T+3** | **Public announcement** inviting claims |
| **T+14** | **Claims** submitted (14 days from the IRP's appointment) |
| **T+23** | **CoC constituted** |
| **T+30** | **First CoC meeting**: RP decided |
| **T+40** | IRP performs the RP's functions until an RP is appointed |
| **T+47** | **Valuers** appointed |
| **T+60** | **Form G** and **invitation for expressions of interest** |
| **T+75** | **Expressions of interest** received |
| **T+95** | **Information memorandum** |
| **T+105** | **Request for resolution plans** |
| **T+135** | **Resolution plans** received |
| **T+165** | **CoC approved plan** to the Adjudicating Authority |
| **T=180** | **Approval** by the Authority |

**Documents:** the **information memorandum** (assets and liabilities, **two years' financial statements**, creditors and claims, related party debts, guarantees, workforce) and the **evaluation matrix** (criteria for plans). **Two registered valuers** estimate **fair value and liquidation value**; the **liquidation value** is the **average of the two closest estimates** where there are differences.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The 180-day statutory limit is the outer frame; the model timeline shows how each step fits within it.

self_check.prompt_text: By which day in the model timeline is the CoC approved plan submitted to the Adjudicating Authority?

items.title: Who cannot submit a resolution plan: section 29A
items.core_explanation_md:
A person (or anyone **acting jointly or in concert** with them) **cannot submit a plan** if they:

| | Ground |
| --- | --- |
| (a) | Are an **undischarged insolvent** |
| (b) | Are a **wilful defaulter** (RBI guidelines) |
| (c) | Have an **NPA account** (own, or of a corporate debtor they manage or control or promote) for **at least one year** before the CIRP began, **unless all overdue amounts with interest and charges are paid before submitting the plan**; **does not apply** to a **financial entity** that is **not a related party** of the corporate debtor |
| (d) | Were **convicted**: **2 years or more** under a **Twelfth Schedule** Act, or **7 years or more** under any law (bar ends **two years after release**) |
| (e) | Are **disqualified as a director** under the Companies Act, 2013 |
| (f) | Are **prohibited by SEBI** from the securities market |
| (g) | Were promoter or in control of a corporate debtor in which a **preferential, undervalued, extortionate or fraudulent transaction** occurred and an order was made |
| (h) | Gave a **guarantee** for a corporate debtor against whom a CIRP is pending or whose **invoked guarantee remains unpaid** |

The section also bars those **ineligible under the laws of another country** and **connected persons** of ineligible persons.
items.expanded_explanation_md: This is the provision that keeps the old promoters from simply buying back the company.

self_check.prompt_text: May a wilful defaulter submit a resolution plan?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No: section 29A(b) bars a wilful defaulter.

items.title: The resolution plan and its approval
items.core_explanation_md:
A **resolution applicant** submits the plan to the **RP** with an **affidavit of eligibility under section 29A**.

**What the plan states (courseware, needs_review):** amounts to **operational and financial creditors**; treatment of **all stakeholders**; **past failures** of the applicant; **term, schedule and management**; how the **cause of default** is addressed; **feasibility and viability**; **approvals** needed; the applicant's **experience and capacity**. It must provide for **insolvency resolution costs** and pay **operational creditors not less than the liquidation value**, ahead of financial creditors.

**Approval**

1. The **RP checks** each plan for compliance.
2. The **CoC** evaluates the plans strictly on the **evaluation matrix**.
3. A plan is approved by **not less than 66 per cent** of the financial creditors' voting share, considering **feasibility and viability**, the **manner of distribution** (which may reflect the **section 53 priority** and the **value of security**).
4. The approved plan goes to the **Adjudicating Authority**.

The applicant may attend CoC meetings as an **observer**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Section 30(2) on plan contents was amended by the 2026 Act, so the list of contents here is the courseware's account.

self_check.prompt_text: What minimum payment does the courseware say a plan must make to operational creditors?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Not less than the liquidation value.

items.title: The order of priority in liquidation
items.core_explanation_md:
| Rank | Dues paid |
| --- | --- |
| **(a)** | **Insolvency resolution process costs** and **liquidation costs**, in full |
| **(b)** | **Workmen's dues (24 months)** and **debts to a secured creditor who relinquished security** (rank **equally**) |
| **(c)** | **Wages and dues of other employees (12 months)** |
| **(d)** | **Financial debts owed to unsecured creditors** |
| **(e)** | **Dues to Central and State Governments (2 years)** and **secured creditor's unpaid balance after enforcement** (rank **equally**) |
| **(f)** | **Any remaining debts and dues** |
| **(g)** | **Preference shareholders** |
| **(h)** | **Equity shareholders or partners** |

**Rules:** within a rank, **pay in full or pro rata**; **contracts that disturb the order are ignored**; the **liquidator's fee** is deducted **proportionately from each class**.

**Secured creditor's choice**

- **Relinquish** the security to the liquidator and join at rank (b).
- **Stay outside** and enforce the security itself; any **shortfall** ranks at **(e)**; any **surplus** goes to the liquidator.
- **2026 clarification:** if the security relinquished is worth **less than the debt**, the creditor is **secured to the value of the security** and **unsecured for the rest**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The relinquishing secured creditor shares rank (b) with workmen, which is why many banks weigh the choice.

self_check.prompt_text: Where does a secured creditor who enforces its security and falls short rank for the unpaid balance?
self_check.expected_takeaway: At rank (e), equally with Government dues for two years.

items.title: Distribution of liquidation proceeds
items.core_explanation_md: Liquidation proceeds are Rs 60 crore. Claims: insolvency and liquidation costs Rs 5 crore; workmen's dues (24 months) Rs 10 crore; a secured creditor that relinquished its security Rs 20 crore; employees' dues (12 months) Rs 5 crore; unsecured financial creditors Rs 25 crore; Government dues Rs 8 crore. Find who is paid and how much is left at each stage, and the share of unsecured financial debts recovered.

worked_steps.description: Rank (a): costs paid in full.
Rank (b): workmen Rs 10 crore and the relinquishing secured creditor Rs 20 crore, paid in full.
Rank (c): employees paid in full.
Rank (d): unsecured financial creditors claim Rs 25 crore but only Rs 20 crore is left.
Share of the unsecured financial claim recovered.
Nothing is left for Government dues and lower ranks.

items.final_answer_with_unit: Costs Rs 5 crore, workmen Rs 10 crore, secured creditor Rs 20 crore and employees Rs 5 crore are paid in full; unsecured financial creditors receive Rs 20 crore (80.00 per cent of their claim); Government dues and lower ranks receive nothing

self_check.prompt_text: If proceeds were Rs 30 crore, who would be paid and how much?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Costs Rs 5 crore, then Rs 25 crore for rank (b): both workmen (Rs 10 crore) and the secured creditor (Rs 20 crore) share Rs 25 crore pro rata, so about Rs 8.33 crore and Rs 16.67 crore.

items.title: The pre-packaged insolvency resolution process (PIRP)
items.core_explanation_md:
**Who can use it:** corporate debtors that are **MSMEs**, and other corporate debtors with a section 4 default, subject to conditions.

**Conditions**

- **No PIRP or CIRP in the last three years**; not now in CIRP; no liquidation order; **eligible under section 29A**.
- **Unrelated financial creditors with at least 66 per cent in value** approve **the proposed RP** and the **filing**; the **base resolution plan** is put before them.
- A **majority of directors or partners** declare the filing will be made **within 90 days**, that the process is **not to defraud**, and name the RP.
- **Members pass a special resolution** (or **three-fourths of partners** a resolution) to file.

**Process**

| Step | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| Admission | Authority admits or rejects **within 14 days** (7 days to rectify) |
| Whole process | **120 days** from the pre-packaged insolvency commencement date |
| Plan submission | CoC-approved plan to the Authority **within 90 days** |

**Contrast with CIRP (courseware):** PIRP keeps the **debtor in management** with a **base plan** prepared in advance; CIRP puts **creditors in control** from admission; CIRP runs **180 days (extendable to 330)**, PIRP **120 days with no extension**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware's "default up to Rs 1 crore" for PIRP misreads section 4, which only caps the minimum default the Government may notify.

self_check.prompt_text: How long must a pre-packaged insolvency resolution process be completed in?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Within 120 days of the pre-packaged insolvency commencement date.

items.title: What compliance and compliance risk mean
items.core_explanation_md:
**Compliance** is **observing laws, rules, regulations and codes of conduct**, including the **voluntary** ones. External requirements dominate, but the bank's **own policies and procedures** and **ethical practice** matter equally.

**Compliance risk** (BCBS, April 2005, as the courseware quotes it): the risk of **legal or regulatory sanction, material financial loss or loss to reputation** from **failing to comply** with laws, rules, regulations, **self-regulatory organisation standards** and **codes of conduct**.

| Kind | Applies to |
| --- | --- |
| **Internal compliance** | **All employees** |
| **Regulatory and legal compliance** | **The bank as a whole** |

**Why the function matters:** it promotes **uniform, proper behaviour**, **reduces systemic vulnerability**, **minimises deviations**, helps **spot violations** for prompt correction and **improves governance**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Compliance goes beyond what is legally binding to integrity, ethical conduct and good governance.

self_check.prompt_text: To whom does internal compliance apply?
self_check.expected_takeaway: To all employees of the bank.

citations.title: Advanced Bank Management (CAIIB courseware)

items.title: Compliance risk and the other risks (courseware)
items.core_explanation_md:
| Risk | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Regulatory** | **Consequences of non-compliance**: financial harm, litigation, **enforcement** |
| **Operational** | Loss from **failed processes, people, systems**: compliance risk is **operational risk come alive** |
| **Legal** | **Lawsuits, adverse judgements, unenforceable contracts** |
| **Reputational** | **Negative publicity**, loss of **confidence, business and market value**, and **liquidity risk** |
| **Annihilation** | **Regulatory action closing down the business** |
| **Business** and **strategic** | Adverse effect on **profitability** or on **strategic goals** |

**Cyber compliance** addresses three breaches: **confidentiality** (data stolen), **availability** (systems intact but **services unavailable**), **integrity** (**data or processing corrupted**).

The **cost of non-compliance** includes **penalties** and **"name and shame"**: compliance should be **everyday practice**, with **empowered employees**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware ranks annihilation risk as the severest regulatory consequence.

self_check.prompt_text: Which risk is the possibility of regulatory action closing down the business?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Annihilation risk.

items.title: Compliance principles, process and procedures (courseware)
items.core_explanation_md:
Held at needs_review: the courseware reports the **2007 guidelines**.

- The **Head office compliance department** plays the **central role** in identifying **compliance risk** by business line, product and process, and issues **instructions** and **circulates failures**.
- It ensures **regulatory guidelines reach the organisation promptly**, monitors **compliance**, and is the **reference point** for **clarifications**.
- It **proactively assesses compliance risk of products**: the **CCO sits on the new product committee**; new products are **monitored intensively for six months**.
- **Function-wise compliance manuals** are built with operating departments.
- It talks regularly to **legal, operational risk, taxation and audit** departments.
- **Compliance officers** can see **all information** and **investigate**; external experts may be used at the **CCO's discretion**.
- **Testing:** **sufficient and representative** compliance testing, results to **senior management**.
- **Independence:** free to report irregularities **without fear**, with **direct access to the Board or Audit Committee**; the **CCO meets the Audit Committee at least annually**.
- An **annual compliance report** goes to the **Board or ACB**; **non-compliance and penalties** are disclosed in the **annual report**.
- **Staff accountability** for compliance failures; compliance record counts in **appraisal**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The 2020 circular strengthens the reporting line, tenure and conflict-of-interest rules.

self_check.prompt_text: For how long are new products intensively monitored for compliance risk?
self_check.expected_takeaway: For the first six months after introduction (courseware).

items.title: Scope of the compliance function, subsidiaries and RRBs
items.core_explanation_md:
| Area | Examples |
| --- | --- |
| **Statutory compliance** | **Banking Regulation Act**, **RBI Act**, **FEMA**, **PMLA** |
| **Regulatory compliance** | Guidelines of **RBI, SEBI, IRDA** |
| **Codes of conduct** | **IBA, BCSBI, FEDAI, FIMDA** |
| **Accounting standards** | As framed by **ICAI** |
| **Listing agreement** | Where the bank is **listed** on a stock exchange |
| **Internal compliances** | **Instruction manual, circulars, policies** |

**Subsidiaries and Regional Rural Banks** also set up a **compliance function** with **Board approval**:

- the **compliance department** there acts like the bank's;
- it **reports periodically to its Board**;
- it gives **quarterly compliance certificates** to the **bank's CCO** in a **consolidated format** for the **bank's ACB**;
- the **Chairman or directors** representing the bank on their Boards ensure **guidelines are implemented** and tell the **bank's CCO** about **failures and corrective steps**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Their failures damage the parent bank's name, which is why the group view matters.

self_check.prompt_text: Which body's guidelines are examples of codes of conduct in the scope of compliance?
self_check.expected_takeaway: IBA, BCSBI, FEDAI and FIMDA.

items.title: Appointing the Chief Compliance Officer
items.core_explanation_md:
| Topic | Rule (RBI circular of 11 September 2020) |
| --- | --- |
| **Tenure** | **Fixed, minimum 3 years** |
| **Transfer or removal before term** | Only in **exceptional circumstances** with the **explicit prior approval of the Board** after a **transparent procedure** |
| **Rank** | **Senior executive**, preferably **General Manager or equivalent**, **not below two levels from the CEO**; may be **recruited from the market** |
| **Age** | **Not more than 55** |
| **Experience** | **At least 15 years** in banking or financial services, of which **at least 5** in **audit, finance, compliance, legal or risk management** |
| **Skills and stature** | Understands **industry and risk management**, **regulations**, **supervisors' expectations**; can **exercise judgement independently** and **deal directly with regulators** |
| **Clean record** | **No vigilance case or adverse RBI observation pending** |
| **Selection** | **Senior executive selection committee** set up by the **Board** recommends names **in order of merit**; the **Board decides** |
| **Intimation to RBI** | **Prior intimation to the Department of Supervision** before **appointment**, **transfer or removal**, with a **profile** and the **MD and CEO's fit and proper certificate** |

Banks that already had a CCO had **six months** to follow the process and could **reappoint the incumbent** if eligible.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The 31 July 2026 Compliance Function Directions, which replace this circular, are after the cut-off and are not taught.

self_check.expected_takeaway: Three years.

items.title: Is this candidate eligible to be CCO?
items.core_explanation_md: A bank considers a candidate aged 53 with 17 years of experience in banking, of whom 4 years were in audit and 2 years in risk management, currently two levels below the CEO, with no pending vigilance case. A second candidate is aged 56 with 20 years of experience and 8 years in compliance. Test each against the RBI criteria and find the earliest date the first candidate's fixed tenure could end if appointed on 1 April 2027.

worked_steps.description: Candidate 1: age 53 is within the limit of 55.
Candidate 1: total experience of 17 years is at least 15 years.
Candidate 1: years in audit, finance, compliance, legal or risk = 4 + 2.
Candidate 1: rank is two levels below the CEO, which is the limit (not below two levels).
worked_steps.intermediate_result: Rank passes, so Candidate 1 is eligible

worked_steps.description: Candidate 2: age 56 exceeds 55.
Minimum tenure is three years from 1 April 2027.

items.final_answer_with_unit: Candidate 1 is eligible; Candidate 2 is not eligible because of age; the earliest end of Candidate 1's tenure is 31 March 2030 (a transfer or removal before then needs the Board's explicit prior approval in exceptional circumstances)

self_check.prompt_text: Would Candidate 1 still be eligible if the specialised experience were only 4 years?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No: at least 5 of the 15 years must be in audit, finance, compliance, legal or risk management.

items.title: The CCO's reporting line, authority and duties
items.core_explanation_md:
**Reporting line:** direct to the **MD and CEO** and/or the **Board or its Audit Committee (ACB)**. If to the MD and CEO, the **ACB meets the CCO quarterly, one-to-one**, **without senior management** present. **No reporting to business verticals; no business targets.** The Board or ACB reviews the CCO's **performance appraisal**.

**Authority:** to talk to **any staff member** and see **all records and files** needed, flowing from the **compliance policy**.

**Duties (at least)**

1. **Apprise** the Board and senior management of **regulations, standards and developments**.
2. **Clarify** compliance issues.
3. **Assess compliance risk at least once a year** and prepare a **risk-oriented activity plan**, approved by the **ACB** and shared with **internal audit**.
4. **Report promptly** major changes or observations on compliance risk.
5. **Report compliance failures or breaches** periodically to the Board or ACB and to functional heads.
6. **Test compliance** by sufficient and representative testing and report the results.
7. **Examine sustenance** of compliance.
8. **Ensure compliance with RBI supervisory observations** in letter and spirit, time-bound and sustainable.

The compliance function itself is **subject to internal audit**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The one-to-one meeting protects the CCO's independence from the executive management.

self_check.prompt_text: How often does the ACB meet the CCO one-to-one if the CCO reports to the MD and CEO?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Quarterly, without senior management present.

items.title: Dual hatting, committees and who is accountable
items.core_explanation_md:
**No dual hatting.** The CCO must not hold a role that brings a **conflict of interest**, **especially a business role**.

- **Permitted where proportionality justifies it** (size, complexity, risk management strategy and structures): roles **without direct conflict**, such as **anti-money laundering officer**.
- The CCO is **not a member of any committee** that conflicts with the role, **including purchases or sanctions committees**; if a member, only **advisory**.

**Mandate (core elements):** **design and maintenance of the compliance framework**, **training on regulatory and conduct risks**, **communication of compliance expectations**.

**Responsibility**

| | Responsible for |
| --- | --- |
| **Board of Directors** | **Overall oversight** of the compliance function and compliance risk |
| **MD and CEO** | Ensuring an **independent compliance function** and **adherence to the compliance policy** |
items.expanded_explanation_md: A CCO who also headed a lending vertical could not objectively test that vertical's compliance.

self_check.prompt_text: May the CCO also act as the anti-money laundering officer?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Yes, where proportionality justifies it, because that role does not attract direct conflict of interest.

items.title: Risk based internal audit
items.core_explanation_md:
**Risk based internal audit (RBIA)** ties audit work to the bank's **risk management framework**. It gives the **Board** assurance that the processes for **identifying, assessing, responding to, monitoring and reporting** risk work properly against the **risk appetite**.

- It audits **how risk is managed**, not the risks as such.
- Every bank adopts it, in line with RBI's requirements.

**What it sets out to do:** test the **control environment**, review the **controls of the first and second lines**, confirm **legal and regulatory compliance**, find **control gaps** and follow their **closure**, spot **dereliction of duty** and **excess use of powers**, check where branches are **exposed to fraud**, and assure the Board on **governance** and **risk management**.

When an audit finds **breaches**, the report goes to the **Chief Compliance Officer** at the central office, with a copy to **risk management** and to the **regional or zonal head**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware stresses that the audit looks at the management of risk, which is why the Board relies on it for assurance and not for risk taking.

self_check.prompt_text: What does risk based internal audit examine?
self_check.expected_takeaway: How the bank manages risk: the processes for assessing, responding to, monitoring and reporting it, not the risks themselves.

items.title: The three lines of defence
items.core_explanation_md:
| Line | Who | Role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **First** | **Business functions** (risk takers) | Own and manage the risk they take |
| **Second** | **Risk management and compliance** | **Oversee** the risk |
| **Third** | **Internal audit** | Give **independent assurance** |

**External audit** and the **supervisor** sit **outside** the three lines. A statement that the supervisor is a **fourth line** is the one the courseware treats as **wrong**.

The **Board and senior management** set strategy and make sure risk is run prudently; the governance and assurance functions are the bank's **internal defences**, which RBI has strengthened through recent instructions.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Compliance is a second-line function, so a business head cannot also act as the compliance officer without breaking the separation.

self_check.prompt_text: Which line of defence does internal audit form?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The third line, risk assurance.

| **Policy and scope** | A **policy**; scope covers **every activity (including outsourced) and every group entity**; adequate cover of **regulatory matters** |

| **Oversight** | **Audit Committee** oversees; the **Head of Internal Audit** upholds standards and ethics |

items.title: Rules for the Head of Internal Audit
items.core_explanation_md:
RBI circular of **7 January 2021** (scheduled commercial banks other than RRBs, plus LABs, SFBs and payments banks):

| Topic | Rule |
| --- | --- |
| **Status** | **Senior executive**, able to use **independent judgement**; access to **any staff** and **all records** |
| **Competence** | Banking, accounting, **IT**, **data analytics**, **forensics** |
| **Staff rotation** | **Minimum period of service** set by the Board (unless career auditors) |
| **Tenor** | **Reasonably long**, **preferably at least 3 years** (unless career auditors) |
| **Reports to** | **ACB**, **MD and CEO** or **whole time director** |
| **If MD and CEO or WTD reports** | **Reviewing authority: ACB**; **accepting authority: Board**; **ACB meets HIA quarterly without senior management** |
| **Business link** | **None**: no business vertical, **no business targets** |
| **Foreign bank branch** | Reports to the **controlling or head office** internal audit |
| **Pay** | Not linked to the **business lines audited** |
| **Outsourcing** | **Internal audit is not outsourced**; experts on contract only if the **ACB** is assured the skill is absent, with **report ownership** staying with regular staff |
items.expanded_explanation_md: The circular took effect on its own date and supplements the 2002 Guidance Note on risk based internal audit.

self_check.prompt_text: May a bank outsource its internal audit function?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No; it may only hire experts on contract if the ACB is assured the expertise is not available in the function.

items.title: Offsite, IS and concurrent audit
items.core_explanation_md:
The courseware describes three verticals inside internal audit:

- **Offsite audit:** monitors **branch and office transactions from the centre**, using **MIS databases** and tools such as **SQL**, and feeds the **on-field auditors**.
- **Information system (IS) audit:** covers **all information systems**, their **process effectiveness**, **input and output controls** and **goal achievement**.
- **Concurrent audit:** the function that makes sure the **concurrent audit system** works, reviews observations and ensures **timely compliance**.

RBI's recent supervisory reforms, as the courseware lists them, cover **concurrent audit**, **standing of internal audit**, **RBIA** for certain UCBs and NBFCs, **strengthening compliance**, **system based NPA identification** and **appointment of statutory auditors**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Offsite audit reduces the load on field auditors by flagging unusual transactions from the centre.

self_check.prompt_text: What tool does the offsite audit team use to query the MIS databases?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Tools such as SQL.

items.title: Reporting and test checking of compliance breaches
items.core_explanation_md:
Held at needs_review (courseware).

**Reporting path:** **branch** → **regional or zonal office** → **Compliance department at central office** (copy to the **Field General Manager's Office**). Breaches come from **branch reports**, **officials' visits**, **audit reports** and **surveys**. **Functional departments at central office** report their own breaches; **overseas branches** follow the same path; **audit** sends the Compliance department a copy of its breach report.

**Test checking:** the **Risk officer** takes a **random sample** of branches from the **compliance certificates** and tests them independently. Sampling weighs **regulatory focus**, **inherent high-risk activity**, the **bank's exposure** and **past major breaches**, and **does not repeat the same branches** each time.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Certificates alone could be wrong, so independent test checking confirms they reflect reality.

self_check.prompt_text: Which officer test checks the compliance certificates at random?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The Risk officer.

items.title: Blocked accounts: inter-branch and Nostro entries
items.core_explanation_md:
| Item | Inter-branch accounts | Nostro accounts |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Credits moved to a Blocked Account** | Outstanding **over 5 years** | Outstanding **over 3 years** |
| **Debit entries** | Unreconciled over **6 months**, netted **category-wise** | Unreconciled over **2 years** |
| **Provision** | **100%** of the **aggregate net debit** | **100%** of those debits |
| **Blocked Account for CRR/SLR** | **Counts as a liability** | **Counts** |
| **Release of Blocked Account** | **Two officials**, one from **Controlling or Head Office** if above **Rs 1 lakh** | n/a |

**No set-off across categories:** a net debit in one category cannot be reduced by a net credit in another. For Nostro accounts, put in **real-time reconciliation** and have **top management** watch pending items.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The Blocked Account is shown under Other Liabilities and Provisions - Others for inter-branch credits.

self_check.prompt_text: After how many years are unreconciled Nostro credits moved to a Blocked Account?
self_check.expected_takeaway: More than three years.

items.title: Provisioning and appropriations: a year-end walk-through
items.core_explanation_md:
A commercial bank closes its year with these inter-branch entries unreconciled for more than six months (Rs crore):

| Category | Debits | Credits |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **A** | 6.0 | 4.5 |
| **B** | 2.0 | 3.0 |
| **C** | 1.2 | 0.7 |

Its Nostro accounts hold a debit entry of **Rs 40 lakh** outstanding for **2 years 3 months** and a credit entry of **Rs 25 lakh** outstanding for **3 years 2 months**. Its profit disclosed in the profit and loss account is **Rs 480 crore**. Find the inter-branch provision, the Nostro treatment and the transfers.

worked_steps.description: Net each category on its own: A is a net debit, B a net credit, C a net debit.
worked_steps.intermediate_result: Net debits in A and C only

worked_steps.description: Add the net debits without setting off B's net credit.
Provide 100 per cent of the aggregate net debit.
Nostro debit entry has been outstanding for more than two years.
worked_steps.intermediate_result: 100 per cent provision of Rs 40 lakh

worked_steps.description: Nostro credit entry has been outstanding for more than three years.
worked_steps.intermediate_result: Rs 25 lakh moves to a Blocked Account (counts for CRR and SLR)

worked_steps.description: Statutory minimum transfer to the Reserve Fund is 20 per cent of profit; a commercial bank transfers at least 25 per cent to the Statutory Reserve.
worked_steps.intermediate_result: At least Rs 120 crore to the Statutory Reserve

items.final_answer_with_unit: Inter-branch provision Rs 2.0 crore (not Rs 1.0 crore); Nostro debit fully provided (Rs 40 lakh); Nostro credit of Rs 25 lakh to the Blocked Account; at least Rs 120 crore to the Statutory Reserve

self_check.prompt_text: What would the provision wrongly be if category B's net credit were set off?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Rs 1.0 crore (2.0 - 1.0), which the Directions do not allow.

items.title: Reserves, fraud provisioning and window dressing
items.core_explanation_md:
**Reserves (2025 Directions):**

- **At least 20%** of profit to the **Reserve Fund** (Banking Regulation Act minimum).
- A **commercial bank** moves **at least 25% of net profit before appropriations** to the **Statutory Reserve**.
- **Prior RBI approval** for any use of the Statutory Reserve or another reserve, unless allowed by regulation.
- **Expenses and provisions** are **above the line**; **approved draw down from reserves** is **below the line** and disclosed.
- **Share premium** may meet **incremental, directly attributable share issue costs** without approval, **never debt issue costs**.

**Fraud provisioning:** reported **on time** → provide over **up to four quarters** from the quarter of detection (spanning years: debit **non-statutory reserves** and reverse later); **late report** → **full provision at once**.

**Other rules:** **unclaimed credits in transitory accounts** never go to profit or reserves. **Window dressing**, short provisioning, NPA misclassification and the like draw **penal action** under the Banking Regulation Act.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Delay in reporting a fraud removes the instalment benefit, which pushes banks to report fast.

self_check.prompt_text: Over how many quarters at most can a timely reported fraud be provided for?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Four quarters, starting from the quarter in which it was detected.

items.title: Segment reporting under AS 17
items.core_explanation_md:
**Primary format:** **business segments**. **Secondary:** **geographic segments** (**Domestic** and **International**).

| Business segment | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| **Treasury** | The **entire investment portfolio** |
| **Corporate / Wholesale Banking** | Advances to **trusts, partnership firms, companies and statutory bodies** not in Retail |
| **Retail Banking** | Exposures meeting the **retail criteria** (orientation, product, granularity, low value) and **individual housing loans** |
| **Other Banking Business** | All the rest, including **para banking** |

A bank allocates expenditure among segments by its **own reasonable, consistent method**.

items.title: Accounting standards that matter to banks
items.core_explanation_md:
| Standard | Point for banks (2025 Directions) |
| --- | --- |
| **AS 5** | Prior period items above **1% of total income or expenditure** (gross), or **1% of profit before tax** (net) must follow the standard; impact is disclosed in **Notes to Accounts** |
| **AS 9** | **No income on NPAs** per RBI norms is **not** a ground for **audit qualification** |
| **AS 23** | **20% or more** voting power **presumes significant influence**; a bank holding **over 20% after converting debt** may show its rights are **protective**; the test is **intent**, not just the percentage |
| **AS 25** | Listed banks' **quarterly results** are not AS 25 interim reports, but AS 25's **recognition and measurement** principles apply |
| **AS 18** | **Related party** disclosures in a set format |
| **AS 24** | Merging or closing **branches inside the bank** is **not** a discontinuing operation |

items.title: Listing Regulations: scope and principles
items.core_explanation_md:
Held at needs_review (courseware).

A company that lists its shares signs a **Listing Agreement** with the exchange. Its disclosure duties now sit in the **SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015**, effective **90 days after 2 September 2015**.

**Covered securities:** **equity on the main board or SME exchange**, **non-convertible securities**, **IDRs**, **securitised debt and security receipts**, **mutual fund units**.

**Principles:** information per **accounting standards** with an **independent audit**; **no misrepresentation**; **adequate, timely, accurate, explicit and simple** disclosure; **equal, timely, low cost access** for investors; filings carry **relevant** information; obey **all applicable laws**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Banks listed on an exchange follow these Regulations in addition to RBI rules.

self_check.prompt_text: Which instrument replaced the Listing Agreement as the home of disclosure requirements?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The SEBI Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements Regulations, 2015.

items.title: Material events (Regulation 30)
items.core_explanation_md:
Held at needs_review (courseware lists; the Schedule has been amended since).

**Para A: disclose always, no materiality test.** Examples: **acquisitions and sales of units, schemes of arrangement**; **issue, forfeiture, buyback, split of securities**; **new or revised ratings**; **board meeting outcomes**; **fraud or default** by the **promoter, KMP or entity**, or **arrest of KMP or promoter**; **change in directors, KMP, auditor or compliance officer**; **loan restructuring or resolution plan**; **one time settlement** with a bank; **winding-up petition**; **proceedings of general meetings**; **amendments to the memorandum and articles**.

**Para B: disclose only if material.** Examples: **start or postponement of production**; **strategic tie-ups**; **capacity addition or product launch**; **order wins and cancellations**; **disruption from calamity or strikes**; **regulatory change**; **pending litigation**; **fraud by directors (not KMP) or employees**; **guarantees for third parties**; **licence grant, withdrawal or suspension**; **delay or default in paying penalties**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The distinction is whether the entity may judge materiality: for Para A events it may not.

self_check.prompt_text: Does a change in the statutory auditor need a materiality test before disclosure?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No; it is a Para A event, disclosed without a materiality test.

items.title: Responsibility of the Board
items.core_explanation_md:
**RBI rule (circular of 11 September 2020):** the **Board is overall responsible** for overseeing the compliance function and compliance risk. The **MD and CEO** makes sure an **independent compliance function** exists and the **policy is followed**. The policy is **reviewed at least yearly**; its **quality assurance programme** has an **independent external review at least once in three years**; the compliance function is **internally audited**.

**The courseware adds (needs_review):** the Board ensures an **appropriate policy** is in place and implemented, that issues are **resolved expeditiously**, that there is **no conflict of interest** and that **compliance and audit stay separate**; it **reviews compliance quarterly** and the **status annually**, and may **delegate to the ACB**. Under the **Companies Act, 2013**, directors must devise systems to ensure compliance with applicable laws, **confirmed in the Directors' Responsibility Statement**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The three-year external review is a floor; the policy itself is reviewed every year.

self_check.prompt_text: How often must the quality assurance programme of the compliance function be reviewed externally?
self_check.expected_takeaway: At least once in three years.

items.title: The compliance department at the corporate office
items.core_explanation_md:
Held at needs_review (courseware).

The department has **formal status** at the **central or head office**, headed by the **CCO**, a **senior executive** (preferably a **General Manager or equivalent**, **not below two levels from the CEO**; may be **recruited from the market**).

| Question | Basis |
| --- | --- |
| **What must be complied with?** | **RBI master circulars and directions**, **RBI guidelines**, **laws and statutes** for banks, **internal guidelines and policies** |
| **How risky is it?** | **Regulatory focus**, **nature of activity** (inherently high risk), **exposure and materiality**, **history of breaches** |

**Independence:** compliance staff are **never given audit or inspection duties**; the function is **independently reviewed**; **compliance and audit stay separate**. Staff should be **adequate and well qualified**, preferably with knowledge of **law, accountancy and IT**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Mixing compliance with audit would let one function mark its own work, so they are kept apart.

self_check.prompt_text: Why are compliance staff not assigned audit or inspection duties?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It creates a conflict of interest.

items.title: Adverse actions, divergence disclosure and Annual Report disclosures
items.core_explanation_md:
**Courseware (needs_review):** non-compliance with regulatory guidelines and **administrative action** taken against the bank, with **corrective steps**, is **disclosed in the Annual Report**. A **strictures, show cause notice, cautionary advice or penalty** is reported to **top management and the MD and CEO** with advice to Compliance; the **head office department** prepares a **point-wise reply signed by its vertical head**, does a **root cause analysis**, tells the **Board** the **reasons and corrective action**, and reports **instantly or monthly** to Compliance.

**Divergence disclosure (2025 Directions, verified).** After a supervisory review, the bank discloses divergence in asset classification and provisioning in the **Notes to Accounts** if **either** holds:

1. RBI's **additional provisioning** is **more than 5% of reported profit before provisions and contingencies**; or
2. RBI's **additional gross NPAs** are **more than 5% of reported incremental gross NPAs**.

The note appears in the **annual statements published right after RBI communicates the divergence**.

**Not taught:** the courseware's SEBI 24-hour disclosure requirement, which was not verified.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Either condition alone triggers disclosure; both need not be met.

self_check.prompt_text: Must both divergence conditions be met before disclosure?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No; either one is enough.

Bank P: additional gross NPAs compared with the threshold.
worked_steps.intermediate_result: Condition (b) met, so disclosure is required (either condition is enough)

items.title: Material compliance failures and accountability
items.core_explanation_md:
Held at needs_review (courseware).

**Two levels of compliance:** **Level 1** is adherence to **external rules** (RBI, SEBI, IRDA, IBA, FIMMDA, FEDAI); **Level 2** is adherence to the bank's **own policies, processes and manuals**. Non-compliance arises from **business verticals**, **Inspection and Audit** findings and **regulatory inspections**.

**Is a failure material?** Weigh the **detriment or risk of detriment** to the bank, the **scale** of the issue, the **overall impact** on the bank and its clients, and the **loss of confidence** in the bank or in providing legal services.

**Accountability:** examples include **breaching laws, rules or policies (including RAR/RMP requirements)**, **wrongful or inaccurate release of data** (accident, negligence or malice), **data hoarding** and **inadequate supervision**. Responses may be **facilitative or punitive** but **proportionate**.

**Inquiry:** the **CCO forms a preliminary inquiry committee of any two of AGM (Risk), AGM (HR) and AGM (Compliance)** (the **senior-most Chief Manager** stands in if an AGM is unavailable); if it finds grounds, the **Inquiry Committee** starts an **investigation** done within a **reasonable time such as 15 working days**; the **CCO reports findings to the ACB and the MD and CEO**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The two-of-three committee spreads the inquiry across risk, HR and compliance so no single function decides alone.

self_check.prompt_text: Who forms the preliminary inquiry committee, and from whom?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The CCO, from any two of the AGMs for Risk, HR and Compliance.

items.title: Control activities and six aspects needing special attention
items.core_explanation_md:
**Control activities (examples):** reviewing **operating performance and exception reports**; **approvals above limits** (for example **dual signatures**); **segregation of duties**, with staff in **sensitive positions absent for two consecutive weeks a year**; **pre-numbered documents**; **access limits** to assets and records; **independent checks** such as **reconciliation**.

| Aspect | Point |
| --- | --- |
| **Information systems** | **Integrity, security, privacy**; a **tested contingency plan** |
| **Segregation of duties** | Adequate separation; may be limited in **small banks** |
| **Audit programme** | **Independent** function reporting to the **Board**; **annual audit plan**; **members' accounts verified at least once every two years** |
| **Record keeping** | Books follow **sound accounting principles** |
| **Protection of physical assets** | **Dual control**, access limits, physical security |
| **Education of staff** | **Training and cross-training** to keep **continuity** |
items.expanded_explanation_md: Mandatory leave of two consecutive weeks makes it harder to hide irregularities.

self_check.expected_takeaway: Two consecutive weeks.

items.title: Compliance issues and modern compliance challenges
items.core_explanation_md:
**Compliance** means following **laws, rules, regulations and codes of conduct**, including voluntary ones, plus the bank's **own policies** and **ethical practice**.

A **compliance issue** is a **single event** in which an **Accountable Employee** breaks **one or more required processes or procedures**.

**Challenges the courseware lists for banks and financial institutions:**

| Challenge | Core point |
| --- | --- |
| **Geopolitics and nationalism** | Protectionism adds **uncertainty** to data protection, KYC and beneficial ownership rules |
| **Divergent regulation** ("merge the diverge") | Cyber, **data privacy**, loan servicing, supervisory expectations that **differ from global standards**, new technology |
| **Data** | **Protect and govern** data, including with **third parties** |
| **Operational resilience** | **Continuity planning**, **operational risk**, **concentration risk**, cyber and environmental threats |
| **Credit cycles** | **Risk layering**, leveraged lending, new channels, climate and health effects |

items.title: Compliance risk management and due diligence
items.core_explanation_md:
Compliance used to be **reactive** (fixing problems after they appeared). Today it is **risk based**, with **due diligence**: the bank can **show it was diligent** because its system is **effective, not just on paper**, focuses on **results as well as process**, and has **working procedures**.

**Essential ingredients of due diligence:** **real commitment**; a **pro-active culture**; **consistent enforcement** (discipline, investigation, corrective and preventive action); **full reporting and action**; **adequate resources**; **monitoring, audit and inspection**; **identifying requirements** that affect the business; monitoring **outsourcing obligations**; **managing risk exposure**; **measuring compliance**.

**The complete function (courseware):** identify and assess risks from **new products and relationships**; advise committees on **integrity and reputation** (checks on borrowing clients and project sponsors); **investigate misconduct** under the CMD's guidance with the head of audit and compliance; handle **conflicts of interest, money laundering, terror financing** and **complaints on bank-financed operations**; **measure compliance risk**; **review the regulatory framework and the Code of Conduct**; run a **risk based annual programme**; **report to the Audit Committee and CMD**; cooperate with **internal audit**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A paper-only system fails due diligence even if every rule is documented.

self_check.prompt_text: What makes a compliance system pass due diligence according to the courseware?
self_check.expected_takeaway: It is effective in practice, not merely on paper, and focuses on results as well as process.

items.title: Operational risk, inherent risk and residual risk
items.core_explanation_md:
**Operational risk:** loss from **inadequate or failed internal processes, people and systems**, or from **external events**. It **includes legal risk** and **excludes strategic and reputational risk**.

- **External causes:** floods, earthquakes, power failure, terrorism.
- **Internal causes:** failure of **IT, risk management or HR systems**, **outsourced providers**, poorly trained staff, **negligence**, **misconduct**, **conflict of interest**, **fraud**.
- **Warning signs of rising operational risk:** **mistrust**, **failure to communicate**, **low morale**, **cynicism**, **higher staff turnover**.

**Inherent vs residual (courseware):**

| Term | Meaning | Courseware formula |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Inherent risk** | Risk a system poses **out of the box**, **before controls** | **Threats x vulnerability** |
| **Residual risk** | Risk **left after controls** | **Inherent risk x control risk** |

Crossing a street: **looking both ways** lowers the high inherent risk, but a small **residual risk** remains.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Controls never reduce risk to zero, so residual risk always remains.

self_check.prompt_text: Does the operational risk definition include strategic and reputational risk?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No; it includes legal risk but excludes strategic and reputational risk.

items.title: Credit, market, liquidity, operations and systems risk
items.core_explanation_md:
| Risk | Meaning | Management point (courseware) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Credit** | Loss when borrowers' finances deteriorate and **principal and interest** cannot be recovered | **Highest priority**; **credit rating** and **self-assessment** systems |
| **Market** | Loss from **interest rate, forex, stock price** and other market movements; includes **credit risk in market transactions** (counterparty failure) | **Limits** set by the **Board and Executive Committee**; results reported **daily** to directors and **monthly** to the Executive Committee |
| **Liquidity** | Running **short of funds** because of falling creditworthiness or a large **maturity gap**, forcing **high-cost borrowing** | Examine **sources and uses of funds**; guidelines on the **funds gap**; **Risk management department** in overall charge; **contingency plans** |
| **Operations** | Losses from **errors, unethical conduct, cash disparities, complaints** in handling transactions | **Operations department** in charge; **Inspection department** does internal checking, including overseas offices |
| **Systems** | Losses from **computer malfunction and unethical conduct** | **Multiple telecom lines**, **backup computer centres**, a **systems office** in the planning department |
items.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware describes one bank's practice; real practice varies with size and structure.

items.title: Assessing compliance risk and planning to mitigate it
items.core_explanation_md:
**Compliance risk assessment** gauges how well the bank complies with **regulatory directives** and which **major compliance risks** it faces. Evidence includes **regulatory examination observations**, **compliance testing**, **implementation of guidelines**, **regulatory reporting** and **compliance culture**; for **overseas establishments** also **enforcement action**, **closure of audit reports**, **AML-CFT compliance** and **training**.

**Courseware scale (illustrative):**

| Score | Level |
| --- | --- |
| **1 to 3** | **Well controlled** |
| **3.1 to 5** | **Meets requirement** |
| **5.1 to 7** | **Needs improvement** |
| **7.1 to 10** | **Needs significant improvement** |

**Mitigation plan:** assess **activity-wise at least yearly** and send a **risk-oriented activity plan to the ACB**, copied to **internal audit**; **report major changes promptly**; **report failures and breaches periodically**; check **sustenance**; meet **RBI's supervisory observations in letter and spirit, on time**.

**Shared responsibility:** **business units and the compliance function** share it, **every employee** must comply, and the **compliance function ensures** it.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A high score is bad: it signals weak control, so the scale reads from best (1) to worst (10).

self_check.prompt_text: What does a compliance risk score of 6 indicate on the courseware scale?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Needs improvement (5.1 to 7).

items.title: Independent testing and an effective audit programme
items.core_explanation_md:
Compliance units **test compliance risk in each business line** periodically and put the results before the **Board or management committee**.

**An effective audit programme** has: a policy suited to the **risk profile**; coverage of **all applicable regulations**; good **scoping and planning**; **adequate transaction testing**; **no gaps**; organised **work papers and paper trails**; clear **exception reporting**; **identified violations and explained risks**; **recommended and tracked corrective action**; results reported to the **Board, Audit Committee and senior management**; documented resolution of observations not in the audit report.

**Before each cycle** consider: the **AML risk profile**, **high risk products and customers**, **new regulations**, **recent audit and examination results**, **past recommendations**, and **changes** in risk profile, the compliance function, IT, monitoring parameters, key staff and products.

**Areas tested (examples):** **policies**, **customer due diligence and enhanced due diligence**, **customer identification programme**, **internal controls and reporting**, **suspicious activity monitoring**, **record keeping**, **cash transaction reports**; **issues tracked to closure and closure validated**.

**Who tests:** an **independent audit function**, **head office audit** or an **outside audit firm**, with **technical expertise and training**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Validating closure matters because an issue marked closed on paper may still be open in practice.

self_check.prompt_text: Who may carry out the testing of compliance?
self_check.expected_takeaway: An independent audit function in the institution, head office audit or an outside audit firm, with the right expertise.

items.title: Inspection versus audit, and the types of audit
items.core_explanation_md:
Held at needs_review (courseware).

- **Inspection:** a **site visit** required as part of a compliance obligation. It deals with things that can cause **immediate accidents or problems**.
- **Audit:** checks that **compliance obligations have been met**, including that inspections were done. It covers the **root causes**.

Both are vital.

**Ten types of audit the courseware lists:** **risk based internal audit**, **concurrent audit**, **statutory and tax audit**, **credit audit**, **forensic audit**, **RBI inspections**, **system audit**, **stock audit**, **foreign exchange audit**, **snap audit**.

**Reporting:** internal auditors capture **breaches** and report them to the **CCO at head office** with a copy to **risk management** at the administrative or controlling office, which uses them in its **random testing of compliance**.

**The Audit Committee's audit role (courseware):** oversee the **whole audit function**, follow up **statutory audit and RBI inspection** findings, **strengthen housekeeping**, fix **accountability of auditors who miss serious irregularities**, review **accounting policies and internal controls**, **sensitise the Board to risk-prone areas**, review **risk management measures** and **ensure statutory compliances**; it can **investigate** and take **external advice**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Audit looks for why a problem arose; inspection looks at what is wrong now.

self_check.prompt_text: Which looks at root causes, inspection or audit?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Audit.

items.title: The loan review mechanism
items.core_explanation_md:
Held at needs_review (courseware).

A **loan review** assesses the **quality of the loan portfolio**: **individual loans** and **repayment risk**, **compliance with lending policies**, **documentation lapses**, **priority findings** and **recommended practices**. Where loans are risk-rated, it tests the **risk grades and their accuracy**.

| A loan review **is** | A loan review is **not** |
| --- | --- |
| Assessment of **individual loans** at a **point in time** | A **portfolio review** (no view of **concentrations**) |
| Quality, compliance and documentation findings | A **trend analysis** |
| Report to the **competent authority** | An assessment of the **loan loss reserve** |

**Checklist:** **credit initiation** (eligibility, underwriting, repayment sources, management, appraisal); **loan structuring**; **approval procedures**; **credit and collateral file documentation**; **normal monitoring**; **problem loan management** (reporting and downgrading); **loan workout**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A loan review gives a snapshot of loan quality, not a view of overall portfolio risk.

self_check.prompt_text: Does a loan review assess the adequacy of the loan loss reserve?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No.

| **Improved effectiveness** | Activities go to the **right people and departments** |
| **Protected reputation** | Risks are managed well, so the **name is protected** |
| **Reduced costs** | Contributes to **return on investment** |

items.title: Compliance culture, its benefits and warning signs
items.core_explanation_md:
**Compliance culture** is **workplace behaviour that naturally meets ethical and legal norms**. It shapes decisions in the moment and goes **beyond what the law requires** to **integrity and ethical conduct**. It should be **visible in senior management**, built into **hiring and training**, ideally **linked to pay and promotion**, and **measured**.

**Benefits:** **lower organisational, individual and reputational risk**; **employee confidence**; **attract and retain talent**; **better transparency and decisions**; **better regulator relationships**; **stronger valuation**.

**Signs of poor culture:** **short-term profit** focus; **dominant individuals** and **no challenge**; **sub-cultures** after mergers; **tick-box** (letter, not spirit) compliance; controls seen as an **irritant**; **ineffective incentives**; **cover-ups**; **employees afraid to speak up**; **no challenge of the status quo**.

**What banks should do:** turn misconduct into **case studies** for staff and see good conduct as **saving penalties**, a **hidden earning**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware also notes that stress-testing banks valued better capital planning and a forward-looking view of risk.

self_check.prompt_text: What is meant by a tick-box attitude?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Following the letter of the law or regulation but not its spirit.

items.title: Ten attributes of a culture of compliance
items.core_explanation_md:
Held at needs_review (courseware). What regulators look for:

| Attribute | What they ask |
| --- | --- |
| **Tone at the top** | Do leaders put compliance above deal value? |
| **Integration across the enterprise** | Does compliance work with all **risk areas** (credit, market, liquidity, operational)? |
| **Silos** | Is compliance **present when business decisions are made**? |
| **Power** | Is the **CCO part of senior management**, and who wins a dispute, business or compliance? |
| **Cowboys** | Are rewards based **only on financial performance**, with **no limits on risk-taking**? |
| **Resources** | Is compliance **funded** compared with business technology? |
| **Employee buy-in** | **Zero tolerance** for misconduct; **continuing training** |
| **Living compliance programme** | **Tailored, tested, modified, enforced**; issues **escalated** |
| **Technology** | Is compliance **automated** or on paper? |
| **Documentation** | Can the bank **prove** testing and sign-off? |
items.expanded_explanation_md: The courseware's labels (silos, cowboys, power) are short prompts for the question a supervisor would ask.

items.title: RBI's minimum supervisory expectations on compliance culture
items.core_explanation_md:
Compliance **starts at the top**, is part of the **organisation's culture** and is a **shared responsibility of every staff member**; **business units are equally responsible** for non-compliance.

**RBI circular (11 September 2020):** the Board-approved policy sets expectations on **tone from the top, accountability, incentive structure and effective communication and challenge**.

| Element | Courseware's detail |
| --- | --- |
| **Tone from the top** | Values of Board and senior management **shown in actions**; Board oversight **not limited to the compliance function** |
| **Accountability** | Senior management **responsible for adherence**; **clear demarcation** of senior management, functional and operational heads; **business is the first line, internal audit the third** |
| **Communication** | **Clear and transparent**; **general standards for all staff** distinguished from **rules for specific groups**; **awareness channels**; **conduct risk process and whistle-blower mechanism** |
| **Incentive structure** | **Built into decision systems and processes** |
| **Ex ante and forward looking** | Compliance is **preventive**, unlike risk management and internal audit |
items.expanded_explanation_md: Compliance prevents non-compliant transactions beforehand rather than detecting them afterwards.

self_check.prompt_text: Which function looks at activities beforehand to prevent non-compliance?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Compliance (it is ex ante and forward looking).

items.title: The GRC framework
items.core_explanation_md:
Many enterprises run **governance, risk and compliance** initiatives **separately**, which causes **silos, duplication and rising cost**. **GRC** brings them together.

| Element | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Governance** | **Oversight** by which risks are managed: **corporate controls, key policies, enterprise risk management, regulatory and compliance oversight, ethics**, and performance tracking through **balanced scorecards, risk scorecards and operational dashboards** |
| **Risk management** | A **structured process** to **evaluate business and regulatory risks and controls** and **monitor mitigation** (financial, operational, IT, brand, reputational) |
| **Compliance** | **Processes and internal controls** meeting **regulator, industry and internal requirements**, made **repeatable** so it is sustained at **lower cost** than the first deadline project |

**A GRC solution** is an **integrated platform** giving an **enterprise view** of risk across **identification, assessment, response and monitoring**. It can be **web-based**, with modules such as **incident management**, **RCSA** (risk control self-assessment), **KRI** (key risk indicators), **issues and action plans**, **compliance and policy management**, **governance and audit management** and **regulatory reports**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Treating compliance as a one-off project makes each new regulation expensive; making it repeatable lowers the cost.

self_check.prompt_text: Name the three elements of GRC.
self_check.expected_takeaway: Governance, risk management and compliance.

items.title: The whistle-blowing process and components of a policy
items.core_explanation_md:
**Raising a concern:** in **writing or verbally** to the **ombudsperson or CVO** (a verbal complaint is **written up** by the ombudsperson). The ombudsperson, CVO or **audit committee** checks whether a breach occurred and **responds within 2 days** of receiving the complaint.

**Identity:** the whistle-blower may or may not reveal it; either way the complaint is **taken seriously**, and the **identity is kept confidential** in all cases. **False allegations** bring **strict disciplinary action**.

**Investigation:** the committee **contacts** the employee, vendor or stakeholder, decides **internal steps**, keeps everything **confidential** and **shares status and findings with the Board**, with a **final report** holding all details and documents.

**Alternative routes:** manager or **head of department**, **HR**, **legal**, **Compliance Head**, **CEO or CVO**, **management committee members**; in an **urgent** case **write directly to the chair of the audit committee**; a complaint received by HR goes to the **director of human resources**.

**Four components of a policy:** a **whistle-blower**, a **wrongful or unethical practice** (grave and serious, not trivial), an **authority** (independent, senior, responsible; a defined escalation process) and **a policy** (with **direct access to the chair of the audit committee**).

**Five reasons staff do not report (ACFE):** **no corrective action**, **no confidentiality**, **retaliation by superiors**, **retaliation by co-workers**, **unsure whom to contact**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The audit committee chair is the escape route when senior management is the subject of the complaint.

self_check.prompt_text: Within how many days does the courseware model say the ombudsperson or audit committee should respond to a complaint?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Within 2 days of receiving it.

items.title: Whistle-blowing law and rules in India (courseware account)
items.core_explanation_md:
Held at needs_review: statutes and circulars cited by the courseware were **not checked** against primary text, and the **Listing Agreement clause 49** it cites has been **replaced by the SEBI Listing Regulations 2015**.

**Companies Act, 2013 (as the courseware describes):** **vigil mechanism** provisions; sections **206 to 229** on **inspection, inquiry and investigation**; **section 177(9)** requires a whistle-blower policy for **listed companies**, companies **accepting public deposits** and companies **borrowing over Rs 50 crore from banks or public financial institutions**. The **Serious Fraud Investigation Office** is created under **section 211**.

**Old clause 49 (non-mandatory part):** a **mechanism to report concerns**, **safeguards against victimisation**, **direct access to the audit committee chair** where **senior management is involved**, **communication within the organisation** and **periodic audit committee review**.

**Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2011:** the courseware says it **has not come into force**; its status at the cut-off was **not verified**, so it is **not tested**.

**PIDPI Resolution, 2004** (after the **Satyendra Dubey** case): the **Central Vigilance Commission** is the **designated agency** for **written complaints** on **corruption or misuse of office** in the central government and its corporations; **anonymous complaints are not acted upon**; the **complainant's identity is not revealed** unless disclosed by the complainant; a **victimised complainant may apply for redress**; a **2013 amendment** made **Chief Vigilance Officers** designated authorities under CVC supervision.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Internal whistle-blowers report within the organisation; external ones go to the media, public or law authorities.

self_check.prompt_text: Does the PIDPI Resolution act on anonymous complaints?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No, anonymous complaints are not acted upon (courseware).

items.title: Why compliance fails
items.core_explanation_md:
The courseware lists reasons from the standpoint of those the rules target:

| Reason | Point |
| --- | --- |
| **Failure to understand the law** | Requirements are **too complex** |
| **Collapse in belief in the law** | Compliance **costs too much**; standards seem **unreasonable** |
| **Overly legalistic regulation** | Technical rules that **do not relate to the purpose** lose confidence |
| **Regulation at odds with market incentives or culture** | Rules that **do not fit market practice** are obeyed less |
| **Failure to monitor** | A rule **not monitored vigorously** draws **little compliance** |
| **Procedural injustice** | People **treated unfairly** comply less |
| **Deterrence failure** | **High rewards** for breaking rules and **low chance of detection** |
| **Failures of administrative capacity** | Agencies do not provide **resources, information or support** for implementation |
| **Failure to understand the problem** | Government misreads the cause |
| **Failure of causal relation** | The rule **does not achieve its objective** |

**For banks:** an **independent** compliance function with **qualified staff** and **formal status**; **local compliance** issues in other jurisdictions handled **within the bank-wide policy**; and a **Board commitment to honesty and integrity**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Deterrence fails when detection is unlikely, which is why monitoring and enforcement matter.

self_check.prompt_text: Which reason says rules are obeyed less when people feel treated unfairly by a regulator?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Procedural injustice.
